Computer systems · a concept-first course

How Computer Systems Produce Results

Learn to follow work, data, and decisions through software, machines, and networks. Connect those ideas to research across systems and hardware conferences.

Start and outcomesConcept lookupConference routes1. Start2. Dependencies3. Numbers4. Memory5. Topology6. Skipping7. Compilers8. Sharing9. Many Chips10. Physical limits11. Correctness12. Security13. Worked service14. Worked update15. Worked training16. Worked science

A faster processor does not always deliver an answer sooner. The request may be waiting for data, another request, or a result from another machine. This course teaches you to trace those steps, calculate which change can help, and check whether the returned answer meets the task's requirements.

Begin with one request and follow the lessons in order. You will then examine shared machines, stored numbers, networks, chip constraints, and recovery after failure. The worked examples use arithmetic and state their assumptions. Technical terms are explained as they become useful.

Conference reading routes apply the common lessons to selected research. Each route identifies its conference year, reviewed sources, and remaining limits. The coverage table shows the distribution of guided paper walkthroughs. Invented examples are labeled separately from authors' reported results, which have not been independently reproduced here.

Start here · no specialist background required

What you will learn, and where to begin

You need basic arithmetic and percentages, not prior knowledge of chip design or distributed systems. The worked examples show their calculations and explain technical terms when they first become useful. Their invented numbers teach a relationship; they are not measurements from a paper.

New to the subject? Begin with one request from arrival to answer and use the next-lesson links. Reading a particular conference? Use its reading route, then follow the lesson links wherever you need an explanation. Looking up a word? Use the concept lookup.

By the end, you should be able to

  • Trace one request from arrival to accepted answer, separating work from waiting and one-request time from completion rate.
  • Follow data through computation, memory, and communication; identify which resource can limit the complete task.
  • Compare designs at the same accepted result, counting setup, movement, checking, accuracy, and failure costs.
  • Read a reported result with its workload, comparison, units, device, and measurement conditions attached.
  • Explain what a paper's evidence supports, what it leaves open, and one condition where its method may stop helping.

How the lessons fit together

For each example, first say what counts as a finished answer. Predict what makes it wait, then work through the calculation with its units. Change one assumption: make two steps share a processor, add a data transfer, or require an update to survive a power loss. Explain which part of the answer changes and why. The links below follow the order of the core lessons.

  1. First, follow the work and the data

    Begin with one request. Count its working and waiting time, then ask which steps can run together. Follow the numbers it uses, the storage it reads, and the connections its data travels through. Finally, compare doing the work again, reusing an earlier result, and changing the execution plan.

    Trace a request · Find required order · Track number meaning · Follow data movement · Find shared connections · Decide when to skip repeated work · Compare execution plans

  2. Next, see what changes when work is shared

    A design that works for one task may behave differently when requests compete, machines exchange data, or a chip runs into power and timing limits. Follow the shared resource and the work needed to coordinate it.

    Understand waiting and queues · Follow communication and recovery · Connect the plan to physical limits

  3. Finally, check a complete result

    Every lesson asks what the task must deliver. Now examine that requirement more closely: is an approximate answer acceptable, what may another user observe, and what must survive a crash? Follow a service request, stored update, training run, or scientific calculation through its final check. Then use the same questions to examine a paper.

    State and test a promise · Examine privacy and observation · Trace an accepted answer · Follow a crash and retry · Check an accepted model · Check a scientific result

What connects the conferences?

The conference names tell you where work was published. They do not divide the underlying problems into separate worlds. Consider storing numbers in fewer bits. That can reduce the bytes a program reads, but the machine may have to convert them before calculating. Rounding can also change the answer. To judge the choice, follow all three consequences: data moved, conversion work, and the result the user receives.

In this course, a concept is an idea you can use in that explanation, such as rounding error or time spent waiting for data. A theme brings papers together around a question, such as when smaller stored numbers make a complete task faster. A subtheme narrows that question: how much conversion work can the saving afford, or when does rounding change a decision? These are the course’s reading groups, not official conference categories.

Carry the question between conferences, not the reported speedup. Two papers may both reduce data movement while studying different programs, machines, and acceptable errors. Compare what causes the saving and what extra work it requires. Only compare their numerical results directly when the tasks and measurement conditions justify it.

How to use a conference route

Start with the route’s evidence notice. It says whether the route is a broad source-backed synthesis or a limited guide built around a small number of papers. Next, read one theme and do its practice question before opening the linked walkthrough. In the walkthrough, separate the paper’s reported observation from the course’s invented calculation. Finally, open the source link and write down the workload, comparison, measured quantity, and condition that limits the claim. If any of those are absent, record the gap rather than filling it with an assumption.

Keep three kinds of statements apart

In your notes, label a statement reported when the paper measured or proved it, calculated when you derived it from the paper’s numbers, and proposed when it is a test you think should happen next. A reported number needs its paper location. A calculation needs its arithmetic and assumptions. A proposed test needs a reason; it is not evidence that the paper already supplied.

Check your starting point

Try each question before opening its answer. Write down the calculation or the observation you would need. If your reasoning differs, use the linked lesson to find the assumption responsible. These examples help you choose what to revisit. After the lessons, work through a guided paper and use the final challenge to assess a paper you have not studied here.

A request spends 4 ms waiting, 3 ms reading, 2 ms computing, and 1 ms sending its answer. Assume the stages happen one after another. How long until this answer arrives?

10 ms. Add all four stages: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1. This is the elapsed time for one request under the stated assumptions; it does not tell you how many requests the server can finish per second.

Review elapsed time and completion rate

In the same example, computing drops from 2 ms to 1 ms. The other stages stay fixed. What is the new total, and why is it not half as long?

9 ms: 4 + 3 + 1 + 1. Only one part got faster; the other 8 ms remain. A faster component does not make the whole task faster by the same factor.

Review the complete request path

A processor often has no work to do while it waits for data. Before buying a faster processor, what would you measure?

Measure how long data takes to arrive, how often the requested data must be fetched, how many requests compete for the same path, and whether valid data can be reused. If transfer or contention is the delay, more compute capacity may sit idle.

Review data access and movement

A service's average response time improves, but one request in every hundred still arrives after its deadline. Has the delay problem been solved for every user?

No. The average improved for the measured requests, but one in every hundred still missed its deadline. Record how late those requests were and what made them wait. Also check whether the service's stated target allows that many misses. An average alone cannot answer either question.

Review queues and unusually slow requests

A paper reports that one operation is faster on one tested device. Does that establish that the full application is faster on other devices?

No. It supports the operation result under the reported workload, device, comparison, and measurement conditions. The full application may include other costs, and a different device may behave differently. Read the paper's evaluation boundary before extending the claim.

1. Follow One Request From Arrival To Answer

Start by separating time spent working from time spent waiting. Then ask which part a proposed improvement actually changes.

Start here. No earlier lesson is required.

Key concepts: Bottleneck · Constant cost (O(1)) · Latency · Throughput

Imagine a request arriving at a server. Before the answer can leave, the server must obtain its input, perform the required calculations, and prepare the output. It may also wait for an earlier request to release a processor or memory space. The user experiences all of that elapsed time, even when the machine is doing no work for this particular request.

Consider a teaching example, not a paper measurement. A request waits 4 milliseconds, reads its data in 3 milliseconds, computes for 2 milliseconds, and sends its answer in 1 millisecond. Assume these stages happen one after another. The answer arrives after 10 milliseconds. Making the computation twice as fast reduces the total to 9 milliseconds. Only the computation changed; the other 8 milliseconds remain.

This gives a concrete first question for reading research: which part of the path does the proposed mechanism change? A faster arithmetic unit changes calculation time. Reusing a valid stored result may remove calculation and data reads. A scheduling rule changes which request waits. Each approach acts on a different cause of delay, so each needs a different measurement.

The rate of completed requests is a separate quantity. Consider a second teaching system with ten independent workers. Each worker takes ten milliseconds to finish a request, including all its required steps, and handles only one request at a time. Start the first worker at time 0, the second at time 1 millisecond, and so on through time 9. Their first answers finish at times 10, 11, through 19 milliseconds. Each worker immediately starts its next request when it finishes. With enough incoming work, answers then continue to finish one millisecond apart. Each request still takes ten milliseconds on its worker.

The elapsed time for one request is called latency; the rate of completed requests is called throughput. In the ten-worker example, throughput after the initial startup is 1,000 requests per second. One worker alone would finish only 100 per second, yet a request that starts immediately still takes ten milliseconds in either system. More workers increased capacity without shortening that request's work. This assumes the workers do not slow each other down by competing for data or another shared resource. Requests waiting for a free worker have additional delay, which belongs in latency measured from arrival.

The earlier four-stage request calculation assumes that its stages do not overlap and that the faster computation leaves the queue unchanged. Real systems can violate both assumptions. If reads overlap computation, adding their durations overstates elapsed time. If faster computation lets the server clear a queue sooner, the benefit can extend to waiting requests. State the assumptions before using the calculation to predict a real service.

Try this: keep the original four stages, but make the data read twice as fast instead. The new total is 4 + 1.5 + 2 + 1 = 8.5 milliseconds. That saves more time than halving the computation because the original read took longer. To choose between these improvements in practice, you would also need their cost and measurements showing whether reading or computation actually delays completion.

Change one stage; keep the rest fixed

This is the same invented, sequential request as above. The queue wait, input read, and answer delivery stay fixed; only calculation time changes. That isolates one cause of latency. It does not predict the completion rate of a server handling many requests.

Use the arrow keys or drag the control. Total = 4 ms waiting + 3 ms reading + calculation + 1 ms delivery.

Sequential elapsed-time model; each stage is counted once.
StageTime
Wait in the queue4 ms
Read the input3 ms
Calculate2 ms
Send the answer1 ms
Request elapsed time10 ms

At the starting value, this request takes 10 ms. Even if calculation took zero, the other stages would still take 8 ms.

Where this shows up

  • Training large models needs many chips to share work without waiting on each other.
  • Phone and laptop AI needs accepted results inside a small power and heat budget.
  • Scientific computing needs large machines where memory, storage, and networks stay balanced.

Work it through

For the 10-ms request, imagine calculation takes no time at all while waiting, reading, and delivery stay unchanged. What is the lowest possible total under those assumptions? Would that establish the completion rate of a server handling many requests?

Read the reasoning

The total cannot fall below 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 ms by changing calculation alone. The largest saving is 2 ms, or 20% of the original elapsed time. This does not determine a many-request completion rate: overlapping requests, shared resources, and queue behavior require their own account. If changing calculation also changes waiting, the assumed fixed-stage model no longer applies.

Dependencies

2. When Can Two Pieces Of Work Run Together?

Prerequisite: the opening lesson on elapsed time and completion rate. Here we distinguish waiting for a result from waiting for a resource.

Review first: Start

Key concepts: Concurrency · Dependency · Parallel execution · Pipeline

Suppose a program reads an image, resizes it, and classifies it. Classification needs the resized image. Resizing needs the original image. These requirements impose an order even if three processors are available. A dependency means that one operation needs something another operation has yet to produce.

Now introduce a second image. Its read does not need the first image's classification. A reader can fetch the second image while another device resizes the first. Different images can therefore occupy different stages at once. This arrangement is a pipeline. The order within each image remains intact while work on different images overlaps.

Use an invented teaching example: reading takes 2 milliseconds, resizing takes 5, and classification takes 3. Give each stage its own resource, allow only one image per stage at a time, and assume transfers between stages cost nothing. Images are independent and arrive ready to be processed. The first image finishes after 2 + 5 + 3 = 10 milliseconds.

The next image can read from time 2 to time 4, but resizing remains occupied until time 7. It must wait. Resizing then runs from 7 to 12 and classification from 12 to 15. A third image can finish at time 20. Once work is flowing, the slowest stage allows one completion every 5 milliseconds, or 200 images per second. That rate describes a continuing stream; a single image still has to pass through all three stages.

For n ready images, this model gives a total time of 10 + (n − 1) × 5 milliseconds: the first image takes 10 ms to fill the stages, and each later image finishes 5 ms after the one before it. The last image still has to leave the pipeline; its remaining work is included in that formula. For ten images, the total is 55 ms, compared with 100 ms if each image is finished before the next begins. The pipeline overlaps work; it does not remove any reading, resizing, or classification.

There is also a storage obligation. The reader can produce one image every 2 milliseconds, or 0.5 images per millisecond; resizing can consume one every 5 milliseconds, or 0.2 per millisecond. Once the stages are flowing, the waiting queue grows by about 0.3 image per millisecond if both keep running. This rate calculation is an invented model, not a measurement. A buffer stores waiting work and absorbs a temporary mismatch, but it cannot make the slower stage faster. If the reader can be paused, it must wait when the buffer is full. If new images cannot be paused, excess images must be dropped or stored somewhere else; otherwise the finite buffer eventually overflows.

The separate-resource assumption matters just as much as the dependency order. If resizing and classification occupy the same processor and cannot overlap, that processor must provide 8 milliseconds of work per image. Its capacity is at most 125 images per second. Drawing three boxes does not create three independent resources. Shared memory connections can introduce a similar limit even when processors are separate.

Check a complete schedule for that shared processor. No image is ready until the first read finishes at time 2. Resize the first from 2 to 7 and classify it from 7 to 10. The reader can prepare the second image while this happens; resize it from 10 to 15 and classify it from 15 to 18. Continuing this order finishes ten images at time 2 + 10 × 8 = 82 milliseconds. Nothing can beat 82 under these assumptions: all 80 milliseconds of processor work must happen after time 2. The schedule attains the bound because reading later images keeps up and waiting images have storage. Merely calculating 80 milliseconds of work would omit startup.

Concurrency means several activities can be in progress over the same period. Parallel execution means work actually occurs simultaneously. A program can make progress on another activity while one waits for input, even on a single processor. The linked OSTEP chapters explain these reasons for using multiple threads and how a producer and consumer share a bounded buffer. Our pipeline calculations are separate teaching examples with explicitly idealized timing.

Two conference papers connect this distinction to model training. WLB-LLM (OSDI 2025) studies documents of different lengths. A batch is a group of inputs processed together. If workers receive equal numbers of documents but some documents are much longer, equal counts can leave one worker with more work. WLB-LLM packs variable-length documents across pipeline batches and splits work by document across workers, aiming to reduce the time spent waiting for the worker that finishes last.

Its tested framework reports 1.23× over Plain-4D and 1.19× over Fixed-4D. Other comparisons report 7.5% and 3.4% improvements over static per-sequence and per-document sharding. Sharding means dividing work or data into portions assigned to different workers; static assignments stay fixed for the comparison. These names identify the paper's comparison systems and policies. The reported gains belong to those configurations and do not determine the gain for another workload.

FSMoE (ASPLOS 2025) studies mixture-of-experts models, which send each token, a unit of input, to selected specialist parts of the model. Its approach measures time spent routing inputs, moving data, running the specialists, and exchanging update values. It then schedules independent communication and calculation together. It also adjusts work division between the forward pass (computing predictions) and backward pass (calculating model updates). The opportunity comes from work whose inputs are already available while another operation waits.

The authors evaluated two groups of graphics processing units, or GPUs, connected for training. They report 1.18×–1.22× over their Tutel/PipeMoE baselines in 1,458 configured mixture-of-experts layer cases, and 1.19×–3.01× over DeepSpeed-MoE/Tutel in tested GPT-2 and Mixtral models. A layer is one stage of a model's calculation. A result for an individual layer and a result for training a model cover different amounts of work.

These reported results come from different experiments and baselines, are not directly comparable, and have not been reproduced by this course. WLB-LLM illustrates reducing uneven work across workers; FSMoE illustrates scheduling independent work together. In either case, trace the dependencies and shared resources before expecting a shorter completion time.

Where this shows up

  • Training: exchange a completed portion of an update while calculating another portion whose inputs are already available.
  • Serving: prepare another request while an earlier request executes, provided memory and execution resources permit it.
  • Chip design: supply storage between stages and check whether shared connections prevent the intended schedule.

Work it through

With separate resources, reduce resizing from 5 to 2 milliseconds. Reading remains 2 and classification remains 3. How long do the first image and ten images take? Which stage now limits the continuing completion rate? Then put resizing and classification on one shared processor. How does the ten-image time change?

Read the reasoning

The first image takes 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 milliseconds. Classification is now the slowest stage, allowing a completion every 3 milliseconds. Ten images finish after 7 + 9 × 3 = 34 milliseconds. The long-stream rate approaches 1,000 ÷ 3, about 333 images per second. With one processor for resizing and classification, each image needs 2 + 3 = 5 milliseconds on that processor. Start at time 2 and finish each image before starting the next: ten images take 2 + 10 × 5 = 52 milliseconds. The first still finishes at time 7, but subsequent completions are five milliseconds apart. These schedules assume independent images, adequate buffering, a separate reader, and no transfer overhead.

Sources and further reading

  • OSTEP, chapter 26, section 26.1: parallel work and progress during I/O waits
  • OSTEP, chapter 30, section 30.2: producer/consumer work with a bounded buffer

  • FSMoE (ASPLOS 2025) author manuscript, sections 3–6: profiled scheduling, communication overlap, and evaluated configurations
  • OSDI–ASPLOS service traces: dependencies in serving and training; illustrative examples

Numbers

3. How Much Detail Does A Number Need?

Prerequisite: work and elapsed time. Learn what rounding changes before judging whether a smaller representation still meets the task's acceptance rule.

Review first: Start

Key concepts: Outlier · Quantization · Rounding

A bit stores one of two values, zero or one. Two bits have four possible patterns: 00, 01, 10, and 11. Each extra bit doubles the number of patterns, so eight bits have 2⁸ = 256. A group of eight bits is a byte. These patterns do not determine their own meaning: a number format assigns a value to each pattern it uses. The number of distinct stored values is therefore limited by the number of available patterns.

To represent measurements between 0 and 1 with eight bits, we could assign 256 equally spaced values including both endpoints. There are 255 gaps between those values, so adjacent values differ by 1 ÷ 255. Choosing this set of allowed values and mapping measurements onto it is called quantization. Many different measurements must share one stored value because there are more possible measurements than available patterns.

In that teaching scheme, round each in-range measurement to its nearest allowed value. The largest rounding error is half the spacing: 1 ÷ 510, about 0.00196. Four bits allow only 16 patterns. Over the same range, their spacing is 1 ÷ 15 and the largest rounding error is about 0.0333. Fewer bits save space by making some formerly distinguishable values share a representation.

Range matters independently of bit count. Spread the same 256 values across 0 to 100 and the spacing becomes 100 ÷ 255, about 0.392. A value outside the chosen range raises a different problem. If 1.2 is forced to the endpoint 1 in the original scheme, its error is 0.2, far larger than the in-range rounding bound. This endpoint replacement is clipping. A claim about small rounding error must state which values it covers.

Now ask what the stored values do. Suppose a calculation adds 100 values, each with an absolute error of at most 0.002. If the additions themselves are exact, the sum can be wrong by as much as 0.2 when all errors point in the same direction. Cancellation may produce a smaller error, but cannot be assumed without evidence about the errors. Rounding during the additions adds another source of error and needs its own bound. Multiplication by a large coefficient can amplify an input error before the values are added.

A final decision can be more sensitive than the size of the numbers suggests. Imagine choosing the larger of two scores, 0.502 and 0.498. If the first falls by 0.003 and the second rises by 0.003, they become 0.499 and 0.501, so the lower score becomes the higher one. Small numerical errors can reverse a choice near a decision boundary. Conversely, some tasks tolerate considerably larger errors. The right question is how the changed values affect the result the user needs.

The storage saving is easier to calculate than the speed improvement. One million values stored in 16 bits each occupy 2 million bytes; eight-bit values occupy 1 million bytes. These are decimal quantities and exclude scales, indexes, padding, and other bookkeeping. At an unchanged transfer rate, the value bytes require half the transfer time. That does not establish half the total request time.

For a teaching counterexample, suppose the original request spends 4 milliseconds moving values and 2 milliseconds calculating, sequentially. Halving the transferred bytes reduces movement to 2 milliseconds. But if converting the smaller representation costs another 3 milliseconds, the new total is 7 instead of 6. A device that consumes the smaller representation directly may avoid that cost. You must inspect the executed path rather than infer execution time from file size.

There are several choices besides reducing every value equally. Different groups can use different scales or ranges; especially sensitive calculations can keep more detail. These choices introduce bookkeeping and additional execution paths. Calibration uses representative examples to choose settings. Evaluation then needs separate examples to check whether the settings still meet the task's acceptance rule when the data changes. A setting chosen and scored on the same examples gives weak evidence about new inputs.

The linked paper by Jacob and colleagues connects integer-only inference with a training procedure intended to preserve model accuracy. Its abstract reports evaluation on image classification and detection using CPUs. That provides a concrete example of designing the representation and execution together; it does not establish a universal precision for other tasks. The arithmetic examples in this lesson are our teaching constructions, not that paper's measurements.

Two MLSys 2025 papers show why fewer bits are not automatically faster. QServe stores weights in 4 bits, values passed between model layers (activations) in 8 bits, and the attention data cached across text-generation steps in 4 bits. Its authors report 20–90% runtime overhead associated with converting INT4 weights or partial sums into forms the GPU could use. QServe therefore pairs its number format with a faster conversion method, a different data order, and changes to attention. The paper reports 1.2× maximum serving throughput for Llama-3-8B on an A100 versus TensorRT-LLM. That result is for this model, device, workload, and comparison—not a general speed guarantee.

MiLo (MLSys 2025) tackles a different case: a mixture-of-experts model, where each input uses only some of the model's expert blocks. It stores weights in 3 bits and adds small correction matrices, each represented by two smaller arrays, to recover some detail that rounding removed. A custom GPU routine handles the packed numbers. The paper reports a 1.2× latency speedup over MARLIN for its evaluated mixture-of-experts models when more than one input is processed together. The correction pieces still consume memory, and the result belongs to MiLo's own models, tests, device, and baseline. Do not compare its 1.2× with QServe's as if they were tested head-to-head.

Together these papers make the design test concrete: choose which values lose detail, check how that error affects the required answer, count conversion or correction work, then test the complete execution path on the intended hardware. The DAC synthesis connects the same reasoning to error that accumulates across layers and repeated steps. A compression ratio is not a speed result, and a speed result on one workload does not establish acceptable answers on another. The paper results are reported evidence; the calculations earlier in this lesson are separate teaching examples.

Where this shows up

  • Inference servers use shorter weights and caches to fit more users on the same hardware.
  • Edge devices use smaller numbers to keep speech, vision, and language models local.
  • Custom chips add arithmetic units built for the exact number sizes the model can tolerate.

Work it through

Use 16 equally spaced values over 0 to 3, including both endpoints. What is the maximum in-range nearest-rounding error? If ten such rounded values are added, what worst-case error bound follows? Does it cover clipping an input of 4 to 3?

Read the reasoning

There are 15 intervals, each 3 ÷ 15 = 0.2 wide. Nearest rounding gives an error of at most 0.1 for an in-range value. Adding ten values gives a bound of 10 × 0.1 = 1, assuming no additional arithmetic error. Clipping 4 to 3 already introduces an error of 1 for that single value. The 0.1 per-value bound does not apply to this out-of-range input, so a sum containing it needs a revised bound.

Sources and further reading

  • Jacob and colleagues: integer-only inference and training; abstract supports the paper example
  • QServe (MLSys 2025): W4A8KV4, conversion overhead, GPU execution changes, and evaluated serving results
  • QServe bounded source record and reported throughput comparisons
  • MiLo (MLSys 2025): INT3 MoE weights, low-rank correction, GPU kernel, and measured latency
  • MiLo bounded source record and reported accuracy/latency evidence
  • MLSys: precision and quantization, including QServe and MiLo
  • DAC: approximation and the final result's error requirements

Memory

4. Having Enough Memory Does Not Mean Data Arrives In Time

Prerequisite: work, waiting, and dependencies. Separate how much fits, how quickly bytes move, and how long one dependent read takes.

Review first: Start · Dependencies

Key concepts: Bandwidth · Cache · Cache ownership · Locality · Key–value cache · Processing-in-memory

Imagine a calculation that reads a large table. Three separate questions determine whether memory can support it. Does the table fit? How many bytes can the connection deliver per second? How long must the calculation wait for the particular value it needs next? These questions concern capacity, bandwidth, and access latency. Distance can affect delay, but queueing, access order, and the number of available connections also matter.

Capacity is an amount, such as 16 gigabytes. One gigabyte, abbreviated GB, is one billion bytes in these examples. Bandwidth is a rate, such as 100 GB per second. Latency is a duration, such as 100 nanoseconds for a read in a simplified example. A millisecond is one thousandth of a second, a microsecond is one millionth, and a nanosecond is one billionth. Adding capacity does not automatically raise the transfer rate. Raising the transfer rate does not automatically shorten a read that must finish before the next can begin.

Capacity is about the peak amount that must be present at one time. During model training, weights are the stored numbers adjusted to improve predictions. Gradients describe how the training error changes with those numbers; the update procedure uses them to choose changes. It may also keep summaries of earlier updates, called optimizer state. These values can coexist with intermediate calculation results. For an invented example, if a step needs 6 GB of weights, 4 GB of intermediate values, 6 GB of gradients, and 8 GB of optimizer state at once, its peak is 24 GB. If the intermediate values are no longer needed before the gradients are created, the peak could be lower because their space can be reused. Whether a job fits therefore depends on when values are produced and when their last use occurs, not just on adding up every value ever created.

APOLLO (MLSys 2025) shows how large one part of a training peak can be. AdamW keeps two running summaries of past gradients for each weight; the paper notes that these optimizer states alone use 28 GB in its cited single-batch LLaMA-7B example. APOLLO reduces this category with a smaller projected summary and shared update scales: instead of choosing a separate scale for every weight, it can use one for a group of related weights (a channel) or for a whole array of weights (a tensor). The authors report about 3× training throughput versus AdamW on eight A100-80GB GPUs by fitting batches four times larger. This is not a claim that each calculation became 3× faster: the larger batch is part of the measured system change, and the result is tied to the paper's model and setup. It is paper-reported evidence, not a result reproduced by this course.

Take an invented calculation that must read 8 gigabytes through a connection sustaining 400 gigabytes per second. Using decimal units, the transfer needs at least 8 ÷ 400 seconds, or 20 milliseconds. If computation then takes 12 milliseconds, the sequential path takes at least 32 milliseconds. Perfectly overlapping these activities could reduce the lower bound to 20 milliseconds, but only if the calculation can process earlier portions while later portions arrive. A formula cannot establish that independence.

Now change the access pattern. Suppose each fetched record contains the address of the next record. The program cannot request the next record until the previous read returns. In a teaching model with 1,000 dependent reads taking 100 nanoseconds each, their chain takes at least 100 microseconds. A wider connection need not help: the program cannot yet name enough future reads to fill it. Independent requests could use the connection together, but that changes the workload and the schedule.

How much independent work is enough? In a separate idealized model, each read returns 64 bytes after 100 nanoseconds. With only one read in flight—requested but not yet returned—the system receives at most 64 bytes every 100 nanoseconds, or 0.64 GB per second. Eight reads in flight permit at most 8 × 0.64 = 5.12 GB per second. Keeping a 64-GB-per-second connection fully occupied would require at least 100 reads in flight on average: during a 100-nanosecond wait, that connection could deliver 6,400 bytes, equal to 100 reads. This is a necessary amount of concurrent work under the model, not proof that the memory can sustain it.

The addresses must be available early enough, the hardware must track those requests, and the memory must be able to serve them. If all requests compete for one restricted part of memory, adding requests may only lengthen the wait. If they belong to the dependent chain above, the next address is unavailable and extra tracking space cannot help. A bandwidth comparison therefore needs both the connection's capacity and evidence that the program supplies enough usable independent work. These counts assume the stated delay remains fixed and omit request overhead and startup effects.

Reuse offers another way to avoid waiting. A cache keeps data or results that may be needed again. Finding the required item is a hit; fetching it from elsewhere is a miss. Every lookup has a cost, and a miss adds more work. In a simple teaching model, a lookup costs 1 microsecond and a miss adds 20. If one lookup in ten misses, the mean cost is 1 + 0.1 × 20 = 3 microseconds. This is an average; each miss still costs 21 microseconds in this model.

Storage is finite, so inserting a new item may require removing another. A replacement policy chooses what leaves. Keeping recently used items is a guess that recent use will repeat. Here is a small invented failure case for least-recently-used replacement: a two-item cache holds repeatedly used items A and B; a one-time read of X and then Y evicts both; the next reads of A and B miss. This does not mean recency is useless, but it shows that a scan can overwhelm the prediction. OSTEP gives a longer example: cycling through 50 pages in a cache that holds 49 produces no hits under LRU for that pattern. The linked chapter also explains replacement policies that try to resist scans. Our cache times and two-item trace are teaching examples, not machine measurements.

Reusing a result also requires checking its identity. A stored model response depends on the input, model version, and relevant execution settings. An identical-looking prompt does not justify reuse after changing the model. A database value may become stale after a write. Systems therefore need rules for matching stored results and retiring invalid copies. The lookup and checking work belong in the cost of reuse.

Moving data to a larger, slower memory tier solves a capacity problem while creating a scheduling problem. If data arrives after the calculation needs it, execution waits. Fetching it early needs a prediction and spare space to hold it. Fetching too much can occupy the connection and displace data needed sooner. A placement policy must therefore account for when data will be used, not merely whether space exists.

Working memory and persistent storage also make different promises. Ordinary DRAM is temporary working space and does not preserve its contents through power loss. An SSD is designed to retain stored data, but an application still needs the right write and flush rules before it can claim that a particular update is durable. Moving data out of DRAM can free working capacity, but it changes the access path; storing it on an SSD alone does not prove that a write will survive a crash. The correctness and recovery lesson treats that separate promise.

These distinctions let you compare conference questions. The MLSys essays examine model state, stored attention calculations, offloading, and reuse. OSDI examines placement across memory and storage together with sharing and recovery. ISCA and HPCA ask how the hardware changes the available access paths. A proposal from any of these areas should identify which quantity it changes and which cost remains. The linked essays provide the paper-specific evidence and its limits.

Where this shows up

  • Language model serving is often limited by reading the stored context again and again.
  • Graph and database work can be limited by scattered memory reads.
  • Scientific simulations can spend more time moving arrays than computing on them.

Work it through

In the illustrative cache, reduce the miss fraction from 10% to 5%, but increase lookup and checking time from 1 to 3 microseconds. Misses still add 20 microseconds. Is the mean access time better? What does the answer leave out?

Read the reasoning

The new mean is 3 + 0.05 × 20 = 4 microseconds, compared with 3 before. Fewer misses do not compensate for the extra work on every lookup. The calculation leaves out queues, overlapping requests, different miss costs, and correctness of reused data. It also does not describe the slowest requests. Both comparisons assume the same request population.

Sources and further reading

  • OSTEP chapter 22, sections 22.1, 22.5–22.6, and 22.12: average cache cost, recency, looping scans, and scan resistance
  • OSTEP chapter 39, section 39.1: working memory versus persistent storage
  • OSTEP chapter 44: SSD storage, internal buffering, and access path
  • APOLLO (MLSys 2025), sections 1, 3–5: optimizer-state footprint, projected updates, and reported throughput
  • APOLLO bounded paper record: source scope, baseline, and evaluation limits
  • MLSys: keeping useful state within memory limits
  • OSDI: keeping state available at the right place
  • ISCA: moving computation closer to data and the resulting costs
Previous: Numbers Next: Topology Concept lookup
Topology

5. Routes Determine Which Connections Must Share the Work

Prerequisites: memory capacity and transfer rate. Trace the actual route before adding up the speeds printed on individual links.

Review first: Memory

Key concepts: Cut · Topology

Topology describes which parts connect to which others. A link is a connection between two parts. A switch receives data on one link and forwards it onto another; data travels in pieces called packets. A route is the sequence of connections a transfer follows. To find how quickly it can finish, we need the capacity of those connections and the other traffic sharing them. Separate these three questions: does a path exist, how much work can pass through it, and how long will this particular transfer wait? All quantities in the examples below are teaching assumptions.

Imagine two senders, each connected to a switch at 10 GB per second. The switch reaches a receiver through one 10 GB-per-second link. Each sender needs to deliver 10 GB. There are three links, each labeled 10 GB per second, but adding their labels to get 30 GB per second is meaningless for this delivery. Both transfers must cross the final link. Its 20 GB of work takes at least two seconds, even if the senders transmit together and the switch forwards immediately. Propagation, packet handling, and waiting can only increase this lower bound.

Draw a boundary separating the senders from the receiver. Every delivered byte must cross that boundary. The combined capacity of the links crossing it bounds the delivery rate. Such a boundary is called a cut. A narrow cut can limit a large network regardless of how many fast links exist elsewhere. The bound applies to traffic that must cross it; local transfers staying on one side do not consume that cut's capacity.

Now give the receiver two independent incoming links, each sustaining 10 GB per second, and assume its memory can accept both streams at their combined rate. Assigning one sender to each link lowers the transfer-time bound to one second. But if both routes still use the same incoming link, the unused second link contributes nothing. A physical option becomes usable capacity only when the route and endpoint can use it.

Traffic size matters as much as the number of transfers. Suppose four transfers carry 9, 9, 1, and 1 GB. Assume they start together, these are the only transfers, and the endpoints can supply and receive data fast enough to keep both paths busy. The two independent paths each sustain 10 GB per second. Assigning the two large transfers to one path and the two small ones to the other gives equal transfer counts but loads of 18 and 2 GB. The busy path needs at least 1.8 seconds. Putting one large and one small transfer on each path produces 10 GB per path and a one-second bound. Balancing counts is not the same as balancing work.

Choosing a route from measured congestion introduces a timing problem. By the time a sender acts on a report, other senders may also have moved to the apparently empty path. The report describes an earlier state, not reserved capacity. An adaptive scheme must explain how it measures load, how quickly feedback arrives, and whether many decisions can reinforce each other. A static scheme avoids some feedback costs but can miss changing traffic or failed connections.

The historical CONGA paper, published at SIGCOMM 2014, offers one concrete response. Its abstract describes estimating congestion along network paths and using feedback from remote switches to assign groups of packets called flowlets. This is a mechanism for using multiple available routes under changing load. It is not evidence that every topology or workload benefits equally, and its reported measurements are not the numbers in our examples.

Extra routes also matter after failure, but surviving connectivity is only the first requirement. Suppose two independent 10 GB-per-second paths normally carry 16 GB per second together. If one fails, a route remains, yet only 10 GB per second of capacity remains. Keeping all 16 GB per second of incoming traffic creates six GB of excess work each second. A three-GB buffer fills in half a second under a steady-rate model starting empty. Rerouting alone cannot preserve the original service rate.

Independence must be checked physically. Two drawn paths may pass through the same switch, share a cable conduit, or depend on one power supply. They can survive one link failure while both disappearing under a different failure. State the failure being tolerated and trace the resources it can remove. Otherwise the diagram can suggest protection the installation does not provide.

The same reasoning applies within a chip. Several processing blocks may each have a fast local connection but share one route to memory. Moving a calculation closer to its inputs can reduce traffic across that route; adding arithmetic units may only increase the demand. Physical placement adds another constraint: a logical connection needs actual wires, space, and time for signals to travel. The graph of allowed connections and the physical layout answer related but different questions.

When reading NSDI networking or architecture papers, mark the busiest shared boundary, the traffic that crosses it, and the rule assigning that traffic to paths. Then repeat the analysis under the paper's failure case. A design may increase total network capacity while leaving one application's route unchanged. A different design may move less data without changing any link. Those are distinct causes of improvement and should remain distinct in the explanation.

Where this shows up

  • Chip design uses topology when placing compute blocks, memory blocks, and wires.
  • Supercomputers use topology when choosing network shapes that avoid traffic jams.
  • Chiplet systems use topology when deciding how many small dies should connect and where.
  • Security uses topology when deciding which data paths must be isolated from an attacker.

Work it through

Two independent paths each sustain 5 GB per second. Transfers of 8, 8, 2, and 2 GB are ready together. What completion-time lower bound follows if both large transfers use one path? What if each path gets one large and one small transfer? If either path fails, what is the bound for sending all 20 GB through the survivor? Assume endpoints can keep up and ignore overhead.

Read the reasoning

The first assignment puts 16 GB on one path and 4 on the other, so completion cannot be sooner than max(16/5, 4/5) = 3.2 seconds. Balanced assignment puts 10 GB on each, giving a two-second bound. With one surviving path, 20/5 = four seconds is the bound. These are achievable only under the idealized assumptions, with routes that can sustain the stated rates; they are not measured completion times. The alternate route preserves delivery, not the original capacity.

Sources and further reading

  • Alizadeh and colleagues, CONGA (SIGCOMM 2014), abstract — feedback-based path assignment
  • NSDI 2026 synthesis — control state, placement, and failure recovery

Skipping

6. When Is Skipping Work Worth The Trouble?

Prerequisites: memory and numerical error. Count the cost of finding, representing, and scheduling the work that remains.

Review first: Numbers · Memory

Key concepts: Sparsity

Suppose a calculation forms a weighted sum. In ordinary real arithmetic, a term whose weight is exactly zero contributes nothing. Omitting that term can preserve the answer. Omitting a small nonzero term changes the answer and needs an error argument. Reusing an earlier sum needs a different argument: the inputs and relevant state must still match. These are three distinct reasons for avoiding work, with three different checks.

Even exact omission depends on the promised number semantics. Computer arithmetic can include infinities, invalid values, signed zeros, and observable exceptions. A compiler cannot always replace a multiplication by zero without considering those rules. For the examples here, assume finite ordinary values, no arithmetic exceptions, and no observable effects from the omitted operations. A real implementation must state its own permitted transformations.

A pattern is sparse when many of its possible positions are zero. A sparse representation stores the nonzero values and enough information to locate them. Consider an invented row of 100 weights, each stored in two bytes. Keeping all positions uses 200 bytes. If only 20 weights remain, storing each with a one-byte position uses 20 × 3 = 60 bytes, before row headers and alignment. With 80 weights remaining, the same representation uses 240 bytes. The position information can make a partly empty row larger than the original.

Storage savings do not settle execution cost. The processor must read the positions, fetch the corresponding inputs, and combine the products correctly. Contiguous values may be easy to process together. Scattered positions can require separate accesses and leave execution units idle. A format that skips whole blocks may save less arithmetic while being easier for the machine to consume than a format that records every isolated nonzero value.

Use a second teaching model. The original operation takes 100 units of time. Suppose the remaining fraction of arithmetic takes the same fraction of that time, and finding and organizing it adds 30 units. Keeping 20% of the work costs 20 + 30 = 50 units, a twofold improvement. Keeping 80% costs 80 + 30 = 110 units, which is slower. Under these assumptions, the retained fraction must be below 70% to improve execution time. Real costs may depend on the pattern, so measure them rather than treating the fixed 30 as a machine constant.

The distribution of remaining work also matters. Imagine four workers that previously processed 25 items each. After skipping, their counts are 20, 0, 0, and 0. Only one fifth of the original total work remains, but completion still takes 20 item-times if work stays assigned to those workers. Redistribution might approach five item-times per worker, but requires moving work and perhaps its data. The total number of retained operations cannot describe this waiting by itself.

Approximate omission introduces another cost: checking that the result still meets the task's acceptance rule. Dropping terms subtracts their combined contribution from the original sum. In an invented example, the retained terms sum to 1 and the dropped products are +0.10 and −0.08. The original result is 1 + 0.10 − 0.08 = 1.02; the shortened calculation returns 1. The new result minus the original is −0.02, so the absolute error is 0.02. Without relying on cancellation, the error bound is 0.10 + 0.08 = 0.18. Small weights alone are insufficient: dropping a term with weight 0.001 and input 1,000 removes a contribution of 1. Later operations may amplify the error, so a local bound still needs a connection to the final task.

Reuse shifts the question from contribution to identity. A stored prefix calculation may save repeated work when the input prefix and model state match. Looking it up, verifying the match, retaining it in memory, and moving it to the executing device all consume resources. A workload with little repetition may pay those costs with few successful reuses. The cache lesson explains why the proportion of hits and the cost per hit must be considered together.

As a historical example, the EIE paper proposes hardware that executes a compressed neural network using sparse matrix-vector operations and shared weights. The abstract establishes that connection between representation and execution. Its reported performance concerns its stated comparisons; this lesson does not transfer those numbers to current models or hardware. Our byte counts and timing examples are independent teaching constructions.

MLSys 2025 uses sparsity in at least three different ways, and they should not be mistaken for the same trick. SparseTransX trains models on a graph of facts, such as “Paris — capital of → France.” Its graph connections are naturally sparse; the method does not discard small values. Instead, it gathers many scattered reads and writes into a bulk sparse-matrix calculation. Its evaluation covers four graph models on CPUs and GPUs, and its reported speedups apply to those training workloads—not to pruning neural-network weights.

Radius targets a different cost: communication between GPUs during training. It leaves out selected entries of the gradient—the calculated signal for how model weights should change—and reuses the chosen positions across steps. It also keeps skipped values and sends their accumulated remainder periodically. Because AdamW, the update rule used here, adjusts new changes using its running history, this delayed correction does not exactly recreate the result of sending every gradient value at every step. For GPT-2.0B pretraining with 40% gradient sparsity, the authors report 21% less time per step and 19% less total training time than dense communication on 64 NVIDIA A100 GPUs connected by Slingshot 11; downstream scores were preserved in their evaluation.

TASD (Tensor Approximation via Structured Decomposition) takes a third route: it represents irregular sparse work as a series of patterns that the accelerator already knows how to run. Its TASDER software searches for a suitable set of patterns for each layer. Fewer patterns can save more operations but lose more of the original calculation; more patterns can improve the approximation while bringing work back. The authors report up to 39% speedup for sparse ResNet-34 on an NVIDIA RTX 3080 using its 2:4 sparse hardware.

These findings come from different models, tasks, machines, and comparisons, so they are not a head-to-head ranking.

To classify the mechanism, ask: Are values naturally absent, deliberately discarded, or merely rearranged? What work is added to find or encode the pattern? Which execution unit can skip work, and which cannot? What error, task-quality, or full-workload measure checks that the saved work was worth it? These questions separate sparse representation, approximate omission, and hardware-friendly reorganization. The MLSys and MICRO readings below connect them to reuse, memory access, and scheduling.

Where this shows up

  • Sparse models route only part of the model for each input.
  • Serving systems reuse cached work when many users ask related questions.
  • Accelerators can omit eligible zero-valued terms; omitting nonzero terms additionally requires checking the resulting error.

Work it through

A row contains 100 two-byte values. A proposed format retains 50 values, each with a two-byte position. Ignore headers. Does it save storage? In the 100-unit timing model with 30 units of overhead, does retaining half the arithmetic save time?

Read the reasoning

The original row uses 100 × 2 = 200 bytes. The new format uses 50 × (2 + 2) = 200 bytes, so it saves no storage even before headers. In the separate timing model it costs 50 + 30 = 80 units, saving 20 units, or a 1.25-fold speedup. These conclusions can coexist because storage size and execution time measure different things. The timing conclusion assumes that remaining arithmetic scales as stated and that all extra work is included in the 30 units.

Sources and further reading

  • Han and colleagues, EIE (ISCA 2016): abstract on execution of compressed networks
  • SparseTransX (MLSys 2025): naturally sparse graph updates reformulated as sparse matrix operations
  • SparseTransX bounded paper record and reported scope
  • Radius (MLSys 2025): gradient selection, residual handling, convergence, and measured training time
  • Radius bounded paper record and optimizer/convergence boundary
  • TASD/TASDER (MLSys 2025): structured decomposition, approximation, and execution evidence
  • TASD/TASDER bounded paper record and hardware scope
  • MLSys: sparsity, pruning, and attention-state reuse
  • MICRO: representation, access order, and scheduling

Compilers

7. The Same Calculation Can Have Different Execution Plans

Prerequisites: dependencies, memory, and number precision. Examine what an implementation may change and what it must preserve.

Review first: Dependencies · Numbers · Memory

Key concepts: Compiler · Fusion · CUDA Graph · Tiling

Consider two instructions expressed as array operations: multiply every input by two, then add one to each result. The program describes a calculation. An execution plan must additionally decide where intermediate values live, which operations run together, and which machine instructions perform them. A compiler constructs such a plan while translating a program into a form the machine can execute.

Here is a teaching example with one million four-byte values. Assume the input, temporary array, and output are separate, and that arithmetic preserves the intended values. Two separate passes read the input, write the temporary array, read it again, and write the output. Counting each array once gives 16 million bytes of transfers at this logical boundary. Combining the passes can read each input, calculate its final result, and write the output directly: 8 million bytes. This combination is called fusion.

The difference is an opportunity to remove intermediate traffic, not a prediction of traffic at every level of memory. A cache may already retain the temporary array. Conversely, a large combined operation may need more temporary values than fast storage can hold, forcing some into slower memory. Measuring the relevant memory connection tells you whether the proposed saving occurred where execution was actually waiting.

Fusion also needs a correctness argument. Suppose another part of the program reads the temporary array after the first pass. Deleting the array without supplying that reader changes behavior. Suppose the arrays share storage in an unexpected way. Reordering reads and writes can then change which input a later operation sees. A compiler needs facts about these uses and storage relationships before applying the transformation.

Change the earlier example's storage assumption to see the problem. Start with four storage positions containing [1, 2, 3, 0]. The input consists of the first three positions, but the output must occupy the last three, so they overlap. The two-pass version first saves the doubled inputs [2, 4, 6] in separate temporary storage. It then adds one and writes [3, 5, 7] into the output positions, leaving [1, 3, 5, 7] in storage. A combined left-to-right pass instead reads 1 and writes 3 into the second position. Its next read sees that new 3 rather than the original 2, so it writes 7 into the third position. It then reads 7 and writes 15 into the fourth. The final storage is [1, 3, 7, 15], which is wrong for the requested two-pass computation. Avoiding the temporary array requires a plan that preserves the original inputs until their last use; removing it alone is insufficient.

For this particular overlap, a combined pass can work from right to left. Read the original 3 and write 7 into the fourth position; read 2 and write 5 into the third; then read 1 and write 3 into the second. Every overwritten input has already been used, and the final storage is [1, 3, 5, 7]. This is a valid alternative under the example's assumptions, not a rule that reversing any loop fixes overlapping storage. The dependency determines the permitted order.

Even familiar algebra depends on the number rules. Consider a deliberately simplified calculator that rounds each addition to three significant decimal digits. Let a = 10,000, b = −10,000, and c = 1. Evaluating (a + b) + c gives 1. In the other order, b + c = −9,999 rounds to −10,000, so a + (b + c) gives 0. Reordering the additions changes the answer because an intermediate result loses information. A compiler must respect the program's required numerical behavior, including any explicitly permitted approximations.

A compiler can also divide an array into blocks that fit fast storage, an approach often called tiling. The goal is to reuse the contents of each block before fetching another. Larger blocks can reduce repeated transfers but consume more local storage. Smaller blocks can leave more room for simultaneous work but increase setup and boundary handling. Choosing the block size therefore connects the memory lesson to the dependency lesson.

A compiler often passes through one or more intermediate representations: internal forms between the program people write and the instructions a machine runs. A graph of operations can preserve facts about a whole matrix operation and which inputs it reuses. A lower-level form may spell out individual reads, additions, and storage, making some patterns harder to see. The form affects which choices are easy to consider; eventually the plan still has to specify concrete instructions and storage.

Finding a good plan costs time too. In a teaching example, a general implementation takes 5 milliseconds per request. A specialized plan takes 3 milliseconds, but creating it costs 200 milliseconds once. For N identical requests, compare 5N with 200 + 3N. They are equal at 100 requests; the specialized plan saves total time only above 100. A workload that frequently changes shape may repeatedly pay the preparation cost.

The TVM paper shows this handoff in one machine-learning compiler: it first represents a model as a graph of operations, then describes tensor calculations and schedules that choose such details as loop order and block size. Its schedule changes are intended to preserve the program's logical result, while an automated search uses a learned cost model to rank choices. This is a specific design described in that paper, not proof that another compiler will find a good plan for every input or device. The arithmetic and timing examples here are teaching examples, not TVM measurements.

Relax (ASPLOS 2025) shows why a compiler's internal form matters when input sizes can change. Suppose one array has n rows and another has 4n values. If the compiler records both sizes as simply unknown, it loses the relationship between them; it may then miss a safe way to combine operations or plan temporary storage. Relax keeps a model's operation graph, lower-level loops, calls to prewritten routines, and symbolic size relationships together as it transforms the program. That lets it consider some optimizations across these levels instead of lowering each one separately and losing those relationships. The authors report competitive LLM performance across several GPUs and deployment to mobile, embedded, and browser environments. This is evidence for their tested models and targets, not proof that every model becomes faster or that the transformations preserve every property a program may expose. The arithmetic and timing examples here remain teaching constructions, not TVM or Relax measurements.

Where this shows up

  • ML compilers turn model graphs into kernels that fit the target chip.
  • Hardware design tools turn a high-level circuit description into gates and wires.
  • Serving systems compile requests into batches and schedules that reduce waiting.

Work it through

A prepared implementation costs 120 milliseconds to build and then takes 4 milliseconds per run. The existing implementation takes 6 milliseconds per run with no extra preparation. At what run count do they tie? Which is faster for 50 runs, including preparation?

Read the reasoning

Set 120 + 4N = 6N, giving N = 60. At 50 runs the prepared implementation takes 120 + 200 = 320 milliseconds; the existing one takes 300. Preparation pays off only above 60 runs under these assumptions. If the plan can be reused later, count those later runs too; if inputs require another plan, count that new preparation cost separately.

Sources and further reading

  • Chen and colleagues, TVM (2018), sections 2–5: graph representation, tensor calculations, schedules, and automated search
  • Relax (ASPLOS 2025), sections 2–5: symbolic shapes, cross-level representation, dynamic-shape optimization, and evaluation
  • Relax bounded paper record; its current local note is abstract-derived
  • ASPLOS: program meaning, intermediate forms, and rewrites
  • OSDI: representing work for execution

Sharing

8. Doing More Work Can Make Someone Wait Longer

Prerequisites: elapsed time and dependencies. Separate waiting, useful execution, and the policy that decides whose turn comes next.

Review first: Start · Dependencies

Key concepts: Batching · Decode · Prefill · Percentile · Queue · Scheduling · Slack · Time to first token (TTFT) · Time per output token (TPOT) · Virtual deadline

A request arrives while a machine is busy. Its calculation may need only a few milliseconds, but it cannot start yet. A queue is the set of work waiting for access. The order in which that work receives access is a scheduling policy. A faster calculation and a better policy solve different problems: one reduces how long the resource is occupied; the other changes who waits. All numerical examples below are invented for teaching.

Suppose a single worker takes 10 milliseconds per request, never overlaps requests, and initially has no work. Five requests arrive together at time zero. If it handles them in order, they finish at 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 milliseconds. The average completion delay is 30 milliseconds even though every calculation takes only 10. The final request spends 40 milliseconds waiting and 10 executing. A benchmark that starts its timer only when execution begins would omit most of that person's experience.

This worker can finish at most 100 requests per second under these assumptions. If 120 arrive every second for a sustained period, unfinished work grows by roughly 20 per second once it is busy. No choice of order can make all that work fit. The system must add capacity, reduce work, slow incoming traffic, or refuse some requests. Refusing work can keep accepted requests responsive, but the refusal rate must remain visible in the results. Otherwise a system can appear fast by discarding difficult work.

Matching capacity exactly can work in a perfectly regular schedule. If a request arrives every 10 milliseconds and each takes exactly 10 milliseconds, the worker finishes just as the next request arrives. None waits. But suppose the first request takes 15 milliseconds and all later ones take 10. The second arrives at time 10 and waits until 15; the third arrives at 20 and waits until 25. Every later request also waits five milliseconds. The queue does not keep growing in this example, but there is no spare time to remove the delay. Another disturbance could add more waiting.

Arriving more slowly leaves room to recover. With arrivals every 12 milliseconds and the same one-time 15-millisecond first job, the first three requests wait 0, 3, and 1 milliseconds; the fourth does not wait. The two spare milliseconds between ordinary jobs let the worker catch up. These regular schedules are teaching cases, not guarantees for variable arrivals. Five requests arriving together can cause a queue even if the next second is quiet. Average requests per second alone does not describe the bursts, job sizes, or ordering needed to explain delays. Nor does one utilization percentage determine waiting time without a model of those variations.

Now suppose each execution has a shared 6-millisecond setup cost plus 2 milliseconds for each request included. Running one request costs 8 milliseconds. Running four together costs 14 milliseconds. Grouping requests this way is batching. For a continuously available backlog, single-request execution finishes 125 requests per second; four-request batches finish about 286 per second. This is a rate comparison under the stated cost model, not a promise that every machine gets faster with larger batches.

Consider four requests arriving at times 0, 3, 6, and 9 milliseconds. Executing them individually as soon as the worker is free produces completions at 8, 16, 24, and 32. Their arrival-to-completion delays are 8, 13, 18, and 23 milliseconds, averaging 15.5. Waiting until time 9 to assemble one batch produces a common completion time of 23. Their delays are then 23, 20, 17, and 14, averaging 18.5. The batch finishes the whole group sooner and occupies the worker for less time, but increases the average delay and makes the first request much slower.

A batching policy therefore needs both a size limit and a waiting rule. Waiting forever to fill a large batch leaves the last few requests stuck when arrivals stop. A timer can launch a partly filled batch, trading some sharing benefit for bounded assembly time. That timer does not bound total delay: earlier batches can still occupy the device, and execution itself can vary. If users have deadlines, the policy must account for time already spent waiting and the work still ahead.

Order also changes who benefits. Let one 100-millisecond job and ten 1-millisecond jobs all arrive together. With the long job first, the eleven completion delays sum to 1,155 milliseconds, for an average of 105. With the short jobs first, their delays sum to 55 and the long job finishes at 110, giving an overall average of 15. Both orders finish all work at time 110. Serving short jobs first improves this average dramatically, but a continuing stream of short jobs could keep a long job waiting indefinitely. Preventing that requires an additional rule, such as increasing priority with waiting time or reserving a share of service.

Averages can hide the people who wait longest. If 99 requests finish in 10 milliseconds and one in 1,010 milliseconds, the mean is 20 milliseconds. That number describes neither the usual request nor the worst one. Report the distribution or clearly defined percentiles as well. A percentile states a delay below which a chosen fraction of observations falls; exact conventions differ for finite samples. Also report how many requests were rejected and whether the timer began at arrival, admission, or execution.

For generated text, one request consists of repeated steps rather than one indivisible calculation. This creates opportunities to reconsider the group between steps. The OSDI 2022 Orca abstract describes scheduling at the level of an iteration and batching selected operations. Its motivation is that a fixed group can hold back finished requests and delay newly arriving ones. This is a historical mechanism example, not a performance prediction for today's services or for the numbers above. The practical limit is that changing groups still requires enough memory for the active requests and a schedule their operations can follow.

When reading the MLSys serving themes, distinguish arrival-to-first-output delay, gaps between outputs, and time until the entire answer finishes. They answer different questions. A service that begins quickly but pauses repeatedly may have a good first-output number and a poor reading experience. Ask which requests share execution, how newcomers enter, what happens to long-running work, and what happens when demand exceeds capacity. Those policy choices belong in an end-to-end explanation alongside the kernel speed measurements.

Where this shows up

  • Model serving: choose batch size and admission rules while accounting for memory and time already spent waiting.
  • Shared clusters: compare scheduling policies using both completion delays and treatment of long jobs.
  • Performance evaluation: include rejected work and state exactly where each timer starts and stops.

Work it through

Three requests arrive at times 0, 2, and 4 milliseconds. Execution costs 4 milliseconds of setup plus 2 per request. Compare immediate individual execution with waiting until time 4 and executing one batch. Calculate completion times, individual delays, average delay, and total worker busy time. Which result would you report to someone who cares about the first request?

Read the reasoning

Individual runs each take 6 milliseconds and finish at 6, 12, and 18. Subtracting arrivals gives delays of 6, 10, and 14, averaging 10. The worker is busy for 18 milliseconds. One three-request batch takes 10 milliseconds, starts at 4, and finishes at 14. Delays are 14, 12, and 10, averaging 12; busy time is 10. Batching finishes the group four milliseconds earlier and saves eight milliseconds of worker time, but the first request waits 14 rather than 6 milliseconds. Report that delay directly rather than substituting the group completion time or average rate.

Sources and further reading

  • Yu and colleagues, Orca (OSDI 2022), abstract — iteration-level scheduling and selective batching
  • MLSys 2025 subthemes — serving schedules, request state, and resource allocation
