Many Chips

9. Dividing Work Creates Communication and Recovery Work

Prerequisites: dependencies and memory. Follow one distributed job through calculation, exchange, waiting, and retrying.

Review first: Dependencies · Memory

Key concepts: Barrier · Checkpoint · Quorum · Recovery

Suppose a job takes 100 seconds on one machine. Can four machines finish it in 25 seconds? Only if the work divides evenly, all four machines have the data they need, and combining their results adds no time. Those conditions are a useful starting model, not a promise. The numbers in this lesson are teaching examples, not measurements from a paper.

Let 20 seconds of the job be a preparation step that cannot be divided. The remaining 80 seconds divide evenly across four workers. Even with free communication, completion takes 20 + 80/4 = 40 seconds. Eight workers reduce this to 30 seconds. No number of workers removes the initial 20 seconds. This is the limit imposed by work that must happen in sequence, often called Amdahl's law. It applies to a fixed amount of work; doing a larger job with more machines is a different comparison.

Now add a result exchange that starts after calculation and takes 12 seconds on four workers. Completion takes 52 seconds, not 40. Suppose eight workers need 24 seconds for their exchange because more data crosses a shared connection. Their total is 20 + 10 + 24 = 54 seconds. More machines make this particular job slower. The exchange times are assumptions, not a general law that doubling workers doubles communication. To evaluate a real system, find the bytes sent, their routes, the shared limits, and which transfers can overlap calculation.

A link's rate constrains everything sharing it. If four workers must each send 1 GB across the same outgoing link, and that link sustains 1 GB per second, transmitting all 4 GB takes at least four seconds. Four senders do not create four links. Independent links could change this bound; so could combining results before sending them. The memory lesson's distinction between access delay and transfer rate still applies, but now the route through the network matters too.

Dividing the input equally does not guarantee equal work. Imagine four workers whose tasks take 10, 10, 10, and 30 seconds, starting together. A following step that needs every result starts at 30 seconds. The mean worker time, 15 seconds, does not predict that wait. This meeting point is called a barrier. The first three workers spend 20 seconds each waiting there. Smaller tasks can make it easier to assign unfinished work to idle workers, but each task also needs assignment, input access, and bookkeeping.

If the slow worker has not finished at second 12, an idle machine could start a second attempt. Suppose that attempt takes 10 seconds with no additional transfer delay. It finishes at second 22, eight seconds before the original attempt would finish. But this spends extra machine time. If both attempts contend for the same overloaded storage, the copy may not help. Nor can two successful attempts both add the same contribution to the final answer: the system must accept one result for that task.

Failure introduces a related uncertainty. A coordinator sends a task, then hears nothing. The worker may have stopped, the network may be delayed, or the reply may have been lost after successful execution. A timeout says how long the coordinator is willing to wait; by itself it does not prove which event happened. Retrying a pure calculation can be harmless if the system accepts only one result. Retrying an instruction to increment a counter is different: two executions change the state twice unless duplicate requests are recognized or another rule prevents duplicate effects.

The original MapReduce paper, published at OSDI 2004, makes the storage boundary concrete. Its map tasks produce intermediate files on worker-local disks. Section 3.3 says completed map tasks are rerun when their worker fails because those files become inaccessible. Completed reduce tasks, which combine intermediate results into final output, need not be rerun: their output is in a global file system. Finishing the calculation is therefore not the same as leaving a result that survives the specified failure.

The same section describes rules for accepting task outputs despite duplicate attempts. For deterministic task functions—ones that give the same outputs for the same inputs—the paper promises the result of a failure-free sequential execution. It describes weaker guarantees otherwise. Recovery also has a control limit: the implementation described in this 2004 paper aborts the job if its master coordinator fails. Section 3.6's backup attempts address slow workers, not that coordinator failure. Ask which component can fail and which result survives; the label fault-tolerant does not settle either question.

Saving progress changes the amount of work a failure destroys. Suppose a job pauses for two seconds to save a complete restartable state after every 60 seconds of useful calculation. With no failures, saving occupies 2/62, or about 3.2%, of elapsed time. If a failure is equally likely anywhere within a calculation interval, it loses an average of 30 seconds of calculation. Saving after every 20 seconds raises the no-failure saving fraction to 2/22, about 9.1%, but cuts that conditional average loss to 10 seconds. Choosing between them requires the failure frequency and the cost of loading saved state. These averages exclude failures during saving and assume earlier saves survive.

A saved state, or checkpoint, must be a state from which the job can actually continue. In a multi-worker calculation, independently saved files might describe different steps. Restarting one worker before it sent an update while restarting another after it received that update can repeat an effect. A recovery design must say which updates are already included, which remain to be delivered, and where that information survives. Saving more bytes is not automatically saving a usable restart point.

Two recent training systems show different ways to pay for recovery. Checkmate (NSDI 2026) starts from a fact about data-parallel training: workers already send each update's gradients through the network. Its network switch copies those gradients to separate CPU machines, which apply the updates to a shadow model. In the paper's tested setup, that kept a recovery copy current every training step with throughput comparable to its ideal no-checkpoint baseline. The pause was avoided, not made free: the design needs a shadow cluster, network support, and reliable delivery of each update exactly once. Its result is for the evaluated training and network setup, not every training job or every kind of failure.

LLMTailor (SC Workshops 2025) makes a different trade: instead of copying every model layer at every checkpoint, it combines selected layers and their optimizer state from partial checkpoints to form a state that can resume training. The authors report lower checkpoint storage and time in their tested language-model tasks. But a file that loads is not automatically an identical recovery. In their filtered Qwen2.5-7B fine-tuning example, several reported benchmark scores were lower than after ordinary checkpointing. The result depends on which layers are selected, when their states were saved, and what quality test is used. These two papers turn the general recovery question into a concrete one: did the design reduce copying, reduce what it saves, or reduce lost work—and what added resources or changed results came with that choice?

Where this shows up

  • Training frontier models depends on fast links between accelerators.
  • Inference services depend on routing requests to available memory and compute.
  • High-performance computing depends on storage and networks that keep processors fed.

Work it through

A fixed job has 12 seconds of sequential preparation and 72 seconds of divisible calculation. Four workers add an 8-second exchange after calculation; eight workers add a 16-second exchange. Assume equal worker speeds, even division, and no overlap. Which finishes first? How much can the eight-worker exchange take before eight workers cease to be faster?

Read the reasoning

Four workers finish in 12 + 72/4 + 8 = 38 seconds. Eight finish in 12 + 72/8 + 16 = 37 seconds, just one second earlier. With eight workers, preparation and calculation already take 21 seconds. An exchange shorter than 17 seconds beats the four-worker case; 17 seconds ties it. Doubling the machines saved nine seconds of calculation but spent eight of them on extra communication. This calculation compares completion time, not cost or energy.

Sources and further reading

  • Dean and Ghemawat, MapReduce (OSDI 2004), sections 3.3 and 3.6 — recovery and backup tasks
  • Checkmate (NSDI 2026): gradient multicast to CPU shadow nodes for per-iteration checkpointing; paper-reported evaluation and scope
  • LLMTailor (SC Workshops '25 / PDSW '25): partial layer and optimizer-state checkpoint merging
  • Author preprint of LLMTailor: evaluation details, including task-specific results after filtered recovery
  • NSDI 2026 research synthesis — coordination and recovery themes
  • Checkmate source-grounded mechanism, result boundaries, and assumptions
  • LLMTailor evaluation setup, baseline boundary, results, and limitations

Physical limits

10. A Calculation Needs Wires, Power, and Time to Settle

Prerequisites: timing, memory, and topology. Connect an abstract operation to a physical implementation without confusing a model with a manufactured chip.

Review first: Start · Memory · Topology

Key concepts: Power · Energy · Physical placement · Physical routing

Imagine adding two stored numbers. In a chip, their zeros and ones are represented by electrical signals. Small circuits combine those signals, wires carry the intermediate results, and storage circuits capture the answer. Each part takes up space, needs energy, and takes time to respond. To understand whether a proposed chip can perform the addition at the promised rate, follow that physical path.

Separate power from energy first. Power is the rate of energy use, measured in watts; one watt is one joule per second. Energy is the accumulated use over time. In a teaching example, a device using 100 watts for two seconds consumes 200 joules. A faster device using 150 watts for one second consumes 150 joules. The faster device has higher power but lower energy for that task. Which one is acceptable also depends on the available electrical and cooling capacity.

Keep the measurement boundary fixed. If the faster device additionally requires a host and memory consuming 80 watts during its one-second run, the included total becomes 230 joules. That does not prove it loses to the first device unless the first device's supporting components are included on the same basis. Idle time, startup, and cooling can matter as well. A chip-only energy number and a complete-system energy number answer different questions.

Changing a signal's voltage requires moving charge onto or off the connected wires and circuit inputs. Capacitance measures how much charge a structure stores for a given voltage difference. In a simplified circuit model, the energy used to charge and discharge it scales with capacitance and voltage squared. Holding the number of these changes and the capacitance fixed, reducing voltage from 1.0 to 0.8 volts reduces this energy to 0.8² = 0.64 of its former value. That is not a 36% whole-system energy guarantee. Leakage, the current that flows even when a circuit is not switching, and other components also consume energy. MIT's linked circuit lesson derives the charging model.

Lowering voltage can also make circuits respond more slowly. If the answer now arrives too late to be stored correctly, the machine needs more time per step. That longer run keeps supporting components powered for longer. Consider an invented example: switching uses 100 joules and supporting components use 20 watts during a one-second task. Total energy is 120 joules. Suppose lower voltage reduces switching energy to 64 joules but stretches the task to three seconds, with the same supporting power. The new total is 64 + 20 × 3 = 124 joules. Less energy per switch can coexist with more energy per completed task. These assumed durations illustrate the accounting; the voltage ratio alone does not predict them.

Heat also has a history. A short run may finish before the device reaches its sustained temperature. A longer run can require reducing its operating rate to remain within a temperature limit. Suppose, as a teaching model, a device processes 100 items per second for ten seconds, then 60 per second for the next fifty. It completes 4,000 items in a minute, averaging about 66.7 per second. A design sustaining 80 per second completes 4,800. The first device's peak rate ranks it first; sustained completed work ranks it second.

The pattern of activity matters along with the total. Concentrating switching in a small area can create a hot region even when average chip power looks acceptable. Many units switching together can also stress the network delivering power. A supply voltage specified at the board is not automatically the voltage available at every cell at every instant. These effects are reasons to examine placement, workload activity, and the power network rather than assuming a single nominal number captures all operation.

Many chips use a repeating electrical signal, the clock, to tell storage circuits when to capture their inputs. The time between successive capture events is a clock cycle. A result must reach its destination and remain stable for a specified interval before capture; this is the setup requirement. It must also remain stable for a specified interval after capture; this is the hold requirement. MIT's sequential-logic lesson explains both. A longer cycle can give a late result more time to arrive, but does not by itself stop the next result from arriving too soon after capture. Timing checks must examine both the latest and earliest possible changes.

A nanosecond is one billionth of a second. In a simplified teaching path, allow 0.6 nanoseconds for calculation, 0.3 for the wires, and 0.2 for storage-circuit delay and timing allowances. Its required interval is 1.1 nanoseconds, so it does not fit a 1-nanosecond cycle. Halving only the calculation delay changes the requirement to 0.8 nanoseconds, not 0.55. This example combines several contributions into one allowance; a real analysis separately handles clock arrival, setup and hold constraints, variation, and the actual paths. Passing this calculation establishes only that this simplified late-arrival limit is met.

Now check the earliest change. In a separate teaching model, both storage circuits receive the clock event at time zero. The destination needs its old input to remain unchanged until 0.08 ns afterward, but the new input can arrive at 0.03 ns. That is 0.05 ns too early. Moving the next clock event from time 1 ns to time 2 ns leaves this conflict unchanged: the problem occurs just after the current event. A slower clock alone does not satisfy this hold requirement.

Suppose an added delay element contributes exactly 0.06 ns in this idealized model. The earliest change moves to 0.09 ns and satisfies the 0.08-ns hold requirement. But delayed signals also arrive later. If the path's latest-arrival requirement was 0.8 ns, it becomes 0.86 ns, still within a 1-ns cycle. Both checks pass here. Real delay elements have ranges that depend on conditions, so a repair must be checked for both its earliest and latest effects, including differences in when the clock reaches each storage circuit.

Wires are not free edges in a diagram. They occupy routing space and add resistance and capacitance, which influence delay and energy. Moving connected blocks closer can shorten a path, but crowding blocks can make their wires detour or leave too little space for the power network. Adding more arithmetic units can therefore increase congestion without increasing useful completed work. Placement chooses locations; routing chooses the physical connections between them.

OpenROAD is software for turning a circuit description into a physical chip layout. Its documented sequence starts by setting the chip area and reserving space for major blocks and power connections: floorplanning. Placement assigns circuit locations. Clock distribution builds the connections that carry the clock to storage circuits. Routing chooses wire paths. Once those paths exist, the tools estimate their electrical effects and repeat timing and physical checks. A wire that takes a longer route than expected can change an earlier timing estimate. The documentation is a source for the flow, not evidence that any design in this course has completed it.

Different checks establish different things. Functional simulation runs a model on chosen inputs. A timing analysis asks whether modeled signal paths meet stated timing constraints. A design-rule check examines geometry against supplied manufacturing rules. A layout-versus-schematic check compares extracted connectivity with the intended circuit. Passing one does not imply passing the others: correctly connected circuitry can still be too slow, and legal geometry can implement the wrong logic. All depend on the models, constraints, rules, and exclusions used.

A post-layout simulation includes electrical effects derived from a particular layout; it is still a simulation. A chip measurement observes manufactured hardware, but only the sampled devices, workloads, and conditions were measured. Manufacturing variation means one successful chip does not establish the fraction of all manufactured chips that will meet the target. Report the evidence stage, tested conditions, and missing coverage rather than using the word validated without qualification.

For the DAC, DATE, VLSID, and circuit-oriented conference material, follow this chain: intended behavior, circuit representation, physical arrangement, predicted behavior, and measured behavior where available. Ask where the reported gain was established and which later stages might change it. A placement improvement can be valuable before fabrication, but its evidence should remain a placement result. A measured energy saving should preserve task quality, operating duration, and system boundary in its comparison.

Where this shows up

  • Device comparisons: distinguish peak power, task energy, and sustained throughput.
  • Architecture proposals: include data movement, layout, and power delivery alongside arithmetic units.
  • Research reading: identify whether a result comes from a model, a routed design, or measured hardware.

Work it through

Design A completes a fixed task in 4 seconds using 60 watts at the measured device. Design B takes 3 seconds at 75 watts. First compare device energy. Then include a common host consuming 20 watts throughout each run. Finally, suppose B needs 1 additional second of preparation at 50 watts total system power, while A has no additional preparation. Which has lower end-to-end energy, and which finishes sooner?

Read the reasoning

Device energy is 240 J for A and 225 J for B. Including the host gives (60 + 20) × 4 = 320 J for A and (75 + 20) × 3 = 285 J for B. B's additional preparation adds 50 J, taking its total to 335 J and its elapsed time to four seconds. A now uses less energy and they tie in completion time. This assumes equal accepted results and includes only the stated intervals and components; changing those boundaries changes the question.

Sources and further reading

  • MIT Computation Structures, Design Tradeoffs — charging energy and switching activity; lesson quantities are teaching examples
  • MIT Computation Structures, Sequential Logic — capture, setup, hold, and clock timing
  • OpenROAD documentation — physical implementation stages and final checks
  • DAC 2025 synthesis — representation, physical execution, and source-coverage limits
  • DATE 2025 synthesis — physical constraints and validation boundaries

Correctness

11. State the Promise Before Checking the Result

Prerequisites: numerical precision and recovery. Distinguish a design mistake, a damaged value, and an interrupted operation.

Review first: Numbers · Many Chips

Key concepts: Error detection · Geometric mean · Safety property · Specification

Before judging a result, write down what the system must do and which failures it must handle. For addition, should the answer stay an exact integer, wrap back to zero when the counter fills, or report that it ran out of room? Must a saved update survive a power loss? May a busy service refuse a request? Different rules can all be valid, but the chosen rule determines whether a design is correct. This written rule, including assumptions about inputs and the surrounding system, is called a specification.

A bit stores one 0 or 1. A counter stored in eight bits that cannot be negative can hold 0 through 255. After 255 increments from zero, it holds 255. On the next increment, a wrapping counter returns to zero. That follows the rule if counting is meant to wrap; it is wrong if the system must keep the exact number of events. A faster circuit or more tests cannot settle which behavior people need. The rule has to be chosen first.

A test runs the system on selected inputs and checks whether the result follows the written rule. For a simple increment operation that takes one eight-bit value as input, testing all 256 values covers every input. If it takes two eight-bit values, there are 65,536 pairs. Add timing, history, or multiple users and the possible cases grow far beyond the input values alone. A test suite can run every line of a program and still miss a harmful order of events.

A proof gives a reasoned demonstration that a rule holds under the stated assumptions. For a queue with a fixed capacity, one rule might be that its item count never falls below zero or rises above capacity. To prove this, show the rule is true at the start and remains true after every allowed operation. That still does not prove each waiting request will eventually be served. The first promise is a safety property: a forbidden event never occurs. The second is a progress property: something required eventually happens. A queue that refuses every request can keep its item count in range and still fail to serve users.

Every proof has limits set by its assumptions. A proof that assumes writes occur in program order does not cover a device that may save them in another order. A proof about a circuit design does not establish that the manufactured chip meets its timing at every temperature. A successful measurement on a few chips, in turn, does not try every possible input sequence. These methods answer different questions and can support each other without replacing each other.

A design mistake is different from a fault during operation. A counter built to the wrong rule can repeatedly produce the wrong result even when every component functions as designed. A correctly designed counter can instead suffer a changed bit in storage. Testing the rule addresses the first problem; checking or protecting stored information addresses the second. Say which failures the design handles: one changed bit, a stopped machine, a lost message, or something else. Protection against one is not automatically protection against the others.

Here is a small error-detection example. Add one extra bit so the total number of ones is even; this is called even parity. The data 1011 contains three ones, so append a one to produce 10111. Any single flipped bit makes the total odd, revealing that something changed. But the check does not identify which bit changed. Flipping two bits leaves the total even and can escape detection: changing the first two positions produces 01111, also with four ones. This check detects every single-bit flip in the protected group; it cannot correct the error or detect every possible corruption.

Multiple copies help only under a stated assumption about failures. Suppose three devices each return a wrong yes-or-no answer 1% of the time, and an error in one device does not affect the others. A working majority rule picks the answer given by at least two devices. The chance that this majority is wrong is 3 × 0.01² × 0.99 + 0.01³ = 0.000298, or 0.0298%. This teaching calculation assumes no shared cause of failure and a correctly working majority rule. A design bug or power loss could affect all three. Repeating the same faulty design does not fix its mistake.

An interrupted operation creates a third problem. Imagine storage that records a value and a separate flag saying that the value is ready. If the flag survives a crash but the new value does not, a reader can accept stale contents as the new result. Checking that both storage locations are readable will not detect that mistake. The recovery rules must preserve the relationship between the value and the flag, not merely the integrity of each location.

Crash consistency means that related stored information still agrees after a power loss. The textbook Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces shows this problem in its file-system chapter. Section 42.1 shows how a power loss can leave related records only partly updated; section 42.2 explains why repairing their structure can still lose the file contents the user expected. A system can pass a structural check and still return the wrong information. The counter, bit-check, and majority calculations in this lesson are separate teaching examples.

A check also needs a next step. If it fails, should the system retry, rebuild from a protected copy, report an error, or stop? Retrying helps only if the cause might have passed and the repeated operation is safe. Returning an old value may keep the service running but break a promise to provide fresh data. A complete evaluation says how many errors the check caught, how many it missed, how often it stopped healthy work, and what the system did next.

PMVerify (ASPLOS 2025) makes the assumptions concrete. A processor can issue several writes before all of them reach persistent memory, which keeps stored values after power loss. A crash may preserve some writes but not the rest. PMVerify asks whether a crash can leave a stored state that ordinary execution cannot reach under the specified memory rules. Excluding such crash-only states is the paper's robustness property. It is not a check of every application requirement: ordinary execution could itself reach an unwanted state. Developers still need to check ordinary behavior and recovery against the application's promise.

Of 26 example programs from the Persistent Memory Development Kit (PMDK), a toolkit for programs that use persistent memory, PMVerify found 12 robustness violations, proved one case robust, and could not decide on 13. The authors say most undecided cases used operations the tool did not support; one supported case timed out. A result the tool could not decide is not a pass, and the single positive result applies only to the program and storage rules it analyzed.

PoWER (OSDI 2025) takes a different route. For each storage operation, it states what must be true for safe recovery; it also sets rules for detecting damaged stored data. The authors used it to verify two example storage systems, checking the proofs with Verus and Dafny. Those proofs cover only the code and failure rules they include; they do not show that every storage system survives every failure. The papers illustrate different kinds of evidence: tests show what happened in selected runs; PMVerify checks which crash states its rules allow, but may leave some undecided; PoWER's proofs show that a rule follows from their assumptions. In every case, ask what behavior was promised, which failures were considered, and what remains unchecked.

Where this shows up

  • Datacenters use error correction and checkpointing to survive long training runs.
  • Chip design uses verification to catch mistakes before manufacturing.
  • Safety-critical devices need bounds on timing, power, and failure behavior.

Work it through

A service increments a counter for each request. It stores an even-parity bit with the counter and repeats an increment if its acknowledgement does not arrive. Does parity prevent a request from being counted twice? If all parity tests pass, what else must be established before claiming the service counts requests correctly?

Read the reasoning

No. Two valid increments can each produce a correctly encoded value, so the parity check can pass even when one request was counted twice. The service needs a way to recognize repeated requests and ensure that its record of a request and the counter cannot disagree after a crash. It also needs a rule for what happens when the counter fills and a promise about which acknowledged updates survive failure. Parity catches some changed bits; it does not identify repeated requests, ensure updates happen in the right order, or prove that an acknowledged update survives a crash.

Sources and further reading

  • OSTEP, chapter 42, sections 42.1–42.2 — interrupted updates and limits of consistency checks
  • PMVerify (ASPLOS 2025), sections 3–6 — modeled persistent-memory crashes, reachability search, and PMDK results
  • Focused full-paper review of PMVerify, including the one robust / 12 violation / 13 unknown result split and its limits
  • PoWER Never Corrupts (OSDI 2025): crash-consistency and media-corruption verification, plus two verified storage systems
  • PoWER source-grounded proof, corruption-model, evaluation, and guarantee boundaries
  • DATE 2025 research synthesis — design evidence and reliability; see its source-coverage limits

Security

12. Keeping Data Private Requires Controlling What Others Can Observe

Prerequisites: memory, queues, and correctness. Follow the connection from private work to shared state to an observable measurement.

Review first: Memory · Sharing · Correctness

Key concepts: False positive · Side channel · Threat model

Start with a specific promise: one user must not learn another user's private input. Denying direct reads is necessary, but it may not be sufficient. Private work changes the machine as it runs. It occupies queues, fills fast storage, and uses shared connections. If someone else can observe those changes, the observations may reveal information even when the private bytes remain inaccessible.

Before evaluating protection, name the attacker and their access. Can they run a program on the same machine, submit remote requests, choose inputs, measure execution time, or physically inspect a device? What remains trusted: the operating system, the chip, another service? This description is a threat model. It prevents a narrow result, such as protection against an ordinary remote user, from becoming an unsupported claim about protection against a hostile administrator.

Consider an invented two-case example. A service performs a short lookup when a private flag is zero and a longer lookup when it is one. Suppose the externally observed response times are always between 4 and 6 milliseconds for zero and between 9 and 11 for one. An observer can distinguish the cases without seeing either lookup's contents. The response time is carrying information the output was not intended to reveal. Such an unintended observable path is called a side channel.

Suppose unrelated background work adds a variable delay from zero to 20 milliseconds in either case. The possible observed ranges then become 4–26 milliseconds for zero and 9–31 for one. They overlap from 9 to 26, so a single observation in that region could come from either case. Overlap makes one reading less decisive; it does not erase a signal. If the background delay is random and behaves similarly in both cases, repeated measurements may still distinguish the timing distributions. A timing difference alone does not prove recovery of a whole secret. A convincing evaluation must connect the measured signal to the protected information, state how many observations were needed, and compare success against what could be guessed without the signal.

Encryption protects message contents, but the surrounding observations still need attention. Suppose an invented service sends one encrypted response for each request. An observer knows that private choice A always produces a visible transmission of 100 bytes and choice B produces 1,000 bytes. Counting bytes identifies the choice without decrypting anything. This conclusion depends on those exact lengths, the known two-choice mapping, and the ability to identify each response; unrelated traffic could complicate that inference.

Making both transmissions 1,000 bytes removes this particular size distinction. It adds 900 bytes to each short response, using filler called padding. But equal lengths do not hide a different response time, number of messages, or destination. The TLS 1.3 specification, which defines a protocol for protecting network communication, discusses these limits in appendix E.3: encrypted traffic can still expose lengths and timing, and padding is a tool for applications rather than a complete traffic-privacy guarantee. The 100-byte and 1,000-byte responses are teaching numbers, not measurements of TLS.

Shared storage creates another possible path. A cache keeps selected data nearby to avoid slower reads. One user's activity can change which entries remain there. Another user's own access times may then depend on the first user's activity. The relevant chain is private behavior, a change in shared state, a measurable consequence, and an inference. A defense can intervene at different points, but must explain which connection it removes.

Yarom and Falkner's FLUSH+RELOAD paper, published at USENIX Security 2014, gives a historical example. In their tested Intel setup, attacker and victim needed to share memory pages and the last-level cache, but not an execution core. The attacker removed a shared memory line from the cache, let the victim run, then read the line and timed that read: a quick read suggested the victim had used it. In the cross-virtual-machine experiment, the authors pinned the two virtual machines to the same physical processor and arranged for them to share pages. This shows why assigning separate cores is not, by itself, enough to eliminate shared-state observations. It does not establish that every present-day machine or application is vulnerable to this particular attack.

One defense is to avoid making observable choices depend on secrets. For example, the program might follow the same access pattern for both values of a private flag. This is stronger than merely delaying the reply: a fixed reply time does not erase changes left in shared storage. Even a source program with no secret-dependent branches needs an argument about the instructions and memory accesses it actually executes. The intended property is independence from the secret for the observations in scope, not identical timing under every unrelated system disturbance.

Another defense limits sharing. Suppose a fast store has 100 entries. With full sharing, one user may occupy 80 while another occupies 20. Splitting it into fixed regions of 50 entries prevents either from displacing entries in the other's region, but the first user's 80 entries of actively used data no longer fit in its region. Some capacity sits unused in the second region while the first user must fetch data from elsewhere. This teaching example exposes a capacity cost, not a universal performance penalty. Partitioning this store also says nothing about a shared memory connection or power supply; those require separate analysis if the attacker can observe them.

A third approach clears shared state between users. Clearing has a time cost and must cover the state relevant to the promised protection. Erasing one cache does not establish that every predictor, queue, buffer, or device state has been reset. Separating users in time can remove simultaneous competition while still leaving traces from the previous user. A proposal must identify what persists and what its reset actually changes.

Privacy is only one security obligation. Integrity means an unauthorized party cannot change protected data or actions. Availability means legitimate work can obtain service under the stated conditions. A system can hide stored contents while allowing another user to monopolize a shared queue. It can also remain responsive while returning corrupted results. These obligations need different tests; calling a design secure without naming the obligation hides the question that matters.

Detection results need a population as well as a percentage. Suppose 100 of 10,000 events are attacks. A detector catches 90% of attacks and falsely flags 1% of ordinary events. It produces 90 true alerts and 99 false alerts. Only 90/189, about 47.6%, of its alerts are actual attacks. These teaching numbers show why a high detection rate alone does not establish that an alert is reliable. Response cost matters too: stopping a user's work on every alert makes false alarms an availability problem.

For the DATE and architecture security themes, ask four concrete questions. What must remain private or unchanged? What can the attacker control and observe? Which shared resource carries the influence? What experiment or argument shows the defense removes that influence under those assumptions? Keep measured attack failure separate from a proof that no permitted attack can succeed. Also keep performance overhead attached to its tested workload: a defense's cost depends on which sharing benefits that workload used.

Where this shows up

  • Cloud AI services need isolation between users sharing accelerators.
  • Phones and laptops need to protect private data while running local models.
  • Critical systems need hardware that resists both software attacks and physical probing.

Work it through

In 20,000 events, 200 are attacks. A detector catches 95% of attacks and flags 2% of ordinary events. How many true and false alerts result? What fraction of alerts are genuine attacks? Would a fixed response delay alone establish that private inputs cannot leak through shared cache state?

Read the reasoning

There are 190 true alerts and 0.02 × 19,800 = 396 false alerts. Of 586 alerts, about 32.4% are genuine attacks. The detector also misses 10 attacks. These counts do not determine whether the detector is useful without the costs of missed attacks, investigation, and false intervention. A fixed response delay only constrains the response-time observation; it does not show that cache contents or another observable resource are independent of private inputs.

Sources and further reading

  • Yarom and Falkner, FLUSH+RELOAD (USENIX Security 2014), sections 2–4 — shared-page/cache requirements, attack steps, and tested GnuPG example
  • TLS 1.3 specification, appendix E.3 — traffic length, timing, and limits of padding
  • DATE 2025 synthesis, theme 3 — shared resources as performance and security state

13. Trace One Request Until Its Answer Is Accepted

Prerequisites: timing, memory, compilation, scheduling, and correctness. Combine the ideas without assuming that independently reported improvements combine.

Review first: Start · Memory · Compilers · Sharing · Correctness

Key concepts: Goodput · Service-level objective (SLO)

Teaching trace: one cold request, sequential stages, original calculation
StageDurationCumulative time
Wait for service8 ms8 ms
Validate and prepare input4 ms12 ms
Load model state20 ms32 ms
Calculate12 ms44 ms
Check and encode output3 ms47 ms
Deliver response3 ms50 ms

Consider an image-classification service. A person sends an image and expects a label within 50 milliseconds of arrival at the service. The requested model version and preprocessing rules are fixed. A completed response must also satisfy the application's quality requirements; speed does not excuse using a different task. The timings below are invented teaching numbers, not measurements of any named paper or a deployed service.

Begin with a cold request: the worker does not yet hold the model. It waits 8 milliseconds for its turn, spends 4 validating and preparing the image, 20 loading model state, 12 computing, 3 checking and encoding the output, and 3 delivering it. Assume these stages execute sequentially, with no retry or overlap. Completion takes 50 milliseconds, exactly meeting the stated deadline and leaving no margin for variation.

Now halve calculation time from 12 to 6 milliseconds. The operation is twice as fast, but the service finishes in 44 milliseconds. Its end-to-end speedup is 50/44, about 1.14 times, not two times. Calculation occupied only part of the original path. A claim about the faster operation remains useful, but it cannot substitute for a claim about the response the person receives.

Next consider retaining model state for later requests. If a request reaches the same worker while the right model version remains resident, remove the 20-millisecond load. Holding every other teaching assumption fixed gives 30 milliseconds with the original calculation, or 24 with the faster one. This saving depends on placement and reuse. A different model version, eviction, or routing to another worker can restore the load. Keeping the model also consumes memory that cannot simultaneously serve another purpose.

Suppose 80% of requests are warm and 20% are cold, with no other variation. With faster calculation, mean response delay is 0.8 × 24 + 0.2 × 44 = 28 milliseconds. But under a stricter 40-millisecond deadline, the cold fifth still misses. The mean cannot establish that every request meets the deadline. Report the warm/cold mix and the fraction meeting the promise, not just the average. Real queueing can make the cold requests delay others too; this two-point model does not include that effect.

Could image preparation overlap model loading? Only if the model is already known without reading the prepared image, separate resources can do both jobs, and concurrent loading does not slow preparation. Under those new assumptions, the 4- and 20-millisecond stages become a combined 20-millisecond interval rather than 24. A cold request with faster calculation then takes 8 + 20 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 40 milliseconds. If image inspection selects the model, the dependency prevents that schedule. Draw the dependency before taking the maximum of stage times.

Memory can invalidate an otherwise attractive schedule. Suppose a device has 16 GB available, the resident model uses 10 GB, and each simultaneously executing request needs 2 GB of private temporary state. Three requests fit in the remaining 6 GB under this simplified accounting. A fourth does not fit merely because execution units are idle. If a fused implementation needs 3 GB per request, only two fit. It may calculate each request faster while allowing fewer to run together. Real accounting must also include runtime metadata, buffers, and reserved space; these numbers deliberately omit them.

Changing representation can add another cost. Suppose compressed state halves cold loading from 20 to 10 milliseconds, adds 5 milliseconds of conversion, and leaves the faster 6-millisecond calculation unchanged. With the original sequential schedule, the cold request takes 8 + 4 + 10 + 5 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 39 milliseconds. Do not multiply a claimed load improvement by a calculation improvement. Replace the affected terms and include the added conversion. If both proposals change the same transfer, counting each saving separately can count the same removed work twice.

The compressed path is acceptable only if its changed numbers satisfy the same declared quality requirement. That requires task-relevant evaluation, not merely a smaller file or matching output shape. Keeping an older cached model also needs an explicit version rule. An answer can be timely and well-formed yet violate the requested model version. The result check must address the promise the caller actually relies on.

So far, the 8-millisecond queue has been fixed to isolate execution choices. In a real comparison it is an outcome, not a constant to assume. Faster service can reduce waiting; larger batches, additional conversions, or lower concurrency can increase it. Re-run the same arrival trace under each complete policy and record accepted, rejected, late, and failed requests. Keep all arrivals in the accounting so dropping difficult requests cannot masquerade as a service improvement.

Failure changes the accepted-result boundary too. If a worker stops before producing a label, retrying classification can repeat calculation without changing external state, provided the request's model and input are preserved. But a retry may miss the deadline or produce two replies unless delivery is controlled. Adding a billing counter or another external update requires stronger duplicate-handling rules. A recovery claim must cover those effects rather than relying on the calculation being repeatable.

The conference routes identify adjacent research questions. MLSys discusses representation, reusable state, and serving policy. OSDI includes loading newly added workers and arranging execution within a device. ASPLOS includes predicting future memory demand and changing where calculation meets data. Their local essays help locate mechanisms to investigate; they do not prove those mechanisms work together. A combined system needs a compatible implementation and a common workload test. The linked service trace explicitly records that its proposed composition tests have not been run.

Finish the comparison with a concrete account: the requested result and quality rule; the model and data versions; the arrival trace; the hardware and memory limits; the baseline; the full timing boundary; and the response after overload or failure. A new paper can change one part of that account. Your job as a reader is to explain which part changed, which assumption permits the change, and what must be checked again elsewhere.

Where this shows up

  • Compare a proposed serving optimization against arrival-to-accepted-response delay, not only operation runtime.
  • Choose between a busy worker with resident state and an idle worker that must load it.
  • Design a common workload test before claiming separately developed mechanisms combine.

Work it through

A different worker has an already resident model. Its queue is 18 ms, preparation 4, calculation 6, and checking plus delivery 6. A second worker is idle but must load the model for 20 ms; its preparation, calculation, and checking plus delivery take 4, 6, and 6 ms. Use sequential execution. Which worker finishes first, and which meet a 35-ms deadline? What changes if the idle worker can overlap preparation with model loading under the stated independence assumptions?

Read the reasoning

The busy warm worker finishes in 18 + 4 + 6 + 6 = 34 ms. The idle cold worker needs 0 + 4 + 20 + 6 + 6 = 36 ms. Only the warm worker meets 35 ms, despite its queue. With valid preparation/loading overlap, the cold worker takes 0 + max(4, 20) + 6 + 6 = 32 ms and becomes the faster choice. Idle versus busy is not enough information: state location and dependencies determine the comparison.

Sources and further reading

  • Cross-conference service traces — teaching constructions, not measured combinations
  • Proposed common-workload composition test — specification, not a completed experiment

14. Follow an Update Through a Crash and a Retry

Prerequisites: correctness and multi-machine recovery. Define what a success reply means, then check every interruption point.

Review first: Many Chips · Correctness

Key concepts: Atomicity · Durability

Crash cases under the teaching model's atomic-publication and persistence assumptions
InterruptionAuthoritative snapshotRetry of R
Before candidate is durableOld: A 10, B 5Execute the move
Candidate durable, not publishedOld: A 10, B 5Execute the move
During atomic publicationOld or new, never halfInspect completion record
Published, reply missingNew: A 7, B 8; R recordedReturn recorded result
Success acknowledgedNew: A 7, B 8; R recordedReturn recorded result

Consider a small inventory service with two locations. It holds 10 items at A and 5 at B. Request R asks to move three items from A to B. The required new state is A = 7 and B = 8. The total must remain 15, readers must not observe half a move, and once success is acknowledged the move must survive the specified failure. This is a teaching model, not production database code or a claim about a conference system.

Name the failure first. Assume a single server can lose power between persistence steps, losing all ordinary memory. Previously confirmed durable storage survives. There is only one writer, readers are paused during an update and during recovery, and there are no malicious writes or later media corruption. Real services may need to handle concurrent writers, disk loss, and replicas; the procedure here establishes nothing about those additional cases.

The tempting implementation writes A = 7 and then B = 8. If only the first write survives, the total becomes 12. Reversing the order permits a total of 18 instead. Keeping readers paused during normal execution does not fix the stored state after a crash. The missing property is an all-or-nothing transition that recovery can interpret, often called atomicity.

Use fresh storage rather than overwriting the only good copy. Keep an old snapshot with A = 10 and B = 5. Prepare a new snapshot containing A = 7, B = 8, request identifier R, its exact operation, and its successful result. Keep completion records for earlier requests too. The new snapshot is a candidate, not yet the published state. Readers must continue using the old snapshot until publication.

Now make two explicit storage assumptions. First, a persistence operation can confirm that every byte of the new snapshot has reached storage that survives the modeled power loss. Second, publishing a reference to that snapshot is itself an atomic durable operation: after a crash, recovery sees either the old reference or the new reference, never a damaged mixture. These are strong assumptions, not properties to infer from an ordinary assignment or file write. A real design must show how its storage interface supplies them.

The server first persists the complete candidate and waits for confirmation. Only then does it publish the new reference and wait for that operation's durable completion. It then permits readers and sends success. A crash before publication leaves the old reference authoritative; an unused candidate can be ignored. A crash after publication leaves the new reference authoritative, and the complete candidate is available because persistence preceded publication. If the publication was interrupted, its atomicity assumption limits recovery to those same two cases.

Durability and atomicity answer different questions. Atomicity says recovery does not expose a half-move. Durability says a move already acknowledged as successful remains present after the modeled failure. Before an acknowledgement arrives, either old or new state can be possible. After a valid acknowledgement, only the new state is permitted. Publishing and replying before persistence finishes could preserve normal reads but violate that durability promise after power loss.

Now suppose publication succeeds, but the reply is lost. The caller cannot distinguish this from a request that never completed, so it retries using the same identifier R. If the service blindly executes the move again, A becomes 4 and B becomes 11. The total is still 15, yet the requested operation happened twice. Checking only the total misses the error. Recovery must retain enough information to distinguish a repeated request from a new move.

Because the successful result for R is stored in the same published snapshot as the changed inventory, a retry finds that completion record and returns the recorded result without moving anything again. The identifier must be unique within a stated client or service scope, and the service must reject reuse of R for a different operation. This combines request identity and state change in one recovery decision. Storing them separately without an ordering or atomicity rule would reopen the same partial-update problem.

Keeping completion records has a cost. Removing R too early allows a delayed retry to look new. A real service needs a retention rule, such as an agreed retry lifetime or a protocol confirming which requests a client will never repeat. Our small model retains all records and does not claim unbounded practical scalability. Similarly, old snapshots cannot be reclaimed while a reader or the recovery procedure still needs them.

For a separate timing example, assume preparation costs 1 ms, candidate persistence 4 ms, durable publication 2 ms, and reply delivery 1 ms, all sequential. Success arrives after 8 ms. Improving preparation to 0.5 ms changes this to 7.5 ms, not 4 ms. Replying after preparation alone would appear faster by changing the promise. Grouping several updates into one persistence operation can share cost, but adds waiting and requires a defined order and completion record for every grouped request.

OSTEP's crash-consistency chapter provides the foundational connection: related persistent structures can disagree after an interrupted update, and a structural repair need not restore the intended contents. Our snapshot publication and retry example is a separate simplified derivation with its own explicit assumptions. In the conference material, F2FSJ and WOFS address durable-state organization, while checking and replay papers address different parts of the evidence. These should not be treated as interchangeable recovery mechanisms.

To evaluate a real proposal, interrupt execution at each persistence boundary and inspect the recovered state before serving new work. Repeat interruptions during recovery itself. Test lost replies and duplicate requests as well as power loss. Record the storage guarantees required, the normal execution cost, the restart cost, and any faults outside the model. Passing these selected tests is evidence for those cases, not a proof of all concurrent histories or all possible storage failures.

Where this shows up

  • Storage services: distinguish a returned write call from an acknowledged durable state change.
  • Request APIs: preserve identity and completion information across retries and crashes.
  • Paper evaluation: check interrupted operations and recovery costs alongside normal write throughput.

Work it through

A proposed variant publishes the new inventory first and writes the completion record for R afterward. Another variant persists R's completion record first and updates inventory afterward. Give a crash point that breaks each variant. Why is a total-items check insufficient?

Read the reasoning

In the first variant, crash after inventory changes but before R is recorded. A retry can move the three items again because R looks new. In the second, crash after R is recorded but before inventory changes. A retry returns success even though the move never happened. Both can preserve the total of 15 while violating the operation's meaning. The inventory and completion record need one coordinated recovery rule; this lesson's single published snapshot supplies one only under its stated storage and serialization assumptions.

Sources and further reading

  • OSTEP, chapter 42, sections 42.1–42.2 — partial persistence and limits of structural repair
  • Cross-conference durable-state trace — related mechanisms, not a tested combined stack
  • OSDI subthemes — crash consistency, protocols, debugging, and replay

15. Follow a Training Update to an Accepted Model

Prerequisites: dependencies, numerical precision, coordination, and recovery. Separate the time for one update from the time required to reach the target quality.

Review first: Dependencies · Numbers · Many Chips

Key concepts: Parameter server · Pseudo-gradient · Stale update

Baseline teaching timeline for one synchronous update
EventTime from step startCondition for continuing
Prepare inputs0–8 msAll assigned inputs ready
Worker calculation8–48 msEvery contribution ready; three workers finish at 32 ms
Exchange and combine48–60 msCombined contribution available
Apply and check update60–64 msRequired workers have accepted the next version

Training repeatedly changes a model using examples. In this simplified synchronous procedure, four workers start each step from the same model version, process separate portions of a batch, combine their update contributions, and apply one agreed update. The next step uses the resulting version. This is one teaching procedure, not a claim that every training algorithm must follow it. All timings below are invented.

Define the final result before timing the loop. Suppose the job must reach a specified quality threshold on held-out evaluation data, using a stated evaluation rule. The threshold, dataset, and rule remain fixed across the compared methods. Completed steps are intermediate work; the accepted model is the result. Faster steps do not necessarily reduce time to that result if the algorithm needs more of them.

For one baseline step, input preparation takes 8 ms. The workers then calculate in parallel for 24, 24, 24, and 40 ms. After all contributions are ready, exchange and combination take 12 ms; applying and checking the update takes 4 ms. Assume these stages are sequential except for the workers' parallel calculation, no other contention, and no hidden setup. Step time is 8 + max(24, 24, 24, 40) + 12 + 4 = 64 ms.

The first three workers each wait 16 ms for the fourth. Their mean calculation time is 28 ms, but using 28 in the step equation would predict 52 ms, which is not a possible completion time under this schedule. The next operation requires every contribution. This is why a mean device-utilization measure can miss the worker that determines progress.

Imagine redistributing work so all four calculations take 28 ms, with unchanged inputs and accepted update semantics. If moving the work adds a 5-ms non-overlapped preparation cost, the step becomes 8 + 5 + 28 + 12 + 4 = 57 ms. The ideal calculation saving was 12 ms; seven remain after movement. If redistribution instead costs 15 ms, total time becomes 67 ms and the change loses. A balanced assignment is not automatically a faster assignment.

What does preserving the update require? In a separate numerical example, three workers each process one training example and report an average contribution of 2. The fourth processes nine examples and reports an average contribution of 10. Suppose all contributions were calculated from the same model version, every example should have equal weight, and the required combined value is their mean. Averaging the four worker reports gives (2 + 2 + 2 + 10)/4 = 4. But the mean over the twelve examples is (1 × 2 + 1 × 2 + 1 × 2 + 9 × 10)/12 = 8. The first calculation gave a one-example worker as much influence as the nine-example worker. Changing the assignment therefore requires checking how contributions are combined, not just where they are calculated. These numbers are invented; another training rule may deliberately use different weights.

Now examine a separate overlap proposal on the original assignment. Suppose the first exchange chunk becomes ready at time 28 ms, twenty milliseconds into the worker-calculation interval. It transfers from 28 to 34 while independent calculation continues. A second chunk is available only when all workers finish at time 48 and transfers from 48 to 54. The final update then runs from 54 to 58. Six milliseconds of transfer are hidden; the other six remain on the completion path. This requires the stated chunk readiness, sufficient buffers, and resources that can transfer without slowing calculation.

Taking max(40, 12) for the entire calculation-and-exchange interval would give 8 + max(40, 12) + 4 = 52 ms for the step, but that optimistic bound is not achieved by this schedule: the final transfer cannot start before time 48, so the step actually takes 58 ms. Calling an exchange asynchronous does not make its data available earlier. Neither may we automatically combine the 57-ms balanced schedule with this overlap plan: redistribution changes when chunks are ready, so the combined dependency timeline must be constructed again.

A representation change adds a different trade. Starting from the baseline with no overlap, suppose compression cuts exchange from 12 to 6 ms but encoding and decoding add 3 ms. The resulting step takes 8 + 40 + 3 + 6 + 4 = 61 ms. If the baseline reaches target quality in 1,000 steps, it uses 64 seconds of step execution. If compression requires 1,200 steps to reach the same target, it uses 73.2 seconds. The step is faster but the accepted model arrives later. Actual step counts must be measured, not assumed from this example.

Holding those illustrative step times constant, compression wins on step-execution time only when its required count is below 64,000/61, about 1,049.18 steps. Thus 1,049 steps finish slightly sooner and 1,050 finish later than the 1,000-step baseline. Real comparisons also include startup, periodic evaluation, checkpoints, and any failure recovery. These may occur at different frequencies after the procedure changes.

Memory can change the feasible schedule. Input prefetching needs storage for a future batch; overlapping exchange needs buffers for data already produced; training also holds model parameters and other update state. A policy that uses all free memory for larger batches may remove the space an overlap plan assumed. Define which values must coexist, not just the largest individual array. Changing batch size can also change the sequence of updates and the number needed to reach target quality.

A stopped worker raises a state question before a speed question. If some workers applied the new update while another still holds the old version, restarting them without reconciliation does not resume the assumed synchronous procedure. A saved restart point needs the model version and all procedure-specific state required to continue, such as update history, random-generator state, and input position when those affect the promised continuation. The exact requirement depends on whether recovery promises identical replay or only an acceptable resumed training run.

The local conference trace links different research questions: WLB-LLM discusses assignment, FSMoE discusses coordinated expert work, ZEN discusses communicated updates under a quality condition, and communication papers examine paths or scheduling. Those are leads to separate mechanisms. This tutorial's schedules are not measurements of those systems and do not establish that the systems compose. A combined proposal needs a shared implementation, workload, quality rule, and failure policy.

A complete final experiment reports time to the accepted quality target, the quality trajectory, resource use, and failed or incomplete runs under stated stopping rules. Include randomness and repeated trials where they affect the conclusion. Then use the step timeline to explain the observed difference. A faster isolated operation helps explain a result, but does not replace the result itself.

Where this shows up

  • Distributed training: explain a step through its slowest dependencies and required exchanges.
  • Algorithm/system comparisons: measure time to the same quality target, not only time per step.
  • Recovery design: state whether saved information supports identical replay or another permitted continuation.

Work it through

Starting from the 64-ms baseline step, halve only the slowest worker's calculation from 40 to 20 ms. The other workers still take 24 ms. What is the new step time? If this modified procedure takes 1,300 steps to reach the same quality target while the baseline takes 1,000, which has lower step-execution time?

Read the reasoning

The new maximum worker time is 24 ms, not 20. The step takes 8 + 24 + 12 + 4 = 48 ms. At 1,300 steps it consumes 62,400 ms, or 62.4 seconds, versus the baseline's 64 seconds. It wins by 1.6 seconds on the stated boundary, not by the slowest worker's twofold calculation speedup. Additional preparation, evaluation, or recovery differences could reverse that narrow result and must be counted if the claim concerns the entire job.

Sources and further reading

  • Distributed-training service trace — separate paper mechanisms and explicit composition limits

Worked science

16. Finish a Scientific Calculation With a Result You Can Check

Prerequisites: numerical precision, dependencies, memory, and coordination. Follow a small heat-flow calculation from physical assumptions to checked output, then account for a larger distributed solve.

Review first: Dependencies · Numbers · Memory · Many Chips

Key concepts: Discretization · Residual · Iteration

Suppose you want the settled temperature along a rod whose ends are held at 0 and 90 degrees. Assume uniform material, no heat produced inside, no heat escaping through the sides, and enough time to settle. These assumptions define the problem being solved. A real rod losing heat to the surrounding air would require a different model. Computing the wrong model more accurately does not repair that mismatch.

Represent the rod by four equally spaced points: the two known ends and two unknown interior temperatures, u and v. In this simplified balance model, each interior temperature equals the average of its two neighbors. Therefore 2u − v = 0 and 2v − u = 90. The values u = 30 and v = 60 satisfy both equations. We have replaced a continuous object with a finite set of values; that replacement is called discretization. This special example agrees with the linear temperature profile under the stated ideal assumptions. It does not show that four points suffice for other heat problems.

For a tiny system, we can solve the equations directly. To illustrate repeated approximation, start at u = 0, v = 0. In each round, compute the next u as old v divided by two, and the next v as (old u + 90) divided by two. Both use the old values, not a neighbor already changed during this round. The first guesses are (0, 45), (22.5, 45), (22.5, 56.25), and (28.125, 56.25). Each round is an iteration. Updating in place would define a different sequence and must not be silently substituted when comparing implementations.

How do we decide when to stop without knowing the exact answer? Put a candidate back into the equations. Define its two residuals as 0 − (2u − v) and 90 − (2v − u): the amounts by which the candidate misses the required balances. At (28.125, 56.25), these are 0 and 5.625. For this lesson, the residual size is the larger absolute value. Our explicit rule accepts a solve when that size is at most 0.1 degree in these scaled balance equations. Merely reaching a time limit is not acceptance.

In exact arithmetic, this particular iteration halves that residual size every round, starting from 90. After nine rounds it is 90/512, about 0.176, which fails. After ten it is 90/1024, about 0.088, which passes. The tenth guess is (29.970703125, 59.94140625). This is a derivation for these two equations and this initial guess, not a general convergence rate. A larger problem or another update rule needs its own analysis and measurements.

A small residual is not automatically a small error in the answer. Consider a separate pair of scaled equations: u = 1 and 0.000001v = 0.000001. The exact answer is (1, 1), but the candidate (1, 0) has a largest residual of only 0.000001 while v is wrong by one whole unit. Multiplying the second equation by a million leaves its exact answer unchanged but changes that raw residual to one. Equation scaling and sensitivity therefore matter when translating an equation check into an accuracy claim. A residual test needs justification for the problem and quantity you care about.

The PETSc solver documentation linked below gives a practical reason to record the stopping rule precisely. Its default test compares a residual norm with the larger of two limits: a relative limit based on a reference residual, and an absolute limit. For an invented example, let the reference residual be 100, the relative tolerance be 0.01, and the absolute tolerance be 0.1. The two limits are 1 and 0.1, so a residual norm of 0.5 passes the test. It is below the relative limit even though it is above the absolute limit. These numbers explain the rule; they are not PETSc's default settings or measurements from a paper.

Passing that test does not mean the answer is within 0.5 of the exact answer. A residual measures how much the candidate misses the stated equations; the relation between that miss and the answer's error also depends on the equations. PETSc's residual norm may be preconditioned—transformed before measurement by an auxiliary calculation intended to make iteration easier—or otherwise depend on solver type and settings, so check which quantity was tested. By default, reaching the iteration limit is reported as failure, not convergence. The largest-component, at-most-0.1 rule in this lesson is a separate teaching rule, not PETSc's default. Interpret a success flag using the configured test and the recorded termination reason.

Now move to a larger, hypothetical heat problem split across four workers. Each owns part of the grid and keeps copies of neighboring edge values needed for its next calculation. Those copies are often called a halo. Fresh edge values must arrive before dependent boundary work can use them. Sending fewer values by reusing an older edge can reduce traffic, but changes which mathematical update is performed. Overlapping exchange with independent interior work can preserve the update, provided the old and new values remain distinct and the boundary waits for the right round.

Invented larger-solve timing model: stages are sequential, with no overlap or failures.
StageElapsed timeWhat must be established
Read and prepare0–2 sInputs, grid, equations, and worker assignments are ready
1,000 update rounds2–12 sEach round uses the required neighbor values and checks the stated stopping rule
Independent final equation check12–13 sThe returned values meet the required equation tolerance
Write accepted output13–14 sResults and interpretation settings are available to the next consumer

Use the invented sequential timing model in the table. Reading and preparing the problem takes 2 seconds. Each of 1,000 iterations takes 5 ms of local work, 3 ms of neighbor exchange, and 2 ms to combine the workers' residual summaries and decide whether to continue. Thus the loop takes 10 seconds. A final independent equation check costs 1 second and writing the accepted result costs another. End-to-end time is 14 seconds. The two-point example establishes the meaning of the checks; it does not predict this larger problem's 1,000-iteration count.

Compare two separate changes, keeping the same problem and acceptance rule. Change A halves only the 5-ms local work. Its loop takes 7.5 seconds and the whole job 11.5 seconds. Change B adds 1 second of preparation but, by a stipulated mathematical improvement, reaches acceptance in 600 iterations at the original 10 ms each. Its whole job takes 3 + 6 + 1 + 1 = 11 seconds. B wins despite having no faster iteration. Establishing that it actually needs only 600 iterations would require evidence; here that count is a teaching assumption.

A third proposal uses fewer bits, reducing local work to 3 ms, but needs 1,400 iterations to pass the same check. Its loop takes 1,400 × (3 + 3 + 2) ms = 11.2 seconds, giving 15.2 seconds overall. It loses to the baseline. If rounding instead prevents it from passing the threshold at all, report a failed solve rather than a fast completion. Do not multiply the gains from these proposals: changing representation or the mathematical method may also change communication, iteration count, or the cost of checking.

Finally, separate equation accuracy from scientific adequacy. A small equation residual says nothing by itself about omitted heat loss, uncertain boundary temperatures, or whether the chosen grid resolves changes that affect the reported quantity. For a real study, examine those assumptions, compare resolutions where appropriate, and check against analytic results or observations available for the problem. Agreement between two grids alone is not a proof of physical truth. Save the input conditions, model, grid, numerical settings, termination reason, final checks, and output together so another reader can tell what was actually established.

This is the question to carry into the SC papers: what accepted result did the measured work produce? A faster data-transfer operation, a smaller compressed field, and a faster iterative solver affect different parts of the job. Compare them only after fixing the physical question, the permitted numerical error, and the timing boundary. Their individual evaluations are not evidence that a combined workflow has been run.

Where this shows up

  • Numerical methods: compare time to the same justified acceptance condition, not just time per iteration.
  • Distributed simulation: distinguish a legal overlap from an update using a different round's data.
  • Scientific reporting: separate solving the chosen equations from establishing their adequacy for the real question.

Work it through

In the 14-second baseline, suppose checking costs 2 ms and the remaining work costs 8 ms per iteration. A new schedule checks only every tenth iteration. Assume this does not change the updates, the candidate remains acceptable once it first passes, and the first passing iteration is 996. At which iteration does the schedule discover success? What is total job time? Why would a maximum-iteration stop at 990 not count as the same result?

Read the reasoning

Success is discovered at iteration 1,000, after four extra updates. There are 1,000 × 8 ms = 8 seconds of update and exchange work, plus 100 × 2 ms = 0.2 seconds of checks. Adding the unchanged 4 seconds outside the loop gives 12.2 seconds. A limit at 990 stops before the first passing candidate, so it is a failure under the stated rule, not an equivalent faster solve. If acceptability does not persist, or checks change the update process, the supplied assumptions no longer justify this calculation.

Sources and further reading

  • PETSc: KSPConvergedDefault, Notes — stopping thresholds, residual configuration, and iteration-limit handling (consulted 21 September 2026)
  • Templates for the Solution of Linear Systems: Stopping Criteria — further reading on accuracy, progress, and work limits
  • SC 2025 synthesis — scientific workflows and numerical-method leads, with source-depth limits
