Practice across lessons

Try these before opening the reasoning. Write down your timing boundary, assumptions, and acceptance condition as well as your answer. All scenarios are invented teaching examples.

1. Choose between a faster operation and a shorter path

An invented service has sequential stages: 6 ms waiting, 8 ms reading, 4 ms computing, and 2 ms delivering. A costs nothing to prepare and halves computing time. B skips the read and computation on a valid cache hit, but always adds a 1-ms lookup. Half the requests hit. Assume the waiting and delivery times remain fixed, misses run the original read and computation, and neither change affects output quality.

Calculate the baseline, A, and B’s hit and miss times. Which has the lowest mean? Which has the most requests meeting a 19-ms deadline? What missing evidence would you ask for before predicting behavior under a burst?

Read the reasoning

Baseline is 20 ms. A takes 18 ms. B takes 9 ms on a hit and 21 ms on a miss, averaging 15 ms with equal counts. B wins on mean delay, but A meets the 19-ms deadline for every request under these assumptions; B meets it for only half, and the baseline for none. Before predicting burst behavior, inspect the arrival trace, shared-resource contention, cache hit pattern and validity, and how either change affects the queue. Fixed waiting was an assumption, not a measured consequence. Combining A with B requires a fresh calculation: misses would take 19 ms, hits 9, and the mean 14 if all other assumptions held.

Review if needed: Elapsed time · Valid reuse · Delay distributions

2. Compare time to the accepted result

An invented solver has 2 seconds of setup, takes 100 iterations at 20 ms each, and spends 1 second checking and saving its accepted answer. A lower-precision version needs 160 iterations at 10 ms each and has the same other costs. Both pass the same justified accuracy test. A third version returns in 2 seconds but fails that test.

Which valid version finishes sooner? What is the largest whole iteration count at which the lower-precision version is strictly faster? If conversion adds 0.6 seconds, what changes? Explain why the third version is not the winner.

Read the reasoning

The baseline takes 2 + 100 × 0.020 + 1 = 5 seconds. The lower-precision version takes 4.6 seconds, a saving of 0.4 seconds, not a twofold whole-job improvement. With no extra conversion, it is strictly faster at at most 199 iterations; 200 ties. With 0.6 seconds of conversion and 160 iterations, it takes 5.2 seconds and loses. Its strict-win limit is then 139 iterations; 140 ties. The third version fails the required result, so its time belongs in a failed-run report, not an equal-quality speed ranking. Check the accuracy rule’s adequacy separately from these timing calculations.

Review if needed: Representation error · Time to quality · Acceptance rules

3. Match a claim to the evidence that would support it

Three fictional reports say: “Our model preserves exclusive write permission”; “our device operation is twice as fast on the tested inputs”; and “our service has a lower average delay on the supplied request trace.” A proposal combines all three and claims a correct, twice-as-fast service that never misses a deadline.

Identify three unsupported steps in that conclusion. Describe the next check that could test each one. Then decide whether more repetitions of the same timing benchmark would fill all three gaps.

Read the reasoning

First, a model property is not automatically an implementation guarantee: inspect the modeled assumptions, omitted behavior, and evidence connecting the implementation to the model. Also check whether exclusive permission is the full correctness promise; it is not the same as correct data or eventual progress. Second, a faster device operation need not halve total service time: measure the complete path, including unchanged work, preparation, movement, and interference in the combined configuration. Third, a lower average does not bound the slowest requests: examine deadline misses and the load and failure conditions under which the deadline promise is intended. More runs can improve estimates for that benchmark population, but cannot supply a missing correctness argument or justify behavior outside its conditions. A finite trace with no misses does not prove that misses are impossible.

Review if needed: Correctness claims · Proof boundaries · Operation and service measurements · Changing capacity

Continue to a conference route

Follow one question across conferences

These connections are teaching interpretations of the course material, not a shared experiment or an official conference taxonomy. Choose a question, follow the worked explanation, then use the links to compare mechanisms and evidence.

  • Two improvements help separately. What happens together?
  • Preparation pays back. Does the prepared state stay valid long enough?
  • The worker is waiting. What is missing?
  • The representation is smaller. Is the result cheaper?
  • An action is possible. Is it allowed yet?
  • The proposed design wins. At which stage?
  • What does “success” mean in this system?

Two improvements help separately. What happens together?

Before combining reported gains, identify which work each change removes and what each requires. Two changes can remove the same transfer, compete for the same storage, or depend on incompatible formats. Their separate measurements do not establish the cost of using them together. A combined implementation needs its own valid schedule and evidence.

Use an original sequential job: movement takes 12 milliseconds and calculation takes 8, totaling 20. Change A halves movement, producing 14 milliseconds. Change B halves calculation, producing 16. If both retain exactly those effects when combined and add no other costs, the joint time is 6 + 4 = 10. Multiplying their whole-job speedups gives (20/14) × (20/16), about 1.79, whereas the joint speedup is 20/10 = 2. The separate ratios use the same original job but change different portions of it; they are not successive measurements of one evolving system.

Overlap can also produce overstatement. Suppose two different changes each remove the same six-millisecond transfer from a ten-millisecond job. Either gives four milliseconds. If their only effect is removing that one transfer, combining them still gives four, not ten divided by 2.5 squared. The saving can be counted only once. Any further effect needs a separate explanation.

Connect the paper readings by following the interfaces. FlashInfer divides execution work, BlitzScale changes worker readiness, the banked-memory example changes access conflicts, and LUT Tensor Core changes how arithmetic is represented and served. These are concrete cases for asking whether inputs, schedules, and storage assumptions remain compatible. Their inclusion in one course is not evidence that they were integrated or that their reported gains compose.

Reading path

  • Start with a complete time account
  • MLSys: dividing work
  • OSDI: making workers ready
  • FCCM: servicing accesses
  • ISCA: preparing and reading tables

Check the distinction

In the 20-millisecond job, suppose combining A and B requires an extra five-millisecond conversion that neither needs alone. What is the joint time? Which of the four choices is fastest under these assumptions?

Read the reasoning

The combined path takes 6 + 4 + 5 = 15 milliseconds. The original takes 20, A alone 14, and B alone 16. A alone wins. Both changes can reduce their own measured path in isolation, but that does not establish that using both is the best choice; the added interface work belongs in the joint comparison.

Preparation pays back. Does the prepared state stay valid long enough?

Many mechanisms pay once to make later work cheaper: a compiler builds an execution plan, a lookup method prepares a table, or a serving system loads state into a worker. The relevant reuse count is not every future request. It is the work that can use that particular prepared state before an input change, eviction, or other event makes it unusable.

Original teaching model: preparation costs 32 milliseconds and reduces each subsequent calculation from 7 to 4 milliseconds. For n compatible calculations, compare 7n with 32 + 4n. Ten uses still lose, at 70 versus 72; eleven first win, at 77 versus 76. Now suppose the state must be rebuilt after every eight calculations. Each complete group costs 32 + 8 × 4 = 64 milliseconds instead of 56. A stream of 80 calculations then costs 640 rather than 560. Counting all 80 as one reuse group would hide nine necessary preparations.

Lifetime is a correctness question as well as a cost question. A table derived from one set of values cannot be used for another merely because its memory address is unchanged. A plan depending on a shape needs that shape to remain appropriate. A loaded worker needs the state required by its assigned requests. State the condition that makes reuse legal, then identify who checks or enforces it.

Connect the LUT walkthrough to HPCA’s specialization example and DAC’s placement example. They expose three different limits: values changing, requests falling outside a supported fast path, and another user needing the storage. Reuse can fail because the state is wrong, because the operation is unsupported, or because keeping the state harms other work. Those need different responses, not one unexplained cache-hit target.

Reading path

  • Preparation and execution
  • ISCA: input-dependent tables
  • HPCA: supported and fallback requests
  • DAC: reuse and displaced data
  • OSDI: state and readiness

Check the distinction

Suppose preparation can safely happen before the first request arrives, but the accounting window includes that preparation. Have you removed its work? What changes if the user measures only arrival-to-completion delay?

Read the reasoning

The preparation work remains in the full cost account. Doing it earlier can remove it from a particular request’s waiting path if the needed state is known in advance, stays valid, and is still resident. Arrival-to-completion delay may therefore improve without reducing total work. State which boundary is being measured and include any prediction failures, rebuilding, or storage costs relevant to that boundary.

The worker is waiting. What is missing?

Distinguish four causes before choosing a fix: the input has not arrived; an earlier calculation has not finished; the required resource is occupied; or the worker is not yet ready to execute. All can appear as an idle arithmetic unit. A utilization graph alone cannot tell you which intervention will help.

Compare the FlashInfer and banked-memory teaching examples. Splitting one long calculation removes an uneven assignment only if the pieces can get their inputs. Requests to one memory bank remain serialized even when more execution workers are available. BlitzScale adds another boundary: a newly allocated worker cannot contribute arbitrary work before the needed model state arrives. These are different causes of waiting, not three names for the same bottleneck.

Make the comparison concrete. If a task needs 8 ms of bank service followed by 2 ms of computation, halving computation produces 9 ms, not 5. If a legal layout change instead halves bank service without preparation cost, the total is 6 ms. If creating that layout costs 4 ms for this single use, the total returns to 10. These invented sequential timings illustrate why the changed stage and the added work must both be named.

Reading path

  • Start with memory service
  • MLSys: divide ready work
  • FCCM: conflicting accesses
  • OSDI: partial readiness
  • NSDI: move state to capacity
  • HPCA: exposing independent work

Check the distinction

What observation would distinguish a dependency stall from contention for a resource?

Read the reasoning

For the stalled operation, record whether its required inputs and predecessor results are ready, then whether the execution resource can accept it. Ready inputs with a busy resource indicate contention at that boundary; a free resource with a missing required result indicates a dependency stall. Both can occur at different times. Use timestamps tied to the same operation rather than comparing unrelated utilization averages.

The representation is smaller. Is the result cheaper?

A smaller representation can mean fewer bits per value, fewer retained values, or less repeated metadata. Those changes have different consequences. Rounding changes represented values. Skipping an exactly zero contribution can preserve a calculation, while deliberately dropping a nonzero contribution needs an error allowance. Encoding repeated data may preserve every value but add decoding work.

Follow one value from producer to consumer. A compressed stored form saves transfer only while it remains compressed. If the next operation needs a larger form, conversion and temporary storage return to the account. A sparse form adds a way to locate retained entries. A layout padded to reduce conflicts can deliberately grow storage while reducing access time. Storage size is therefore not a sufficient ranking of execution cost.

Hold the data fixed and change only the connection. In an original example, 120 megabytes are already stored either unchanged or compressed to 60 megabytes. The compressed path needs 7 milliseconds of decoding and copying after transfer; the unchanged path needs neither. At 10 megabytes per millisecond, the paths take 12 and 13 milliseconds, so compression loses. At 5 megabytes per millisecond, they take 24 and 19 milliseconds, so compression wins. At 20, they take 6 and 10 milliseconds, so it loses by more. The compressed size did not change. The time saved by sending 60 fewer megabytes changed, while the added work stayed fixed. These sequential timings exclude the earlier creation of both stored forms; producing them during the measured job would require counting that work too.

The numerical lessons and scientific workflow supply the acceptance side of the comparison. Keep the required answer fixed, then count conversion, movement, and any extra repetitions. For physical computing proposals, also inspect the conversion between physical signals and represented numbers. The linked venue routes provide reading questions and source limits; they do not establish that all the proposed changes preserve the same accuracy.

Reading path

  • Rounding and range
  • Finding work that remains
  • Time to an accepted answer
  • ISCA: usable representations
  • MICRO: producer–consumer formats
  • VLSID: updates and conversion
  • SC: movement and numerical change

Check the distinction

A format halves transfer time from 12 to 6 ms but adds 4 ms of decoding and 3 ms of copying. Does it save time for one sequential use? In the 120-to-60-megabyte example, how much transfer time must compression save to be worthwhile?

Read the reasoning

No. The changed path takes 6 + 4 + 3 = 13 ms versus 12. With 7 ms of added work, it must save more than 7 ms of transfer time to finish sooner; saving exactly 7 produces a tie. At a connection rate of b megabytes per millisecond, it saves 60/b milliseconds. It wins when b is less than 60/7, about 8.57 megabytes per millisecond, under the stated assumptions. It may still save storage even above that rate. Ask whether the consumer can directly use the compact form and whether conversion can legally overlap other work; either would change this timing model.

An action is possible. Is it allowed yet?

Distinguish physical availability from permission. Bytes may be present in a cache after access permission has been revoked. A write may have reached a volatile buffer before it is durable. A partial result may be ready before its prerequisites for publication are satisfied. Executing early is permitted only when the required behavior allows that order.

Read the CXL permission example beside the durable-update lesson. The first follows rights to use one shared location; the second follows which inventory state and request-completion record may survive a crash. Both need intermediate states and messages, but their properties differ. Exclusive write permission does not make a multi-object update atomic, and a durable update does not supply a cache-coherence protocol.

Security introduces a further question: who can observe effects outside the intended output? Correct results can still expose private information through shared state. A sound cross-paper comparison states the protected property before examining the mechanism. Preserve the difference between a proof about a model, tests of selected executions, and measurements under an attacker model.

Reading path

  • ASPLOS: permission proof
  • OSDI-related durable state
  • Unintended observations
  • DATE: shared state and observation
  • OSDI: enforcement boundaries

Check the distinction

A request returned success before a crash, and only one writer ever held permission. Is that enough to establish durable completion?

Read the reasoning

No. The permission fact excludes particular conflicting accesses, not loss of volatile data. Inspect what the success reply promises, which required state reached durable storage, and how recovery distinguishes completed work from a retry. A property about access rights cannot replace a property about persistent state.

The proposed design wins. At which stage?

A design goes through different descriptions: intended behavior, an executable or circuit structure, physical placement and connections, and eventually measured operation if hardware exists. A result belongs to the stage that produced it. An early estimate can guide a decision without establishing what a later implementation will achieve.

Separate two questions when comparing design-search and chip papers. First, did the chosen candidate meet the required constraints at the evaluated stage? Second, what did finding and checking it cost? A method that tests fewer candidates can save search time even if its final circuit is no faster. A measured efficient circuit does not establish that the method used to find it is cheap or reliable.

Use an invented comparison with a required clock interval of 1 nanosecond. Before placement and wiring are included, design A has an estimated path delay of 0.7 ns and B has 0.8 ns. After those details are included, the estimates become 1.1 ns and 0.95 ns. A looked faster in the early check but fails the later timing requirement; B passes that check. Neither estimate establishes how a manufactured chip behaves. The example shows why each result needs its design stage and included effects attached.

Suppose a separate energy estimate gives A 2 picojoules per operation and B 3 under the stated conditions. Choosing A on energy alone would accept a design that misses the clock requirement. Allowing A to run more slowly changes that requirement and calls for a new comparison of completion time and energy at the allowed operating point. A sound review first records which candidates satisfy all mandatory conditions, then compares the costs of those candidates.

The DAC and ICCAD routes discuss representations, estimation, and search; DATE connects candidate validity to physical constraints; ISSCC discusses the boundary of chip measurements. These are entry points into the current course drafts, not claims of equally deep source coverage. Follow each route’s evidence notice before comparing results. At every stage preserve workload, output quality, operating conditions, and included components.

Reading path

  • Physical stages and checks
  • DAC: estimates that drive decisions
  • ICCAD: finding and checking a result
  • DATE: physical constraints
  • ISSCC: limits of chip evidence

Check the distinction

A search checks 20 candidates instead of 100, but each check costs six times as much. Has total checking work decreased?

Read the reasoning

No: using the original check cost as one unit, work grows from 100 to 120 units. Parallel execution might still reduce elapsed time if resources are available, but that is a different claim requiring a schedule and resource account. Neither candidate count nor elapsed search time alone establishes the quality of the selected design.

What does “success” mean in this system?

A result such as “99% success” leaves several questions unanswered. What was counted: requests, answers, messages, or tested crash cases? What had to happen for one to pass? Who checked it, and when? A percentage is a count of passing cases divided by a count of included cases. Changing either count changes the claim.

QServe compares compact model execution while separately checking answer quality on named tasks. SOLA counts a request as meeting its service promise only when both its first-token delay and later-token spacing meet their limits. Picsou’s delivery guarantee concerns a message reaching at least one correct replica in the destination group; that alone does not mean the destination committed it or exposed it to clients. PMVerify’s robustness check asks whether a post-crash state could also occur in ordinary execution under its model; that alone does not establish that ordinary states satisfy the application’s own rules.

These claims can all be true at once because they check different requirements. A fast response may contain a wrong answer; a delivered message may not yet be available to a reader; a program may recover to a state it can also reach without crashing, yet that state may violate the application’s rules. Before comparing percentages, write a sentence saying exactly what one case must do to pass. Include who can observe the result and when it must be available.

Consider an invented service test with 100 requests. A request passes only if its answer is both correct and on time. Ninety answers are correct, and ninety are on time. That does not establish ninety successful requests. If the same ten requests fail both checks, ninety pass both. If ten are wrong but on time and another ten are correct but late, only eighty pass both. Both arrangements have the same two separate 90% rates. To count joint success exactly, retain the two results for each request and count requests that pass both checks.

Multiplying 0.9 by 0.9 gives 0.81, but the two observed percentages alone do not justify an 81% joint-success claim. A probability model can predict 81% if each check has a 90% chance of passing and the checks are independent: learning whether one passed must not change the chance that the other passes. That is a model prediction, not a count of this test’s successful requests. Without the paired results, the observed joint count here can be anywhere from eighty to ninety. Also keep the included requests fixed. Dropping ten unanswered requests and reporting ninety successes out of ninety answers would hide those missing outcomes if the promise applies to all 100 arrivals.

This rule transfers beyond these four papers. In a chip evaluation, “works” might mean it meets timing at one voltage and temperature. In scientific computing, it might mean the result meets a numerical tolerance. In a service, it might mean a required fraction of requests meets a deadline. Do not let a headline metric silently stand in for another property.

Reading path

  • MLSys: answer quality and serving throughput
  • MLSys: two per-request latency limits
  • OSDI: delivery versus destination commit
  • ASPLOS: robustness versus application correctness

Check the distinction

In the 100-request example, ten answers are wrong and ten are late. Four requests belong to both groups. How many pass both checks? Then choose one of the linked papers and name something its stated guarantee does not establish.

Read the reasoning

There are 10 + 10 − 4 = 16 distinct failing requests: subtract four because those requests were counted twice. Thus 84 pass both checks, or 84% of the 100 arrivals. Separate 90% rates concealed which requests failed. For the paper comparison, Picsou’s delivery guarantee does not establish that the destination has committed the message. PMVerify’s crash-robustness property does not establish that every ordinary state obeys the application’s rules. SOLA’s two delay checks must both pass; reporting only one is insufficient. QServe’s quality tests do not establish accuracy on every untested task. Keep the condition being checked and the cases included in the count attached to each result.
