NSDI 2026: make decisions across machines with incomplete information

Ten themes with worked examples and explained exercises, plus focused FastServe, Di-PS, and HydraServe walkthroughs based on the final USENIX papers. Selected theme discussions have been checked against official paper abstracts. Review of the complete conference and the remaining teaching claims is unfinished.

Imagine a service receiving a request while its machines are already busy. It must choose a worker using measurements that may be old, provide the data that worker needs, and return an answer before the user's deadline. If a machine fails or an input is wrong, the service must still follow its stated rules. The first three themes examine observation, scheduling, and data placement. The next three follow delay, hardware assignments, and recovery. The final four ask how to collect evidence, protect access, decide what information may be discarded, and use predictions without treating them as guarantees. Read each example by following the same request: what does the next action need, what must happen first, and what would prevent the answer from being accepted?

Evidence boundary

This route draws its theme map from the local synthesis of 150 NSDI 2026 papers. That synthesis reports paper records, extracted text, and review notes; their existence does not establish that every claim in this tutorial has been checked. Selected mechanism summaries cite official USENIX abstracts and state that scope in their evidence notes. The FastServe, Di-PS, and HydraServe walkthroughs inspect their final conference PDFs and give separate source boundaries; their results have not been independently reproduced. Invented quantities illustrate reasoning and are labeled as teaching examples. The three focused PDF reviews do not turn the wider abstract-based synthesis into a paper-by-paper review.

Paper walkthrough: FastServe: a useful stopping point still has a cost

Paper walkthrough: Di-PS: train across clusters without treating every update as equally fresh

Paper walkthrough: HydraServe: make a cold worker useful before every stage is finished

1. Represent the state needed for the decision

Suppose a service must choose which worker receives the next request. Counting waiting requests is easy, but ten short requests can finish before one long request. The decision needs an estimate of the work ahead. Even that estimate has an age: by the time a reply reaches the service, the worker may have finished some work or received more. A controller is the part of the system that uses such observations to choose an action. Its state description is the information it keeps for that choice. Ask both whether that description contains the relevant facts and whether they still apply when the action takes effect.

History and context
Use prior behavior when a snapshot cannot distinguish a burst from sustained demand. State how changed conditions can invalidate that history.
Apply it

Compare a queue with two long jobs against one with four short jobs, then account for work that finishes or arrives while the measurement travels. The controller needs the work remaining and the observation time.

Where it fails: A detailed old reply can still send work to the wrong worker when new jobs arrive before assignment.

Evidence boundary: UNUM’s official abstract supports using measurement history to construct learned network state. The worker-queue calculation is original and does not describe its evaluated controller.

Inspect the named source

Probing and uncertainty
Collect additional evidence when the existing estimate is not trustworthy. Include the traffic and delay caused by probing.
Apply it

Charge six milliseconds for the teaching probe and one millisecond saved per later decision. Six decisions repay the cost; seven are needed for a net saving under the stated assumptions.

Where it fails: The transfer may end, or conditions may change, before later decisions recover the cost of gathering evidence.

Evidence boundary: PolicyCache’s official abstract describes exploration and learning within a single flow. The probe duration and savings are teaching quantities, not reported measurements.

Inspect the named source

Service state tied to the result
Measure progress or user experience where raw link traffic is an inadequate substitute. Identify the rule connecting the measurement to the desired result.
Apply it

For video delivery, distinguish bytes arriving from whether playback has enough data to continue. For a worker assignment, distinguish request count from work remaining. Choose observations that address the user’s required result.

Where it fails: A high transfer rate measured after a playback interruption cannot undo the interruption the viewer already experienced.

Evidence boundary: UNUM’s official abstract identifies adaptive video bitrate selection and congestion control as evaluated tasks. The playback example explains why the task matters; it makes no numerical claim about UNUM.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

In this invented service, worker A has two waiting jobs that each need 8 ms; worker B has four that each need 1 ms. Each runs one job at a time, neither is currently busy, and a new 2 ms job joins the end of its chosen queue. Choosing the shorter queue sends it to A, where it finishes after 18 ms. Choosing the smaller amount of waiting work sends it to B, where it finishes after 6 ms. Request count is accurate but insufficient for this decision.

Suppose querying remaining work takes 3 ms during which both workers continue processing. At the reply, A has 13 ms left and B has 1 ms left. Sending the new job to B still finishes at time 6 ms from the original decision. It would be wrong to add the query's 3 ms to the original 6 ms: some queued work happened during the query. If new requests arrive meanwhile, however, the reply may already be stale. The controller needs both what was measured and when it was measured.

Network senders face the same observation problem. Sending too quickly can build a queue along the path; sending too slowly leaves available capacity unused. UNUM processes a history of measurements at intervals related to the time for a message and its reply to travel the path. A trained model turns that history into a collection of numbers supplied to a controller. Those numbers are called an embedding. Training uses examples from different network settings. The idea is to give the controller information that a single current measurement or average leaves out. The paper's evidence still needs checking against the network conditions where the controller will be used.

PolicyCache learns during an individual flow, meaning one ongoing network transfer. It uses observations from that flow to learn how sending choices affect the result, tries choices to gather more evidence, and switches between exploration and its learned rule. This moves some learning into the transfer being controlled. It raises a practical question: how much of the transfer still produces accepted output after the system has gathered enough evidence? As a teaching example, suppose probing costs 6 milliseconds and saves 1 millisecond on each later decision. Six later decisions only recover the probing cost; seven produce a net saving if no other costs change. A short transfer or a changing path can leave too little time to recover that cost. These numbers illustrate the question and are not PolicyCache measurements.

Check your reasoning

Before the controller acts at time 3 ms, another 10 ms job joins B behind its remaining 1 ms of work. The new 2 ms job must join behind both. Compare its completion time on A and B, measured from time zero. What did the stale reply omit?

Read the reasoning

A finishes it at 3 + 13 + 2 = 18 ms. B finishes it at 3 + 1 + 10 + 2 = 16 ms. B still wins, but not by the margin suggested by the old reply. If the intervening job needed 15 ms instead, B would finish at 21 ms and A would win. A measurement of outstanding work needs a policy for arrivals between observation and action; a precise old measurement does not reserve the measured queue position.

Evidence boundary. UNUM and PolicyCache (NSDI 2026) make different choices about where learning happens. The official USENIX abstracts support the mechanism summaries here. UNUM's abstract reports improvements in network sending control and video-quality selection in real and synthetic settings; PolicyCache's reports a Linux implementation evaluated in emulated and real networks. These statements do not establish which would win on the same workload. The worker queues and probe costs in this theme are original teaching examples. Geminet and BayWatch remain further reading leads in the local synthesis.

Review: Waiting and service time · Result boundaries

2. Choose when work can be interrupted or reassigned

A worker busy with a long request may keep a short request waiting even when the short one needs little work. A scheduler, the part of the system that chooses what runs next, can give the short request a turn if the long one can pause. Pausing means preserving enough progress to resume correctly. Moving the paused work to another machine adds a transfer. Find the points where those actions are possible, then count what they cost and whose completion time they change.

Natural stopping points
Pause where enough state is available to resume without repeating unsafe effects. A possible pause is not necessarily a cheap pause.
Apply it

Split work only at a point where the current output and state form a legal restart boundary.

Where it fails: Interrupting in the middle of a dependency can force recomputation or change the answer.

Evidence boundary: The FastServe walkthrough’s preemption threshold motivates the example; the stopping points are original.

Inspect the named source

Dependencies across calls
Schedule for the chain that determines the program's result rather than optimizing each remote call independently.
Apply it

Draw the dependencies between request segments and mark which cached values must arrive before each segment can continue. Count the transfer before assigning a start time.

Where it fails: Moving a later segment without its required earlier state can force repeated calculation or prevent correct continuation.

Evidence boundary: Libra’s official abstract describes cooperating segments and chunked attention-cache transfers across workers. The dependency-accounting exercise is original.

Inspect the named source

Batch and trial units
Apply resource or statistical requirements to the group they actually concern. A per-request rule can miss a constraint on the whole batch.
Apply it

For each worker’s batch, identify which requests have a first-output, between-output, or completion-time target. Include waiting and movement between segments when checking each target.

Where it fails: A batch that finishes quickly can still contain a request that waited too long before joining it.

Evidence boundary: Libra’s official abstract describes local batches formed with service targets in mind. The three possible timing targets are teaching questions, not an assertion that its evaluation covers all three.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

A teaching request has four sequential 3 ms stages on one worker. Another request needing 1 ms arrives at time 1 ms. Without interruption, the first finishes at time 12 and the second at time 13, so the second waits 12 ms from arrival to completion. Suppose a safe stopping point exists after each stage. Pause after stage one at time 3, spend 1 ms saving state, run the short request from time 4 to 5, spend 1 ms restoring state, then run the remaining stages until time 15. The short request now takes 4 ms from arrival, but the original request finishes 3 ms later.

Those stopping points must also preserve effects. If stage one sends an external notification, resuming by rerunning the whole stage could send it twice. Either save enough progress to resume after the effect or use a receiver-side rule that recognizes the same logical operation. Merely copying the worker's memory does not establish that an external recipient will forget the first notification.

FastServe uses the repeated steps of text generation as stopping points. A token is a unit of text handled by the model; generation produces successive tokens using the earlier context. FastServe can pause a request between output tokens, a scheduling action called preemption. It uses the known input length to choose an initial priority queue and manages intermediate state between GPU memory and host memory. That state movement is part of making the pause usable. The end of a generation step provides a place to reconsider the schedule; it does not make saving and restoring state free.

Libra divides a request into cooperating segments at token boundaries. One scheduler chooses where to split requests across GPU workers, while each worker forms batches, groups of work processed together, with service targets in mind. The design transfers cached attention state in chunks so execution can continue across workers. That cache holds intermediate values needed to process the text context without repeating all earlier calculations. Splitting creates more assignment choices, but a later segment still needs its required earlier state. Treating the segments as independent requests would omit that dependency.

Return to the teaching schedule: the short request finishes earlier because it receives a turn before the long request ends. The long request finishes later because it gives up processor time and pays save-and-restore costs. Both effects belong in the evaluation. A serving result should state whether the target concerns the first output, pauses between outputs, or the finished response. Meeting one of those targets does not automatically meet the others, especially when partially completed requests wait for another turn.

Check your reasoning

Both requests must finish by absolute time 14 ms. Does either schedule meet both deadlines? What if saving and restoring each take only 0.5 ms?

Read the reasoning

Without interruption, completions at 12 and 13 meet both deadlines. With 1 ms save and restore, the original request finishes at 15 and misses. At 0.5 ms each, the short request finishes at 4.5 and the original at 14, so both meet. Improving the short request's delay does not by itself establish that the schedule meets the full set of obligations.

Evidence boundary. FastServe and Libra (NSDI 2026) use token boundaries to create scheduling choices. Their official USENIX abstracts support the mechanisms discussed in this theme. FastServe reports comparisons with vLLM; Libra reports serving results on A100/H100 GPUs under specified service targets. Those separate evaluations do not establish a head-to-head ranking. The millisecond schedule and notification example are original teaching cases. JITServe, Agentix, and CCEval remain further reading leads for different scheduling or evaluation units.

Review: Dependencies · Scheduling

3. Count capacity only after state can reach it

Suppose a worker has room for a model but the model is stored on another machine. Before that worker can answer a request, the required data must cross a connection and become usable locally. If the source keeps changing, copying its initial contents is only part of the job: later changes must also arrive in the right order. Separate three questions: where the data fits, how soon the worker can use it, and which copy is allowed to accept the next update. Each question needs its own evidence.

Movement across storage tiers
Separate frequently changing placement decisions from expensive movement of persistent state. Include lookup and reconstruction costs.
Apply it

Separate the parameters needed for model execution from the history needed to update them. List which bytes must move when a different machine takes on more expert work.

Where it fails: Moving all associated state with every assignment change can consume the time and network capacity the reassignment was meant to save.

Evidence boundary: SYMI’s official abstract describes fixed optimizer-state partitions and changing expert-parameter placement. The six-GB copy timeline is an original teaching model.

Inspect the named source

Topology and ownership
Trace the connections and permissions needed to use a remote pool. Total storage size alone does not establish usable capacity.
Apply it

For each part of the state, identify where it is stored, which machine uses it, and which machine may update it. Include the path and transfer time between those roles.

Where it fails: A finished copy does not by itself grant exclusive permission to accept the next write. Placement and update authority need separate rules.

Evidence boundary: SYMI provides the state-placement example. Its abstract does not define the generic copy-and-handoff protocol in this lesson; that protocol is a teaching question.

Inspect the named source

Reuse without duplicate state
Share logs, cached results, or related model representations only when their identities and validity rules allow it.
Apply it

Count one ten-GB base plus three one-GB differences: thirteen GB rather than forty for four separate ten-GB models, before bookkeeping.

Where it fails: A missing or wrong base prevents exact reconstruction. Lower storage consumption alone does not establish faster loading or a smaller execution footprint.

Evidence boundary: ZipLLM’s official abstract describes lossless differences and array-level deduplication. The sizes and loading questions are original teaching examples.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Suppose a new worker needs a 6 GB state image before it can serve requests. Its only incoming path carries 2 GB/s, so transfer alone takes at least three seconds. Checking and installing the image takes another second after transfer. The worker contributes no service capacity during those four seconds, despite being idle and having enough memory. If other traffic leaves only 1 GB/s for the image, readiness moves to seven seconds.

Now allow the source state to change. Assume, in a simplified continuous-flow model, the initial copy is a consistent snapshot, later changes are recorded, and copying those changes has a dedicated 2 GB/s path. During the three-second initial copy, changes accumulate at 0.5 GB/s, leaving 1.5 GB to catch up. With updates continuing, the backlog shrinks at 2−0.5 = 1.5 GB/s, taking one more second. This is only the copying time. A real handoff still needs a rule for the final change, checking, and which worker may accept the next write. If changes arrive as fast as they can be copied, this catch-up phase cannot empty its queue.

SYMI separates two kinds of training state. A mixture-of-experts model sends each input to selected model blocks, called experts. As their popularity changes, the system may need to assign more processing capacity to one expert. Its parameters are the numbers used in the model calculation; its optimizer state records information used to update those numbers during training. SYMI keeps the optimizer state divided across training machines in a fixed arrangement, while changing the placement of expert parameters through existing weight updates. The lesson is to ask which state must follow an assignment change. Treating every associated byte as one movable bundle can add transfers the design could avoid.

ZipLLM addresses storage for related language models. It combines keeping a single copy of identical arrays, called deduplication, with storing compressed differences between related models. Its BitX method compares corresponding bits using exclusive OR: the resulting bit is zero when they match and one when they differ. With the correct base model and the recovered difference, that operation can reconstruct the original bits. This is lossless compression, meaning reconstruction preserves the stored values exactly. The base's identity is therefore part of the stored representation, not optional bookkeeping.

Consider an invented model collection: one 10 GB base and three 10 GB variants occupy 40 GB as separate copies. If each variant can instead be represented by a 1 GB compressed difference from that base, the collection occupies 13 GB before indexes and other metadata. A worker that lacks the base cannot reconstruct a variant from its 1 GB difference alone. Loading also requires decompression and enough working space. These assumed sizes illustrate storage sharing; they do not predict ZipLLM's compression ratio, startup time, or device-memory use.

Check your reasoning

Keep the three-second snapshot copy and 2 GB/s change-copy path, but raise the change rate to 1.5 GB/s. How much change data waits after the snapshot, and how long does catch-up take? Does that prove the worker is ready to own writes?

Read the reasoning

The backlog is 3×1.5 = 4.5 GB. It shrinks at 2−1.5 = 0.5 GB/s, requiring nine seconds, or twelve seconds from the start of the snapshot copy. This excludes installation and final handoff. Receiving all copied bytes does not by itself establish exclusive write authority or that the snapshot and changes form a valid recoverable state.

Evidence boundary. SYMI and ZipLLM (NSDI 2026) illustrate changing placement and changing stored representation. Their official USENIX abstracts support the mechanism summaries in this theme. SYMI reports training comparisons with DeepSpeed and FlexMoE; ZipLLM reports storage reduction for its studied model collection. These are different outcomes, and neither establishes the other's cost. DistVS, FalconFS, and Sandook remain further reading leads. The copy, catch-up, and base-plus-difference quantities here are original teaching examples.

Review: Memory · Paths · Persistent identity

4. Explain the events that make a request unusually slow

A user whose request takes a second still waits a second when most other requests finish in milliseconds. To describe these unusually slow requests, arrange completion times from shortest to longest and examine the slow end, often called the tail. That description identifies which requests need attention, but does not explain their delay. A request may be waiting for a model to load, for another user to release a processor, or for permission to transmit over a shared wireless channel. Record when each wait begins and ends before choosing what to change.

Startup and queues
Identify which preparation stages can overlap and which must finish before the first response the user can accept.
Apply it

Draw the startup dependencies before adding their durations. In the teaching example, independent 60 ms and 40 ms stages finish together after 60 ms; a dependency forces them to take 100 ms.

Where it fails: Even independent stages may compete for the same network or processor, making the assumed overlap unattainable.

Evidence boundary: HydraServe’s official abstract describes overlapping startup stages and placing workers to reduce network competition. The stage durations and deadline are original teaching quantities.

Inspect the named source

Remaining time and state lifetime
Use the work still required and the expected departure of stored state, not only time already spent or bytes currently allocated.
Apply it

At each preemption, count remaining work and the lifetime of the state that must survive until resumption.

Where it fails: Saving state for a request that will finish soon can cost more than waiting; evicting it can make resumption slower.

Evidence boundary: The paper’s output-aging and proactive management provide source context; the lifetime calculation is original.

Inspect the named source

Enforcement and fairness
Apply resource shares at a point that can actually control contention. Report which requests improve and which lose service.
Apply it

For a shared wireless channel, record each transmitter’s waiting intervals and delivered packets. Ask whether shorter waits for one leave another without a useful turn.

Where it fails: An aggregate delivery rate can improve while one participant experiences longer interruptions. Decide which participants and deadlines the evaluation must cover.

Evidence boundary: BLADE’s official abstract describes adjusting contention windows and reports fairness in its evaluated conditions. The per-participant reading questions are teaching guidance, not an additional measured result.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Use two groups of 100 invented requests. Every request needs 2 ms of execution. In group A, 99 requests start immediately and one waits 100 ms for startup: delays are ninety-nine 2 ms values and one 102 ms value. In group B, every request waits 1 ms in a queue: all delays are 3 ms. Both means are 3 ms, but their causes and worst cases differ. A five-millisecond deadline is missed once in A and never in B.

Suppose startup consists of a 60 ms state load and a 40 ms code preparation step. If they are independent and have resources to run together, startup falls from 100 to 60 ms, not to zero. The cold request then takes 62 ms and still misses the deadline. If the code preparation requires the loaded state, that overlap is not available. The event sequence, not just the average, determines which intervention is possible.

HydraServe addresses this preparation problem for language-model services that start workers when needed. A cold start is the work required to make a worker ready before it can serve a request. HydraServe distributes model data across servers in advance, overlaps startup stages within workers, and chooses worker locations to reduce competition for network transfers during startup. The connection to the teaching example is the dependency: stages can run together only when their inputs and resources permit it. Starting many workers can also make them compete for the same transfer capacity, so readiness depends on the other startups happening at the same time. The 60 and 40 millisecond stages above are invented, not HydraServe measurements.

BLADE addresses a different wait: a ready packet may still wait to use Wi-Fi. Nearby transmitters share a channel and use waiting rules to compete for turns. The range used to choose a waiting interval is called a contention window. BLADE adjusts those windows according to competition on the channel. Its authors identify short intervals with little packet delivery as a cause of cloud-gaming delays in their study. Faster server computation would not directly remove that wireless wait. Evaluation therefore needs the timing of delivered packets and playback interruptions, together with how service is divided among competing transmitters. A high average delivery rate alone can hide a gap long enough to interrupt playback.

Check your reasoning

In group A, halve execution from 2 ms to 1 ms while leaving the 100 ms startup unchanged. What are the mean and the slow request's delay? Does the deadline failure disappear?

Read the reasoning

The mean becomes (99×1 + 101)/100 = 2 ms. The slow request still takes 101 ms and misses the five-millisecond deadline. The mean falls by one millisecond, but the specific failure remains. Report the distribution and cause, not just the mean.

Evidence boundary. HydraServe and BLADE (NSDI 2026) give concrete examples of preparation delay and wireless transmission delay. The linked official USENIX abstracts support the mechanism summaries here. HydraServe reports lower cold-start delay and improved attainment of service targets in its evaluated settings. BLADE reports simulation and commercial Wi-Fi access-point experiments, including reduced transmission tail delay under heavy competition for the channel. They measure different events on different systems, so their improvements cannot be ranked as a common result. Titrate, CacheCatalyst, and Themis HBM remain further reading leads.

Review: Delay distributions · Complete serving trace

5. Define the work that crosses a hardware boundary

A request arriving from the network may travel to the main processor just to be examined and sent somewhere else. A network device that can perform that examination may shorten the path. But it has its own instruction, memory, and processing limits. First list which operations it can finish and which still need the main processor, called the host. Then describe what crosses between them: input data, intermediate results, and enough progress information to prevent missing or repeating an action.

Common and exceptional paths
Make ordinary cases cheap while keeping less common operations correct. Include the cost of transferring a case between paths.
Apply it

Separate operations completed by the network card from features handled by the host proxy. Use the teaching timings to count both the short path and the longer handoff path.

Where it fails: A faster ordinary path can coexist with an eight-millisecond exceptional path that misses the seven-millisecond deadline.

Evidence boundary: HybridMesh’s official abstract describes its SmartNIC and CPU-side proxy. The one-, two-, and five-millisecond costs are original teaching quantities.

Inspect the named source

Compatible interfaces
Specify how differently implemented modules interpret requests, state, and completion. Matching data formats alone may not match behavior.
Apply it

At the handoff, state which data is being passed and which effects have already happened. The counter example requires the receiver to distinguish work still needed from work already completed.

Where it fails: Matching the request format does not prevent the host from repeating an increment the device already performed.

Evidence boundary: HybridMesh provides a concrete hardware/software division. Its abstract does not establish the counter protocol; that example teaches a separate interface requirement.

Inspect the named source

Matching rates
Check whether input, processing, and output can sustain the same workload. A fast device can still wait on a slower neighboring stage.
Apply it

Compare the number of feature records produced each second with the number the next stage can process. In the teaching case, 200 arriving and 150 processed leave 50 more waiting each second.

Where it fails: Five hundred extra buffer slots absorb ten seconds of the imbalance but cannot sustain it indefinitely. Reducing records also requires checking classification quality.

Evidence boundary: FENIX’s official abstract describes rate control between switch feature extraction and FPGA inference. The rates and queue arithmetic are original and do not specify its implemented selection rule.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

An invented device handles an ordinary request in 1 ms. For an unsupported request, it spends 1 ms discovering that fact, transfers the request to the host in 2 ms, and the host takes 5 ms to complete it. With no queueing or overlap, the exceptional path takes 8 ms. If nine of ten requests are ordinary, mean completion time is 0.9×1 + 0.1×8 = 1.7 ms, compared with 5 ms when all requests go directly to the host. The exception nevertheless becomes slower.

The handoff must say whether anything has already happened. Suppose the operation increments a counter. If the device increments it and then forwards an unmarked request, the host might increment again. A correct interface must either hand off before the effect, report completed progress unambiguously, or recognize repeated logical operations. Agreement on the request's byte format alone does not supply that behavior.

These isolated-request times are not a throughput calculation. If responses all cross a path limited to 100 responses per second, the device's 1 ms ordinary-case time cannot make the complete service deliver 1,000 responses per second. Queueing at the output boundary changes the observed delays.

HybridMesh places traffic analysis and routing on a SmartNIC, a network card that can execute processing work. It also retains a proxy, a program that handles traffic on behalf of the service, on the main CPU for features unsuitable for that card. Its target is the ingress gateway: the entry point for outside requests into a group of communicating services. The division matters because making the entry path faster does not eliminate every traffic-management operation. To judge the whole design, follow a request through both parts and count their work and communication. The counter example above explains a general handoff obligation; it does not describe a reported HybridMesh bug.

FENIX splits traffic classification across two kinds of hardware. A programmable switch chip extracts features, measurements that summarize the traffic for a model. A field-programmable gate array, or FPGA, is a chip whose logic can be configured after manufacture; it runs the neural-network calculation. FENIX controls the rate of feature streams sent between them because the two stages have different processing rates. This makes the connection itself part of the design. A fast first stage cannot force a slower second stage to accept unlimited work.

For a separate teaching model, suppose the first stage produces 200 feature records per second and the second can process 150. With no reduction in arrivals, unfinished records accumulate at 50 per second: 500 after ten seconds. Adding room for those 500 records postpones overflow but leaves the rate mismatch. Reducing the sent records can control that queue, yet the application must still check whether the retained information supports accurate classifications. This calculation explains the capacity question; it does not specify FENIX's selection rule or measured rates.

Check your reasoning

What exceptional-request fraction makes the invented mean equal to the host-only 5 ms? Would a seven-millisecond deadline be met by every request below that fraction?

Read the reasoning

For fraction p, the mean is 1 + 7p ms. It equals five when p = 4/7, about 57.1%. Below that fraction the mean improves, but every exceptional request still takes 8 ms and misses a seven-millisecond deadline. A favorable mean does not establish a per-request guarantee.

Evidence boundary. HybridMesh and FENIX (NSDI 2026) illustrate different divisions of work. Their official USENIX abstracts support the mechanism summaries in this theme. HybridMesh evaluates a gateway combining a network card and a CPU-side proxy; FENIX evaluates traffic analysis on an integrated Tofino switch chip and ZU19EG FPGA using network traffic datasets. Neither result establishes the performance of the other's task. BURST, SONiC DASH, and Queue-Mem remain further reading leads. The request times, counter handoff, and rate examples are original teaching constructions.

Review: Execution assignment · Stage rates · Physical limits

6. Pay for recovery before the failure

When a worker disappears, its replacement needs more than an empty machine. It needs the inputs and saved progress required to continue, a way to obtain them, and enough processing capacity to serve the waiting users. Preparing those things while the service is healthy consumes resources. Leaving them unprepared shifts work into the recovery interval. Start by naming what can fail, what remains available, and how the replacement knows where to resume. Then count the cost before the failure and the time until users receive accepted results again.

Prepared state and paths
Keep reconstructible state or reserve a route before it is needed. Ask which shared failure can remove both the original and reserve.
Apply it

List what must reach a replacement worker: a usable saved state, later updates if required, and the authority to continue. Count the machines and network traffic used to keep that state ready.

Where it fails: A recent copy cannot help if it fails with the original or cannot reach the replacement in time.

Evidence boundary: Checkmate’s official abstract describes maintaining a CPU model copy using gradients already exchanged during training. The joint-failure and transfer-deadline questions are teaching extensions.

Inspect the named source

Local recovery
Repeat only the affected dependent work when the saved information permits it. Define the boundary that prevents repeated external effects.
Apply it

Mark which earlier results survive a failed command and which later commands depend on them. Restart from retained usable results, while separately checking whether an external recipient has already acted.

Where it fails: Repeating an earlier calculation can be harmless while repeating its notification changes the outcome. A restart point must account for both.

Evidence boundary: Fractal’s official abstract describes tracking dependencies and progress to limit repeated regions. The file, filter, sort, and notification example is original; command support must be checked in the paper.

Inspect the named source

Shared reserves
Share spare resources only under explicit assumptions about simultaneous failures and priorities when reserve demand exceeds capacity.
Apply it

Use the reserve example: two failed services need 8 GB and 80 requests per second. A spare with 8 GB but only 60 requests per second stores both states while accumulating unfinished work.

Where it fails: The queue grows by 20 requests each second even with instantaneous transfer. Enough storage does not supply the missing processing rate.

Evidence boundary: This shared-spare calculation is original. Checkmate’s separate CPU cluster provides a concrete example of resources maintained for recovery; its abstract does not establish the shared-spare sizing rule used here.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Imagine three services, each requiring 4 GB of state and 40 requests per second of processing capacity. They share one spare with 8 GB of storage but only 60 requests per second of capacity. One failed service fits both limits. Two failed services fit the memory exactly but require 80 requests per second, exceeding the spare's rate. Enough space for the recovered state is not enough capacity to keep up with its users.

If two services fail together and their traffic remains at 80 requests per second, the spare's unfinished work grows by 20 requests each second. After five seconds it has accumulated 100 requests, even if transfer and activation were instantaneous. Reserving more storage would not remove this rate deficit. Sharing the spare is a choice based on which simultaneous failures the service is required to handle.

Recovery also depends on what the failure leaves intact. A spare in the same failed power domain cannot serve as an independent reserve. Saved state needs a surviving path and a checked restart point. If replay can repeat an external action, the recovery protocol must address that action as well as reconstructing local memory. These are explicit conditions of the teaching example, not claims about the papers discussed in this theme.

Checkmate prepares a restart copy during model training. The training machines already exchange gradients, numbers used to update the model. Checkmate also sends those numbers to a separate group of CPU machines, which applies the updates to its own model copy. This gives recovery a recent saved state, called a checkpoint. The paper reports checkpointing after every training iteration without slowing training in its evaluation. That speed claim still requires the additional machines and network delivery described by the design. Keeping the copy current and moving it to a replacement worker are separate jobs; the latter still belongs in the recovery timeline.

Fractal concerns command sequences, called shell scripts, distributed across machines. It separates regions that can be recovered from regions with effects that require special handling, and tracks which regions depend on which earlier results and how far they have progressed. That information limits how much earlier work must run again. For an invented example, if reading a file and filtering it produced a retained intermediate result, a failed later sort could restart from that result. Sending a notification introduces a different question: did the receiver already act on it? This example explains why dependency tracking and repeated external actions require distinct rules; it is not a claim about which commands Fractal supports.

PILOT asks whether the recovery action itself could cause trouble. Its execution model simulates a recovery action within a running distributed system so that its effects can be examined before the action is applied. This addresses interactions that a test of one component may miss. Its reported detection of 17 among 20 evaluated recovery failures leaves three undetected cases in that evaluation. A successful trial therefore provides evidence about the simulated action and conditions; it does not remove the need for a surviving copy, sufficient replacement capacity, or a correct restart rule.

Check your reasoning

Upgrade the spare to 100 requests per second but keep its 8 GB storage. Which resource prevents recovery of all three services at once? Would adding storage alone solve the entire problem?

Read the reasoning

Three services require 12 GB and 120 requests per second, exceeding both limits. Adding storage to 12 GB fixes capacity for their state but leaves a 20-request-per-second service deficit. A reserve plan must satisfy simultaneous storage, processing, transfer, and failure-survival requirements; changing one does not imply the others are met.

Evidence boundary. Checkmate, Fractal, and PILOT (NSDI 2026) address maintaining restart state, limiting repeated work, and examining recovery actions, respectively. The official USENIX abstracts support the mechanism summaries in this theme. Fractal reports evaluation on 4- and 30-machine clusters; PILOT reports finding 17 of 20 recovery failures in five evaluated systems. Neither observation establishes coverage of every possible failure. The reserve arithmetic is an original teaching model. Lemonshark and HEDGE remain further reading leads with their own failure assumptions.

Review: Recovery costs · Surviving path capacity · Retries

7. Collect evidence that can distinguish competing explanations

Suppose a request takes ten milliseconds. Did it wait eight milliseconds for a worker and run for two, or run for all ten? The total alone cannot tell you. To separate those explanations, record when execution began. A trace is a record of such events during a run. Decide which explanations you need to distinguish before choosing what to record or discard. Recording also takes processing time and storage, so the measurement can change the run being measured.

Summaries and escalation
Keep compact measurements for ordinary operation and collect more detail when they cannot resolve a question.
Apply it

Use the ten-millisecond example to identify the missing event: execution start. Before replacing a trace with a summary, list which distinctions that summary must preserve.

Where it fails: Recording more detail later cannot recover an earlier event that was never retained. Recording everything can also change the measured execution cost.

Evidence boundary: μView’s official abstract supports compact streaming measurement processing and identifying informative data. The missing-event example and one-millisecond recording cost are original.

Inspect the named source

Comparing executions
Use shadow runs or different implementations to find disagreements, while checking that they represent the same inputs and required behavior.
Apply it

Before comparing a changed controller with the original, match the relevant network state and traffic. Identify the time resolution needed to reproduce the event being investigated.

Where it fails: A replay can agree with broad traffic totals while missing the order or timing that caused a short queue to form.

Evidence boundary: MirrorNet’s official abstract describes historical state reconstruction and alignment with a production network. The queue example is a question to test, not a reported failure of MirrorNet.

Inspect the named source

Coverage and realism
Search states and failures deliberately. State which workloads and error cases the test population represents and what remains outside it.
Apply it

Separate the number of naturally observed incidents from the number and kinds of errors deliberately introduced in simulation. Record both detections and false alerts with their observation periods.

Where it fails: Detecting one observed incident does not establish detection of every error type. No false alerts over a finite interval does not establish a zero future probability.

Evidence boundary: CrossCheck’s official abstract reports one detected invalid-input incident during four weeks of production checking and separate simulation results. These provide different evidence about coverage.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Two invented traces both report a 10 ms request. In trace A, admission occurs at time 0, execution starts at 8, and delivery occurs at 10. In trace B, admission and execution start at 0, while delivery occurs at 10. The same total is consistent with 8 ms of queueing plus 2 ms of execution, or 10 ms of execution. A summary containing only total delay cannot distinguish them. Recording the execution-start event separates these explanations, assuming the timestamps use the same clock and delivery has no separate cost in this model.

Suppose detailed recording adds 1 ms to the execution path. An instrumented total of 11 ms then cannot be directly compared with the old 10 ms as evidence that the service itself regressed. Measure or bound observation cost and compare equivalent recording conditions. Keeping detailed traces only for slow requests can help diagnosis, but those selected traces do not estimate how common slow requests are unless the selection counts are also retained.

μView moves measurement processing to infrastructure processing units, or IPUs: processors used for infrastructure work alongside the application machines. It updates compact summaries as service measurements arrive. These summaries are called sketches; their purpose is to retain information needed for selected questions without storing every observation. The paper describes using them to anticipate violations of service targets and identify measurements to examine. When reading such a design, ask which questions its summary can still answer. A summary of total request duration, for example, cannot recover a missing execution-start event. That information-loss example is our teaching case, not a description of μView's particular sketch.

MirrorNet addresses the next step: reproducing the conditions in which a network behaved unexpectedly. An emulation is a separate running environment that recreates selected behavior of another system. MirrorNet records changes and replays them to reconstruct historical network state, including the controller, packet-forwarding behavior, and traffic. Its abstract describes reconstruction at one-second intervals and a method for keeping the emulated network aligned with the live network. This supports testing a change against a recorded situation. It still leaves the reader to check whether the timing and behavior needed for a particular question are reproduced; the word mirror alone does not establish that every packet-level event is identical.

CrossCheck examines the inputs used by a controller for a network connecting distant sites, called a wide-area network. A controller can follow its algorithm correctly and still make a harmful decision when its input is wrong. CrossCheck checks for invalid inputs and alerts operators. Its authors report four weeks of checking alongside a production controller: the system detected the one invalid-input incident observed and produced no false alerts during normal operation. They also report separate simulation tests. One observed incident is a small sample of possible failures, and no false alerts in that interval does not establish a zero future false-alert probability. Keep the deployment observation and the simulated tests separate when judging coverage.

Check your reasoning

Two implementations process the same input list and produce the same set of items in different orders. Is that a bug? What must a comparison record establish before treating this as a disagreement?

Read the reasoning

It depends on the promised output. If order is unspecified, the difference can be legal; if the contract requires input order, at least one result may violate it. Establish the same logical inputs, relevant initial state, and required ordering before choosing a comparator. Agreement also does not prove correctness if both implementations share the same mistake.

Evidence boundary. The official USENIX abstracts for μView, MirrorNet, and CrossCheck (NSDI 2026) support the three mechanism summaries here. They concern measurement, emulation, and input checking, respectively. A disagreement remains evidence to investigate; deciding which behavior is wrong requires the expected behavior and relevant inputs. NIDSFuzz, ServeGen, and CCEval remain further reading leads. The ten-millisecond traces and their recording cost are original teaching examples.

Review: Tests and promises · Measurement boundaries

8. Protect the inputs and helpers the result depends on

Encrypting a message protects only a particular path and property. The result can still depend on manipulated location, time, routing, helper access, or model behavior outside that path.

Minimum disclosure
Reveal only the information needed by the intended query. Measure which required answers remain possible and what observations still leak.
Apply it

Limit the information exposed to a scheduler or helper to the fields needed for its decision.

Where it fails: Extra prompt, tenant, or model information can leak data without improving the decision.

Evidence boundary: PrvTel connects compact telemetry retention with differential privacy; the minimum-disclosure question here is broader, and its example is original.

Inspect the named source

Authorization and environmental inputs
Distinguish code that is safe to execute from an action the caller is allowed to request. Include unauthenticated inputs that influence it.
Apply it

Check both authorization and environment: model version, device, filesystem, and request identity.

Where it fails: A correctly authorized request can still use an unsafe helper or unexpected environment.

Evidence boundary: Wallet is a primary example of defining a trust boundary for sensitive serverless data; the authorization checklist here is original, not a claim about Wallet.

Inspect the named source

Collaboration and output checks
Define what participants may learn or change and how contributed results are checked. Decentralization alone supplies no trust guarantee.
Apply it

Validate output shape, content, and provenance before returning a collaborative result to the caller.

Where it fails: A fast response with the wrong model version or incomplete tokens is not an accepted result.

Evidence boundary: The over-threshold private-set-intersection paper defines what a collaborative result reveals; output validation is an original extension, not a reported mechanism.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Consider an invented authorization rule: a caller may retrieve only its own report. A transport protects the request from modification while it travels, but the service chooses the report using an account number supplied by the caller. If it never checks that number against the authenticated identity, a caller can request someone else's report through a perfectly protected connection. Protection in transit preserves the submitted request; it does not decide whether that request is allowed.

Information limits also concern combinations of allowed answers. Suppose a statistics helper reports an exact total of 40 for a group, then an exact total of 33 for the same group excluding one person. Subtraction reveals that person's contribution, seven. Neither answer names the contribution directly. An access rule claiming to conceal individual contributions must consider which related queries are permitted together. This constructed example is not a claim about a named privacy system.

Check your reasoning

Would using an encrypted connection for both total queries prevent the caller from learning seven? Would returning only signed answers make an incorrect contributed total correct?

Read the reasoning

No. Encryption can protect the transport from specified outside observers, but the intended caller still receives both totals and can subtract them. A signature can establish that a particular signer endorsed particular bytes; it does not establish that the underlying arithmetic or input data is correct. Confidentiality, authorization, origin, and correctness require distinct checks.

Evidence boundary. Wallet, Securitas, PlanetServe, PrvTel, and SwitchBFT are leads under distinct threat models. Preserve their differences rather than summarizing the theme as encryption or secure networking.

Review: Threat models · Checked properties

9. Change the representation only with a stated acceptance rule

Before reducing a message, write down what its receiver must do. Restoring an archived file requires the original bytes. Raising an alarm may require only knowing whether any reading crossed a threshold. A picture that looks plausible may still omit the object a detector needs. These are different requirements. Once two distinct inputs become the same transmitted message, the receiver cannot distinguish them from that message alone. A smaller representation is acceptable only if the lost distinctions do not change the required result.

Task-relevant communication
Retain information needed for the downstream task. Evaluate missed cases rather than assuming similar-looking output is equivalent.
Apply it

Compare the two sensor traces with average two. Only one exceeds five, so their common average cannot support the alarm decision. Choose the representation from the question the receiver must answer.

Where it fails: Discarding the difference between two inputs with different required answers makes exact decision-making impossible from that message alone.

Evidence boundary: KDC’s official abstract describes task-oriented representations. The four-sample alarm is an original information-loss example, not a measured KDC workload.

Inspect the named source

Reconstruction and user experience
Distinguish visual fidelity from the experience or decision that matters. Prior knowledge can help reconstruction while failing on unusual inputs.
Apply it

Count reconstruction time and check the downstream decision after reducing transmitted data. Include unusual inputs where the receiver’s prior knowledge may suggest the wrong reconstruction.

Where it fails: A plausible image or likely sensor trace does not establish that the missing input has been recovered exactly.

Evidence boundary: KDC’s official abstract describes receiver-side knowledge and updated context. The proposed unusual-input tests are reading guidance, not reported failures.

Inspect the named source

Temporal and cache validity
Preserve event order when timing relationships matter. Check whether a semantically similar cached result is actually permitted for the new request.
Apply it

Separate finding a similar query from deciding that its old answer applies. In the teaching command example, preserve the requested software version before accepting reuse.

Where it fails: A relevant-looking answer can describe an older version and change the user’s result. Include the cost and accuracy of the reuse check.

Evidence boundary: Cortex’s official abstract describes candidate retrieval followed by a small language-model judge. The version example is original and does not assert a Cortex bug.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

In an invented four-sample sensor trace, values are 0, 0, 8, 0. The receiver must report whether any sample exceeds five. Sending only the average, two, saves data but loses the required distinction: the trace 2, 2, 2, 2 has the same average and should not trigger the alarm. Once both traces have the same transmitted representation, a receiver using only that representation cannot answer correctly for both.

For the narrower task of detecting any exceedance, sending the maximum, eight, is sufficient. For locating when the exceedance happened, the maximum alone is insufficient; include its position or another representation that retains the needed timing. For reconstructing all four original samples exactly, neither summary suffices. The application's question determines what can be discarded.

Reuse has a similar condition. A cached alarm result for a particular sensor and interval remains valid only for that interval and its specified data version. A nearby interval with a similar average may contain a new spike. Choosing a cache key by superficial similarity does not preserve the alarm's meaning.

Knowledge-Driven Communication, or KDC, uses trained models to turn source data into compact representations and prioritize information relevant to a task. At the receiver, trained knowledge and updated context help reconstruct information for that task. The intended answer may therefore depend on what the receiver already knows as well as what arrives. In the sensor example, prior knowledge might make one missing trace seem more likely, but it cannot establish which of two indistinguishable traces actually occurred. Evaluate the task on cases where a plausible reconstruction could change the decision, and include reconstruction time when comparing delivery costs. These are reading questions, not claims that KDC fails those tests.

Cortex tries to reuse previously retrieved knowledge when a language-model application asks a related query. It first finds candidates using an embedding, a numerical representation of a query, then uses a small language model to judge whether a candidate is suitable. The separation matters: similarity narrows the search, while the second stage decides whether reuse is appropriate. The judge itself consumes processing resources; Cortex's abstract describes sharing resources and scheduling it alongside the main model. A fair comparison must count that checking cost and evaluate answer correctness as well as retrieval speed.

For an invented reuse failure, consider two similarly worded questions about a software command, one for version 1 and one for version 2. If the command's behavior changed, the older answer may sound relevant and still be wrong. Preserving the version requirement is part of accepting the answer. A learned judge is a mechanism to evaluate, not proof that every such distinction will be preserved. This example asks what a reuse test must cover; it does not report a Cortex defect.

Check your reasoning

Can the same maximum and its first position distinguish traces 0, 8, 0, 0 and 0, 8, 7, 0? Is that representation enough to count samples exceeding five?

Read the reasoning

Both summaries say maximum eight at position two, but the first trace has one exceedance and the second has two. The summary answers whether any exceedance exists, not how many. If counting is the only required question, transmitting the count can suffice; if later queries are unknown, retaining only that count restricts what can be answered later.

Evidence boundary. KDC and Cortex (NSDI 2026) illustrate task-oriented reconstruction and reuse across related queries. Their official USENIX abstracts support the mechanism summaries in this theme. KDC reports a prototype evaluated across data types and wireless networks; Cortex reports search and coding workloads. Their task-accuracy results must remain attached to those tests. Neither summary establishes exact reconstruction or correct reuse for every input. Morphe, Stimpack, and CascadeNet remain further reading leads. The sensor and version examples here are original teaching cases.

Review: Approximation · Reuse validity · Acceptance rules

10. Bound what a predictive model is allowed to decide

A forecast or simulated comparison can support a choice without having tested that choice in the live system. The evidence must say where predictions are calibrated and what happens when their error is too large.

Error and action limits
Connect a statistical bound to the particular action it permits. State the assumptions and failure probability rather than calling it simply safe.
Apply it

Set an explicit error or delay limit before allowing a predictive model to change scheduling or admission.

Where it fails: A model with good average error can make unsafe decisions near a hard boundary.

Evidence boundary: CCEval uses repeated trials and confidence intervals to reason about uncertain performance estimates; the per-job admission bound in this lesson is original.

Inspect the named source

What-if comparisons
Predict an intervention's consequence while keeping the model's omissions visible. A modeled improvement is not a measured deployment gain.
Apply it

Change one arrival, length, or state condition at a time in a what-if comparison and recompute the whole path.

Where it fails: A scenario that changes several conditions cannot show which factor caused the result.

Evidence boundary: Slowpoke directly studies modeled what-if changes to end-to-end throughput; the lesson’s counterfactual arithmetic is original.

Inspect the named source

Configuration search
Include the cost of trying candidates, monitoring drift, and returning to a known acceptable setting when predictions stop matching observations.
Apply it

Search configurations only after defining the feasible region, evaluation budget, and independent validation check.

Where it fails: A search can choose a noisy lucky configuration or discard a valid one through an unsafe early screen.

Evidence boundary: CCEval’s evaluation of trial variability motivates the evidence boundary; the configuration-search protocol here is original.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Suppose an invented controller may admit a job only when its peak memory will fit within 10 GB. It predicts 8 GB. If an independently justified bound guarantees that actual peak is at most prediction plus 1 GB for this job class, admission fits: at most 9 GB is needed. If all the controller knows is that mean prediction error on old jobs was 1 GB, it has no such per-job bound. A mean can hide a rare error large enough to exhaust memory.

For a concrete record, nine jobs have zero prediction error and one is underpredicted by 10 GB. Mean absolute error is 1 GB, yet the worst error is ten times that mean. A controller must connect the kind of evidence it has to the action it takes. An empirical average, a probability estimate under stated conditions, and a guaranteed upper bound permit different claims.

Trying settings also consumes work. If exploring a candidate costs 30 seconds and the candidate saves 2 seconds per later job, fifteen jobs merely repay exploration and sixteen are the first whole-number net saving. This assumes the same saving persists and ignores no additional monitoring or rollback costs. If the workload changes after ten jobs, the measured local improvement has not recovered the search cost.

Check your reasoning

A valid per-job upper bound is now prediction plus 2 GB. With 10 GB of available memory, what is the largest admissible prediction? If another admitted job can occupy 1 GB before allocation, what must change?

Read the reasoning

With the full 10 GB reserved for this job, predictions up to 8 GB fit the bound. If only 9 GB remains, the threshold is 7 GB. The controller must reserve capacity or recheck the applicable available space at admission; a valid demand bound does not prevent two callers from relying on the same unreserved capacity. If the bound itself no longer applies to the workload, neither threshold establishes safety.

Evidence boundary. PERCs, Slowpoke, SyncWise, OpenOptics, and CCEval are leads. Check whether the evidence is a model, a statistical claim, a hardware experiment, or a live deployment before transferring its conclusion.

Review: Evidence scope · Models versus measurements · Decision consequences

Practice reading a paper

A controller sees 4 GB waiting on a 2 GB/s path. It predicts two seconds to drain the queue. If new work continues arriving at 1 GB/s, the queue instead shrinks at 1 GB/s and takes four seconds to empty under constant-rate assumptions. If arrivals rise to 3 GB/s, it grows. Explain what additional state the controller needs, how old its measurements may be, and what action remains safe if arrivals change before that action takes effect. Then locate a paper record that states an observation-to-action delay rather than inferring one from a throughput result.
