Vary access pattern, sparsity, and reuse in the worked comparison until the extra organization cost exceeds the saving.

Where it fails: The mechanism stops helping when its setup or movement cost dominates the skipped work.

Evidence boundary: The VQ-LLM and MVE reviews record profiling and transition limits. The worker timings and break-even changes are original.

Inspect the named source

Hardware changes
Recheck conversion support, timing, capacity, and calibration on the new device. A fitted model is not automatically portable.
Apply it

Recheck conversion support, timing, capacity, and calibration when moving the design to another device.

Where it fails: A fitted model for one device does not automatically predict a different memory, clock, or power environment.

Evidence boundary: The DynamoLLM review limits its hardware evidence to a homogeneous H100 setup. The faster-worker comparison is original.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching workload: four workers each process two nonzero entries, one per cycle, from a row assigned to that worker. With no setup or transfer cost and no sharing of rows, eight entries finish in two cycles. Now keep exactly eight entries but distribute them as 5, 1, 1, and 1. Completion takes five cycles because one worker has five entries. The total amount of retained work stayed fixed; its placement changed the longest queue.

A revised scheduler can divide entries freely, assigning two to each worker. Suppose it adds two cycles for preparation and one for combining results, all sequential with calculation. Its total is 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 cycles, tying the uneven original schedule rather than beating it. On the evenly distributed input it would take five instead of two. An available redistribution mechanism therefore needs its own cost account.

Now suppose a new device processes two entries per worker per cycle but retains the same three-cycle preparation-and-combination cost. The uneven fixed assignment finishes in three cycles: the longest row needs the ceiling of 5/2. Redistribution needs one calculation cycle plus three extra cycles, totaling four. Faster arithmetic made the unchanged overhead more important. These are discrete-cycle teaching assumptions, not a performance prediction for either paper named in the reading leads.

The VQ-LLM review records codebook-access measurements tied to the model and hardware. If different entries become common, the old placement may no longer save as many reads from slower storage. The MVE review records time spent changing cache modes and work that cannot use its wide-vector operations. Shorter calculation phases can leave those costs as a larger share of a job. These are specific reasons to repeat a comparison, rather than assuming that a similar model name means a similar result.

The DynamoLLM review assumes H100 devices of the same kind. Moving its evaluated configuration to a mixed collection of devices would require new completion-rate, memory-capacity, and power evidence. The worker example makes the same reasoning visible with smaller numbers: changing arithmetic speed alone reversed the choice between fixed assignment and redistribution. A result for one device can identify what to measure on another without predicting the answer in advance.

Check your reasoning

Return to one entry per worker per cycle, but put all eight entries on one original worker. Under the stipulated redistribution cost, does splitting now help? What changed compared with 5,1,1,1?

Read the reasoning

The fixed assignment takes eight cycles. Redistribution still takes 2 + 2 + 1 = 5, saving three. The amount of work is still eight entries; only its original imbalance increased. That larger removable delay now exceeds the added scheduling cost. A claim based only on the total nonzero count would miss this change.

Evidence boundary. The local synthesis identifies model/hardware-dependent profiling for VQ-LLM, cache-transition assumptions for MVE, and homogeneous H100 assumptions for DynamoLLM. These are explicit reading boundaries, not reasons to dismiss the mechanisms or assume universal gains.

Review: Changed service conditions · Device boundaries

Practice reading a paper

A hypothetical special execution mode removes 6 ms of movement per job but costs 8 ms to enter and leave once per group. For one job it loses 2 ms. For four jobs sharing that transition it saves 4 × 6 − 8 = 16 ms in aggregate. This does not determine individual response delays: requests may wait for the group to assemble. List the arrival pattern, extra memory, output quality, and transition behavior needed before choosing the mode. These are teaching numbers, not reported HPCA measurements.

  • DynamoLLM — request-specific energy/SLO profiles, hierarchical control, and cluster results
  • DynamoLLM — combined serving-instance, model-division, and frequency control
  • LEGO — generated connections, memory arrangements, and intermediate storage
  • VQ-LLM — codebook placement, traffic-aware fusion, and generated kernels
  • EXION — inter/intra-iteration sparsity, compaction, and accelerator evaluation
  • MVE publication abstract — multidimensional instructions for in-cache calculation
  • IRIS — ISP/software saliency, mixed resolution, and machine-vision evaluation
  • Choco-Q — hard constraint encoding, circuit compilation, and NISQ evaluation
  • MVE author artifact — device benchmarks and proposed-engine simulation
  • HPCA evaluation review — measured and modeled components, comparisons, and limits
  • HPCA bounded synthesis — sample, mechanisms, and unresolved generalization

Back to the lessons

MICRO 2025: explain the small state change behind the larger result

Eight-theme route with explicit subtheme teaching blocks and two full walkthroughs (TRRIP and Pimba). Eighteen other source-backed records inform the synthesis, while broader paper coverage remains unfinished.

A processor does not execute from a blank slate. Cached values, ownership permissions, buffer occupancy, and earlier predictions affect its next action. Read a MICRO mechanism by naming the state before an event, the rule that changes it, and the work or waiting that changes afterward. This makes the hardware explanation concrete enough to connect to a software service.

Evidence boundary

The local synthesis covers 123 proceedings records. Twenty have extracted paper text and detailed written reviews of their evaluations; two of those records also have full learner walkthroughs here. The other 103 have only abstracts or titles; two attempts to obtain paper sources failed. Detailed claims in the synthesis use the 20 reviewed papers. Results remain author-reported. Device measurements, programmable-chip prototypes, design-tool estimates, simulations, and projections are identified separately.

Paper walkthrough: TRRIP: carry knowledge of code reuse to the cache

Paper walkthrough: Pimba: move repeated model-state work closer to where that state lives

1. Check what the machine already holds before the next request

The same request can take different amounts of time depending on what the machine already holds. A cached value may be ready to read, a missing value may need fetching, or an earlier fetch may still occupy the space needed by the next one. Start with those conditions, then follow the rule that changes them.

Which remembered information changes replacement?
Separate recent accesses from software predictions about future use. Ask how an outdated prediction can be revised or outweighed.
Apply it

Compare the recent-use rule with the invented permanent reservation. Track what remains in each slot when the program changes its accesses.

Where it fails: Keeping unused code indefinitely can leave too little space for the code that now runs. Replacement prediction does not establish shared-data validity.

Evidence boundary: TRRIP supplies code-use labels through page attributes. The permanent-reservation failure is original and is not TRRIP’s replacement policy.

Inspect the named source

What space does unfinished work occupy?
Count pending fetches as well as stored values. Mark when each occupied tracking record becomes available again.
Apply it

Keep the single fetch-tracking record occupied until A finishes at time 10. Only then start B’s fetch.

Where it fails: Ignoring the occupied record predicts B’s completion at 12 instead of 20, despite using the same ten-unit fetch duration.

Evidence boundary: The fetch-record example is original. The local TRRIP review records simulation and proxy workloads, not a fabricated cache or this exact capacity.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching cache: two slots hold recently used blocks. A hit takes one time unit; a miss, including loading the block, takes ten. On a miss with both slots full, remove the block used least recently. All accesses are sequential. Starting empty, the sequence A, B, A, C, A gives miss, miss, hit, miss, hit, totaling 32 units. When C arrives, B is removed because A was used more recently.

Change only the starting state to contain A and B. The same sequence gives hit, hit, hit, miss, hit, totaling 14 units. The program's requests did not change; the remembered state did. Comparing an empty-cache baseline with an already-filled alternative would mix a policy change with a starting-condition change.

Retaining a value also requires a rule for when it stops being valid. If another participant changes the underlying value of A, a fast read of an old cached A may return the wrong answer unless the system updates, removes, or otherwise coordinates that copy. A high hit rate describes reuse, not whether the returned value is permitted by the program's consistency rules.

TRRIP addresses cached instructions: the program steps the processor must fetch before executing them. Its compiler labels code according to expected use and passes that information through the operating system using attributes attached to code pages, fixed-size regions of program memory. The cache uses these labels to make replacement decisions. In the paper, hot and cold describe expected code use, not physical temperature. This supplies information beyond the most recent access, which is the only history used by our two-slot teaching rule.

A reuse label is a prediction, not a promise. In a separate invented example, suppose one slot is reserved indefinitely for code labeled frequently used, but that code stops running. With only one other slot available, alternating B and C always misses. Releasing the reservation lets both fit after their first loads. This is deliberately not TRRIP's policy; it shows why a reader should ask how stale predictions lose influence. The local TRRIP review records simulated mobile hardware and proxy workloads, not a manufactured cache test.

Unfinished work also occupies resources. Suppose an invented machine has one record for tracking a missing block while its fetch runs. A fetch for A starts at time 0 and finishes at 10. An unrelated B request arrives at time 2, but it cannot start its own ten-unit fetch until that record becomes free. B finishes at 20 and has waited 18 units since arrival. A model that gives B a free tracking record predicts completion at 12 instead. Both calculations use the same fetch duration; only one respects the stated capacity.

Check your reasoning

Starting empty, repeat A, B, C twice with the same two-slot rule. How many accesses hit? Why does knowing there are only three distinct blocks not determine the earlier sequence's timing?

Read the reasoning

All six accesses miss, totaling 60 time units. Each reuse occurs after the other two blocks have displaced the needed block. The earlier sequence repeatedly revisits A before it is displaced. Capacity and the set of requested blocks are not enough; the order and initial state determine which values survive until reuse.

Evidence boundary. TRRIP's publication abstract supports the compiler-to-cache prediction explanation. The local evaluation review records its simulated hardware and workload limits. The replacement traces, permanent-reservation failure, and single-fetch-record timeline are original examples, not reconstructions of TRRIP's algorithm. The shared-value validity paragraph raises a separate correctness requirement, not a guarantee supplied by replacement prediction.

Review: Reuse · Buffers · Model behavior

2. Count what still travels after moving the calculation

Calculating near stored data can replace a large transfer with a smaller result. First check that the smaller result contains everything the next step needs. Then count the local calculation, remaining transfers, and any work needed to put results in the right order. Fewer transferred values alone do not establish an earlier answer.

Which values no longer need transferring?
Write down the original inputs and the smaller result. Check that the next step does not need information discarded by the local calculation.
Apply it

Place a consumer beside its input and then count the values that still cross the partition boundary.

Where it fails: Moving one operation near data does not help if its partial results must immediately return across the same boundary.

Evidence boundary: Pimba’s abstract describes near-memory update units shared across banks. The subtotal and transfer arithmetic is original.

Inspect the named source

Can the next step identify and use each result?
Keep the meaning of each partial result separate from its arrival order. Count any tags, storage, or rearrangement needed before the next operation.
Apply it

Track R1 and R2 by identity even if R2 arrives first. The required subtraction is R2 − R1, not an operation chosen by arrival order.

Where it fails: Without result identifiers or a guaranteed order, the next operation can produce −4 instead of 4.

Evidence boundary: The labeled-subtotal example is original, not a Pimba protocol. The local review records Pimba’s modeled execution and remaining state-update dependencies.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching calculation: two partitions each contain four numbers. The desired answer is their sum. Sending all eight numbers to a host requires eight transferred values. Summing locally and sending one subtotal from each partition requires only two. Under exact integer arithmetic with adequate width, adding those two subtotals gives the same answer. The saving depends on the consumer needing the sum rather than the individual numbers.

Suppose the next consumer instead needs every original value in sorted order. Two subtotals are insufficient: partitions [1,1,1,5] and [2,2,2,2] both sum to eight but have different sorted values. A smaller intermediate representation has discarded information the new consumer requires. The local reduction is appropriate for one output contract, not all later uses.

For the sum task, assume a connection carries two values per millisecond, and ignore all other costs except two milliseconds of local subtotal calculation. Sending eight values takes four milliseconds; calculating locally and sending two takes 2 + 1 = 3. If the connection instead carries eight values per millisecond, the paths take one and 2.25 milliseconds. Less traffic still loses when the added calculation costs more than the transfer it removes. These are sequential teaching schedules, not measured hardware results.

Pimba targets language-model operations that repeatedly update stored state, meaning values carried from one generation step to the next. Its proposal puts calculation units near memory banks, the separately accessed regions of a memory device. Rather than duplicating an expensive update unit at every bank, it shares a unit between two banks and alternates their accesses. It also uses lower-precision arithmetic. This is a combined change to placement, hardware sharing, and numerical representation, not simply the same computation moved a shorter distance.

The local evaluation review records simulated Pimba timing and estimated hardware area and power, with output quality checked on listed tasks. It also records waiting caused by sequential state updates. Putting calculation near memory cannot make a later step independent of the state produced by an earlier one. When explaining its gains, keep the precision changes and comparison hardware visible; the evidence does not isolate proximity as the sole cause.

Output order is another separate cost. In an invented variant, two local units produce labeled subtotals R1 = 8 and R2 = 12, but the next operation needs R2 − R1. Receiving R2 first does not make it the first operand: labels still determine the answer, 4. If results arrive without identifiers and completion order can vary, subtracting the first arrival from the second can instead return −4. Reordering or tagging may be cheap, but its information and storage requirements belong in the design. This is a teaching example, not a Pimba output protocol.

Check your reasoning

At what transfer rate do the two sum paths tie? Keep the two-millisecond local calculation and assume the host's final arithmetic is free in both comparisons.

Read the reasoning

With rate r in values per millisecond, compare 8/r with 2 + 2/r. Equality gives r = 3. Below that rate the local sum wins; above it the direct transfer wins under this model. Finite-width rounding, transfer startup, and a different consumer would require revisiting the assumptions.

Evidence boundary. Pimba's publication abstract supports the shared update-unit, bank-access, and lower-precision explanation. Its local evaluation review records simulation, comparison differences, and sequential-update limits. The sums, transfer times, and labeled-subtotal example are original calculations rather than Pimba measurements or protocol details.

Review: Memory movement · Connection limits

3. Explain what the stored bits mean before calculating with them

A stored code is not necessarily the number the program needs. Its meaning may depend on a scale, an offset, or a table shared by several values. The operation reading those bits must use the same rules as the operation that stored them. Count the information needed to interpret the code as well as the code itself.

What information is shared by the group?
Count scales and offsets and check how one unusually large value affects the representation of smaller values.
Apply it

Change the invented group’s largest value from 7 to 28, then decode the smaller values using the new scale of four.

Where it fails: Making the largest value fit can coarsen the available steps for smaller values; fitting in range does not preserve every value.

Evidence boundary: MX+ supplies the outlier-representation connection. The unsigned codes, scales, and rounding convention are original.

Inspect the named source

Does the arithmetic use the same interpretation?
Follow the decoding rule through the operation. A sum of codes is not automatically a valid code for the sum.
Apply it

Decode codes 3 and 5 separately, then compare their sum with decoding raw code 8. Account for the offset once per original value.

Where it fails: Treating a sum of two codes as one encoded value subtracts the offset the wrong number of times.

Evidence boundary: The arithmetic is original. The MX+ evaluation review separates model quality, GPU software timing, and modeled arithmetic hardware.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching format: each stored code c represents the value 0.5 × (c − 3). Codes 3 and 5 therefore mean zero and one, not three and five. Their sum is one. Adding codes gives eight; decoding eight as if it were a single original code gives 2.5, which is wrong. The offset belongs to each input, so the correct decoded sum is 0.5 × (3 + 5 − 2 × 3) = 1.

For n values using the same scale and offset, the sum is scale × (sum of codes − n × offset), assuming exact arithmetic and enough accumulator range. If different groups use different scales, their raw code sums cannot simply be merged with one group's scale. The consumer needs the metadata and a valid combination rule, not merely the packed bits.

Storage accounting must include those rules' data. In an invented four-value group, one byte per code plus two bytes for scale and two for offset takes eight bytes, equal to four ordinary two-byte values. With sixteen values sharing the same metadata, the total is twenty bytes instead of thirty-two. That storage gain alone does not establish acceptable rounding, support for every value, or efficient decoding.

Shared scales can make an unusually large value determine the representation used by every other value in the group. Consider an original format with unsigned codes zero through seven and a shared scale of one. Values 1, 2, 3, and 7 fit exactly. Replace 7 with 28 and choose scale four so that the largest value still fits. Rounding each value to the nearest representable multiple of four, with ties rounded upward, turns the group into 0, 4, 4, and 28. The largest value fits, but the smaller values have changed. This illustrates a shared-scale tradeoff, not the actual MX encoding.

MX+ addresses large, unusual values within groups that share scaling information. In floating-point formats, an exponent selects a range of magnitudes while a significand supplies detail within that range. The MX+ publication abstract explains that the selected outlier does not need its usual per-value exponent field; the proposal reuses those bits for additional significand detail. That works because the consuming arithmetic knows the changed interpretation. An ordinary decoder cannot simply assume those bits still mean what they meant before.

The local MX+ review separates three kinds of evidence: model-quality tests, GPU software execution, and modeled hardware with estimated circuit cost. Higher model quality does not by itself prove faster execution. Nor does a small predicted arithmetic cost establish a measured complete-system result. Preserve those distinctions when connecting a format change to a serving-time claim.

Check your reasoning

Using the same scale 0.5 and offset 3, decode codes 2 and 6 individually and compute their sum. Compare the correct combination with decoding their raw sum as one code.

Read the reasoning

They decode to −0.5 and 1.5, summing to 1. Correct combination gives 0.5 × (2 + 6 − 6) = 1. Decoding the raw sum eight as a single code gives 0.5 × (8 − 3) = 2.5. The same bits have different meanings depending on whether they represent one value or the sum of two codes.

Evidence boundary. MX+'s publication abstract supports the outlier-bit reinterpretation mechanism; its local evaluation review separates quality, software timing, and modeled hardware. The offset arithmetic and unsigned shared-scale example are original teaching formats, not MX or MX+ encodings.

Review: Precision · Executable representations

4. Count the work needed to divide and schedule other work

Dividing a long job can let several workers finish it sooner. But someone must find the pieces, assign them, track their progress, and combine their results. Smaller pieces give more scheduling choices while creating more of this management work. Compare complete schedules, not just the time spent calculating.

Does dividing the job save more than it costs?
Include preparation and result assembly in the seven-versus-eight-versus-five comparison. Also check whether reassignment adds data fetches.
Apply it

Compare grouped and dispersed activity while charging grouping metadata, setup, and synchronization.

Where it fails: A more balanced grouping can lose when per-group control work exceeds the saved idle time.

Evidence boundary: The Task-LP review separates hardware task placement from precomputed server groupings. The split-job timings are original.

Inspect the named source

Which event makes the next operation wait?
Track items entering and leaving storage. A full buffer can stop the producer even when the long-run average rate looks acceptable.
Apply it

Draw the event timeline instead of using only an average rate; include full-buffer and refill events.

Where it fails: An average can hide the moment a buffer fills and legally blocks the producer.

Evidence boundary: The OmniSim review describes conditional queues, dependencies, and deadlock tests against detailed simulation. The two-slot burst is original.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching schedule: two workers receive jobs needing seven and one time units. With one indivisible job per worker, completion takes seven. If the long job can be divided into seven independent one-unit pieces and the short job is one more piece, four pieces per worker finish in four units. But suppose splitting requires two units of preparation and two of result assembly, both outside the parallel stage. Total completion becomes eight, slower than the original seven.

Now use two coarse groups for the long job, of sizes four and three. Put the short job beside the three-unit group, giving four units of work per worker. If this coarser plan needs 0.5 units to prepare and 0.5 to assemble, completion is five. Both split plans achieve the same arithmetic balance; different control costs determine which finishes sooner. All three plans must preserve the same required result.

A controller also needs enough detail to enforce storage limits. Suppose a producer emits four items together, a consumer cannot start for two cycles, and only two item slots are available. A long-run average rate below the consumer's eventual capacity does not make that four-item burst fit. The producer must wait, use other storage, or follow another legal schedule. Ignoring the burst changes the allowed execution, not merely the predicted average.

Task-LP studies another cost of assigning work: whether a task runs near data that a previous task has already brought into a processor's cache. Its local evaluation review describes a hardware placement engine on a programmable FPGA device, tested with 24 processor cores and room to track 128 unfinished tasks. The review attributes gains to fewer reads that miss in the nearest data cache. This makes placement different from simply equalizing task counts: two equally busy workers can still spend different amounts of time fetching data.

The same review separates that hardware experiment from an experiment on a larger server using task groups computed in advance. The latter can test the effect of those groups, but does not measure the complete proposed placement hardware running in that server. The review also records sensitivity to the relationships between tasks and to how many tasks can no longer be reassigned. A grouping decision has value only while enough legal placements remain and its management cost is covered by the saving.

OmniSim addresses the timing-detail side of this theme. Its local review describes tests that include conditional queue accesses, cycles of dependent work, and deadlock: a condition in which unfinished operations wait on one another and none can proceed. The authors compare outputs and timing with a more detailed hardware simulation. A simpler average-rate model cannot explain the two-slot burst above because it has removed the event that fills the storage. The review limits OmniSim's evidence to its supported queue and execution rules and tested examples, not every possible hardware program.

Check your reasoning

For either split plan with four time units of parallel calculation, how small must total preparation plus assembly be to beat the unsplit seven? Does that inequality establish enough buffer space?

Read the reasoning

The combined extra cost must be strictly less than three time units. Exactly three ties; more loses. This timing inequality says nothing about simultaneous stored items. Capacity requires a separate check of the schedule and which values remain live at each step.

Evidence boundary. The local MICRO evaluation review supplies Task-LP's placement and experiment boundaries and OmniSim's event-model tests. The split-job timings and two-slot burst are original teaching examples, not measurements from either paper. Task grouping and simulation detail answer different questions; neither is automatically preferable merely because it operates on smaller events.

Review: Stage boundaries · Grouping costs

5. Check the fast path's conditions before using it

A fast implementation may support only certain inputs or instructions. Name that restriction and the software responsible for enforcing it. Then explain what happens when the restriction does not hold: use another implementation, handle the remaining work separately, or reject the request explicitly. A past record of suitable inputs is not proof that the next input is suitable.

Does the generated program cover every required entry?
Check complete groups and the remainder separately. Producing instructions that run does not prove that they process the full requested input.
Apply it

Compare the generated instructions with an independent reference behavior, including boundary and state cases.

Where it fails: Successful code generation or parsing does not prove that the emitted instruction sequence preserves behavior.

Evidence boundary: The RISSP evaluation review requires retargeting and verification for unsupported instructions. The four-entry implementation is original.

Inspect the named source

What does a timing prediction actually establish?
Keep resource and waiting assumptions visible. A time estimate does not prove that omitted instructions or input cases have valid replacements.
Apply it

List which cache, memory, and timing details the model retains before trusting its scheduling prediction.

Where it fails: A model can rank policies incorrectly if it omits the resource that actually becomes full.

Evidence boundary: The OmniSim review bounds the supported queue/execution model; the RISSP review bounds instruction compatibility. Neither proves this invented fast path correct.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching implementation: a vector operation handles four entries at a time. A fast path works only when the vector length is divisible by four. For length eight it processes two complete groups. For length ten, applying that same path without a remainder rule either omits the last two entries or accesses values outside the requested vector. Generating executable instructions has not established that those instructions implement every allowed input.

A guarded implementation first checks the length, then uses either the fast path or a general implementation. Suppose this check costs one time unit, a supported request costs four more, and a fallback costs ten more. For ten requests, eight supported and two unsupported, total cost is 10 × 1 + 8 × 4 + 2 × 10 = 62 units. Using the general implementation directly for every request costs 100. The guard pays for itself in this workload while preserving a stated route for unsupported inputs.

If all ten requests are unsupported, the guarded route costs 110 and loses. A profile reporting that most requests used to be supported is not a substitute for checking the condition when inputs can change. Conversely, if a compiler can establish the condition for every execution of a particular call, a repeated runtime check might be unnecessary. The responsibility is to justify the assumption at the point where the fast path relies on it.

Falling back for the entire request is not the only possible implementation. For a length-ten input, two four-entry groups could use the fast operation and the final two entries could use a separate routine. But that combined path needs its own checks: each entry must be processed exactly once, the last operation must stay within the input, and any required output order must be preserved. Its execution time is also a new measurement; the four-unit fast-path cost above covers only the originally stipulated supported request.

The local RISSP review gives a hardware example of restricted support. A processor's instruction set is the collection of operations its program can ask it to perform. RISSP generates processors with application-specific subsets, based on records of the instructions used by the application. Removing unneeded support can reduce hardware cost. If later software uses an omitted instruction, however, a changed program must express that work using supported instructions and be checked for the same required behavior. The review does not establish automatic compatibility with arbitrary future programs.

The RISSP evaluation uses selected applications and a specialized flexible-chip technology, with circuit generation and physical-layout analysis. Those results support the stated design comparison, not a general guarantee for other processors. OmniSim, discussed in the preceding theme, supplies a complementary reminder: a timing model must retain the queues and dependencies that determine execution. A model that predicts a fast instruction sequence still does not prove that the sequence handles the final two entries correctly. Timing evidence and evidence of correct behavior answer different questions.

Check your reasoning

For ten requests with these costs, how many must use the fast path before the guarded implementation is strictly faster? Would a timing win excuse processing only eight entries of a ten-entry request?

Read the reasoning

With s supported requests, cost is 10 + 4s + 10(10 − s) = 110 − 6s. Beating 100 requires s > 10/6, so two supported requests suffice, giving 98 units. Omitting entries still violates the requested operation. The timing comparison applies only after the implementation preserves the specified result on both paths.

Evidence boundary. The local MICRO review records RISSP's application-specific instruction support and verification limits, alongside OmniSim's supported execution model. The four-entry fast path, length checks, and remainder alternative are original examples, not RISSP instructions or measured compiler behavior.

Review: Compilation · Evidence for transformations

6. Name the requirement before choosing the score

Finishing sooner, producing a close numerical answer, and preventing an unauthorized change are different requirements. A test of one does not establish the others. State what the user needs to remain true, then choose a measurement that checks that requirement.

What must the attacker be unable to change?
State the unwanted effect, the access the test grants, and the tested hardware. Count attack outcomes separately from useful application performance.
Apply it

State the attacker’s allowed observations and the exact forbidden effect before interpreting the attack trace.

Where it fails: A failed attack in one setup does not prove protection against a different observer, input, or placement.

Evidence boundary: The local ρHammer review records real-platform attack results with privilege and memory-configuration limits. The ten-trial example is original.

Inspect the named source

Which error matters to the next operation?
Check each required output property, not just average numerical closeness. A fast image update can still give an unacceptable position estimate.
Apply it

Check both frame rate and position error in the toy tracking example. The 40-frame-per-second case fails its separate error limit.

Where it fails: A favorable average image score or high frame rate can hide an unacceptable position estimate.

Evidence boundary: The RTGS review separates rendering quality, camera-estimation error, and modeled hardware timing. The 5 cm threshold and toy results are original.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching output: the exact two-value result is [0, 10]. Approximation A returns [0.2, 9.8]; approximation B returns [0, 9.5]. A's mean absolute error is 0.2, smaller than B's 0.25. But if the consumer decides whether the first value is strictly above 0.1, A changes that decision and B preserves it. A better average numerical score does not necessarily preserve the decision the consumer needs.

A different requirement can reverse the choice. If every output value must be within 0.3 of its exact value, A passes and B fails because its second value is off by 0.5. Neither requirement is inherently the right one for every application. State the consumer's obligation before selecting the metric or accepting the approximation.

Security outcomes require another boundary. An invented test campaign might observe a forbidden effect in three of ten trials under one fixed setup. That is a count for those trials, not a throughput score, a general failure probability, or proof about other conditions. Seeing no forbidden effect in a different ten-trial campaign would not establish that the effect is impossible. Specify the allowed actions, observed effect, and tested conditions separately from performance and numerical quality.

ρHammer studies RowHammer, where repeated memory activity can disturb stored bits that the program did not directly write. Its reported bit-flip rate counts unwanted changes, not accepted results delivered to a user. The local review ties its experiments to named processor and memory configurations and administrator-level privileges. It also excludes other memory and protection configurations. Those conditions belong beside the result: the study does not establish that every machine is affected or that an untested machine is protected.

RTGS raises a different question about reduced work. Its local review separates image quality, the accuracy of the estimated camera position and orientation, and the number of frames processed each second. It records that aggressive removal of scene elements can cause the camera estimate to drift. A visually similar image is therefore not sufficient evidence that the system tracks its movement accurately. As with the two-value example, the acceptable error depends on what the next operation uses the output to do.

For a concrete original acceptance check, suppose a toy tracking application requires at least 30 frames per second and position error no larger than 5 cm on every tested frame. One configuration produces 40 frames per second but reaches 8 cm error; another produces 32 and stays within 4 cm. Only the second passes both stated rules on those tests. Averages over frames would answer a different question from the per-frame limit. These thresholds and results are invented, not RTGS measurements or requirements for a real navigation system.

Check your reasoning

A third approximation returns [0.05, 9.75]. Check both the first-value decision and the per-value error limit of 0.3. What is its mean absolute error?

Read the reasoning

The first value remains below 0.1, preserving the exact result's decision. Absolute errors are 0.05 and 0.25, both within 0.3. Their mean is 0.15. This candidate satisfies both stated requirements on this example; it does not establish either property for untested inputs or say anything about a separate security requirement.

Evidence boundary. The ρHammer publication record establishes the attack study; its local review states platform and privilege limits. The RTGS review separates visual quality, camera estimates, and modeled hardware performance. All tiny numerical outputs, trial counts, and tracking thresholds here are original teaching examples.

Review: Security boundaries · Correctness · Numerical quality

7. Convert the proposed schedule into time and required space

A design that needs fewer clock cycles can still take longer if each cycle lasts longer. A schedule that overlaps more work can still fail if its temporary results do not fit. Check time and space together, using the operating conditions of the device being compared.

Operating limits
Name memory capacity, link rate, frequency, and transition costs. Check whether the evaluated workload exercises the limiting condition.
Apply it

Place memory size, link rate, clock, and transition costs beside the workload’s actual request volume.

Where it fails: A design that fits the average case can fail when the workload reaches the limiting capacity.

Evidence boundary: The ReGate review records workload-dependent power-control costs. The frequency, capacity, and idle-energy calculations are original.

Inspect the named source

Technology assumptions
Separate parameters obtained from hardware from those synthesized, modeled, or projected. Changing technology can change the tradeoff, not just scale every cost equally.
Apply it

Label every technology parameter as measured, synthesized, modeled, or projected before changing it.

Where it fails: A new process or device can change leakage, routing, conversion, and clock tradeoffs in different directions.

Evidence boundary: The ReGate review separates circuit estimates and calibrated simulation from measured processor observations. Its complete-workload savings remain modeled.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching comparison: implementation A needs 100 cycles for a job and runs at 1 GHz, giving one nanosecond per cycle and 100 nanoseconds total. Implementation B needs only 70 cycles but runs at 500 MHz, giving two nanoseconds per cycle and 140 nanoseconds total. Reducing cycle count by 30% has increased elapsed time by 40%. The operating rate is part of the implementation, not a unit conversion that can be omitted from the result.

Suppose both jobs also require a separate, sequential 60-nanosecond transfer. Complete times become 160 and 200 nanoseconds. If a redesigned B sustains 800 MHz with the same 70-cycle count and transfer cost, its total becomes 87.5 + 60 = 147.5 nanoseconds. This is a conditional calculation: changing the operating rate may change other costs, and the stated rate still needs supporting evidence.

A physical implementation can also trade storage for timing. If the faster version requires three simultaneously live 3-MB buffers on a device with 8 MB available, that proposed schedule does not fit. Reusing storage is legal only after the old contents are no longer needed. Additional transfers or a different schedule must be counted before applying the faster timing estimate to that device.

ReGate provides a related power question. Its local review describes selectively disconnecting power from unused parts of a neural-network processor, a technique called power gating. The potential saving depends on how long those parts remain unused and on the timing and hardware costs of controlling their power. The review separates estimated circuit costs from whole-workload energy predicted by a simulator checked against available processor observations. Agreement with those observations does not make every proposed power-gating result a device measurement.

For an original example, suppose keeping a unit powered while idle consumes 2 watts, while switching it off and restoring it costs 6 millijoules in total. Ignore off-state power and assume no added waiting. Three milliseconds of idle time would otherwise consume 6 millijoules, so that interval only ties; a longer interval can save energy under these assumptions. If restoring the unit delays needed work, the energy calculation alone cannot decide whether switching it off is acceptable. These costs are invented, not ReGate parameters.

Check your reasoning

With the same 60-nanosecond transfer on both paths and an unchanged 70-cycle count for B, what operating rate makes B tie A's complete time? Does meeting that rate resolve the buffer shortage?

Read the reasoning

The equal transfer costs cancel, leaving B 100 nanoseconds for 70 cycles: 0.7 cycles per nanosecond, or 700 MHz. Faster than that wins only under the fixed-cost assumptions. Three simultaneous 3-MB buffers still need 9 MB, exceeding 8. A timing threshold does not establish storage feasibility.

Evidence boundary. The local ReGate evaluation review records technology, power-control, and workload assumptions, including omitted or abstracted energy costs. It supports the power-gating connection, not the invented frequency, buffer, or switching-energy numbers. Each calculation here states the costs held fixed; a physical implementation must justify them.

Review: Physical constraints · Routes

8. Match the conclusion to the experiment that produced it

When two systems differ, identify what changed before assigning credit for the result. Did the rule change, the machine change, or both? Then label each number as measured or predicted and state the work it includes. A detailed prediction can explain an idea without being a measurement of a built device.

Controlled comparisons
Keep input, accepted result, and resource assumptions comparable. Explain which change caused the gain and which other settings changed with it.
Apply it

Hold input trace, accepted result, resource budget, and comparison settings fixed while changing one mechanism.

Where it fails: A gain cannot be assigned to the proposed policy if the workload or resource allocation changed with it.

Evidence boundary: The commercial compute-in-SRAM review records separate layout/transfer optimizations and their combination. The four-combination timing tables are original.

Inspect the named source

Scope of observation
A paper can combine a measured component with a projected full design. Label each result at its own boundary rather than giving the whole paper one evidence label.
Apply it

Separate a measured kernel or simulator component from the projected full design that surrounds it.

Where it fails: One measured component does not make estimated caches, links, or software integration measured.

Evidence boundary: The commercial compute-in-SRAM review identifies directly measured device components combined with simulated external-memory timing in the retrieval study.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching experiment: the old rule takes 100 milliseconds on an old machine; the new rule takes 60 on a new machine. Those two observations establish a 40-millisecond difference between the combined configurations. They do not isolate how much came from the rule, the machine, or their interaction.

Now measure all four combinations on the same workload and acceptance requirement. On the old machine, the old rule takes 100 and the new rule 90 milliseconds. On the new machine, they take 70 and 60. The rule saves 10 milliseconds on either machine in this invented table; changing the machine saves 30 under either rule. The savings happen to add here. A different table could show that a rule helps on one machine and hurts on another, so this separation must be measured rather than assumed.

Keep the evidence stage attached to each number too. Suppose a component is measured to take 4 milliseconds, while an unbuilt surrounding system is modeled to add 6 sequential milliseconds. Ten milliseconds is then a combined measured-and-modeled estimate, not a measurement of the full system. If the modeled part actually takes 9, the total is 13 even if the component measurement was exact. A trustworthy component measurement does not remove uncertainty from everything around it.

The MICRO study of a commercial compute-in-SRAM device provides a concrete case. It measures calculation on a GSI Leda-E device, which performs operations within its memory arrays. The local review records separate versions with changes to reduction placement, transfer grouping, and data layout, as well as their combination. Those separate comparisons help ask which changes reduce the time spent moving and organizing data. A comparison only between the original version and the combined version would not isolate each contribution.

The same study's retrieval application mixes direct device measurements with simulated timing for a different external-memory arrangement. The local review explicitly identifies that combined result as partly measured and partly modeled. This is not a reason to discard it; it tells the reader which remaining component could change the prediction. Keep the measured device result, the proposed memory configuration, and the complete application estimate as three distinct claims.

Check your reasoning

In a second experiment, keep old-machine times at 100 and 90 milliseconds, but let new-machine times be 70 for the old rule and 80 for the new rule. Does comparing 100 with 80 establish that the new rule helps?

Read the reasoning

No. The combined change still reduces time from 100 to 80, but on the new machine the rule makes execution 10 milliseconds slower, from 70 to 80. On the old machine it saves 10. The effect depends on the machine. The four-combination comparison reveals this interaction; the two combined endpoints hide it.

Evidence boundary. The local commercial compute-in-SRAM review supplies the separate-optimization comparisons and the mixed measured/simulated retrieval result. The four-combination timing tables are original. No MICRO experiment has been independently reproduced by this course, and combining results from separate papers requires a new complete-system comparison.

Review: Projection versus measurement · Whole-service comparison

Practice reading a paper

An illustrative cache policy avoids ten misses costing 100 ns each, but adds a 2-ns lookup to each of 1,000 serial accesses. It saves 1,000 ns and adds 2,000 ns, so total time increases by 1,000 ns. If the extra lookup overlaps other independent work completely, that conclusion may change—but overlap needs a resource and dependency argument. Identify the access count, miss behavior, and timing model a paper must report before a lower miss count can be called a speedup.
