Back to the lessons

DATE 2025: test whether a changed design still does the intended job

Eight-theme route with explicit subtheme teaching blocks and two full walkthroughs (CorrectBench and High-Throughput SAT Sampling). Thirteen other source-backed records inform the synthesis; broader paper review remains unfinished.

Begin with the difference between an intended design and its actual behavior. A generated test may check the wrong property. A simulated structure that meets its modeled timing target may still be impossible to manufacture. A memory policy may behave differently under pressure. The DATE route follows how systems expose, test, and respond to those gaps rather than assuming that producing a design description finishes the work.

Evidence boundary

The local synthesis reports 425 records, with 15 locally extracted source-backed records; two of those records now have full learner walkthroughs here. The remaining 410 are discovery-level records: six source attempts failed and 404 records had no PDF URL. This route teaches from that bounded synthesis. The full proceedings have not received equivalent review, the results remain paper-reported, and no independent reproduction or composed cross-paper system is claimed.

Paper walkthrough: CorrectBench: who checks the generated checker?

Paper walkthrough: High-Throughput SAT Sampling: make many valid candidates at once

1. Show which values each operation needs

Changing how a program or problem is written can reveal work that runs in parallel. It can also hide a dependency or change the allowed answers. Before claiming a faster execution, check which values each operation reads and whether the rewritten problem still describes the intended task.

What can run together, and what must wait?
Name the specific value each operation reads. Keep a dependency whenever a later operation needs a result that has not yet been produced.
Apply it

Use the execution example to count what can run independently and what must wait for a shared value.

Where it fails: A regular or smaller description can still preserve a dependency that prevents the expected speedup.

Evidence boundary: The SAT-sampling review connects logical rewriting to GPU operations. The old/new-y schedule is original, not a paper benchmark.

Inspect the named source

Does rewriting preserve the allowed answers?
Check how solutions of the rewritten problem map back to the original constraints. Preserving the existence of a solution is not the same as checking every returned answer or its variety.
Apply it

Enumerate the allowed x/f pairs, then compare the two constraints with the explicit f = not x operation.

Where it fails: An existence-preserving transformation alone does not certify the validity or variety of every returned sample.

Evidence boundary: The SAT paper describes an equisatisfiable transformation and valid, distinct solutions. The two-variable explanation illustrates its inverter relation.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching program: set y to x + 1, then set z to twice the new y. Initially x is 3 and the old y is 10. The requested result is y = 4 and z = 8. If two workers start together and the second reads the old y before the first writes, z becomes 20. Two available workers do not make these operations independent.

Give the values different names: y_old is 10, y_new is x + 1, and z is 2 × y_new. This description exposes the dependency that the schedule must preserve. With one millisecond for each operation and no other costs, the earliest correct finish is two milliseconds. A one-millisecond finish obtained by reading y_old computes a different function, even if its output happens to match on a particular input.

The same question arises when code accesses memory through names whose locations are chosen at runtime. Suppose one operation increments the value at location p, then another reads location q. If p and q name the same location, the read needs the updated value. If they are known to be different and there are no other shared effects, this particular dependency disappears. A tool must retain that distinction, prove it, or check it before using a schedule that relies on it.

DATE's High-Throughput SAT Sampling paper applies rewriting to logical constraints. SAT asks whether there is an assignment of true or false values that satisfies all the constraints; sampling seeks multiple satisfying assignments. The paper reconstructs logical operations from a flat collection of constraints and arranges the work for GPU execution. Its transformation produces an equisatisfiable problem: a solution exists for the transformed problem exactly when one exists for the original. That is an existence statement. A sampler must also recover assignments that satisfy the original constraints; producing many duplicates does not establish distinct answers or their selection probabilities.

A small example makes the recovered structure visible. Let x and f each be either false or true. Require both 'f or x' and 'not f or not x'. The first rule forbids both values being false; the second forbids both being true. The only allowed pairs are (x=false, f=true) and (x=true, f=false), so the rules express f = not x. Writing that operation explicitly reveals a direct way to produce f from x. It does not make all other operations independent: anything using f still needs its value.

Validity, variety, and selection probability answer different questions. In an invented sampler for those two allowed pairs, suppose each independent draw chooses the first with probability 99% and the second with probability 1%. Every answer is valid, and both answers are possible, yet the sampler strongly favors the first. The chance of missing the second in 100 draws is 0.99 raised to the power 100, about 36.6%. Removing duplicates afterward does not recover an answer that was never drawn. Uniform sampling would give each allowed pair the same probability, here 50%; it would not require exactly equal counts in every finite run.

The paper's section IV counts unique, valid solutions per second; section V separately identifies an approximate-uniformity guarantee for the UNIGEN3 comparison method. A throughput result alone does not establish the same guarantee for another sampler. For testing, a rarely drawn valid input may exercise behavior the frequent inputs never reach. State whether the application needs any valid answer, many different answers, or a specified chance of selecting each answer before choosing its speed measure. The two-pair probability example above is original, not a measured bias in the paper's sampler.

The local evaluation review records public benchmark problems, limits on run time, and requirements on the solutions returned. These matter because a faster search answers the task only if its outputs satisfy the original requirements. The two-variable truth table and the earlier millisecond program are teaching examples, not reported benchmark results. The paper's GPU results do not imply that every rewritten program gains the same parallelism.

Check your reasoning

With x = 3, a test using old y = 4 passes even when the second worker reads the old value. Does that validate the parallel schedule? Give a distinguishing test and its expected outputs. Separately, does a sampler returning both allowed pairs once establish that it selects them with equal probability?

Read the reasoning

No. Old y happens to equal the new y, hiding the missing ordering. Set old y to 7 instead: the intended result is still y = 4, z = 8, while a read of the old value gives z = 14. The test distinguishes these two behaviors. It does not by itself check every possible memory-location relationship or every other effect of the program. Seeing both allowed pairs establishes coverage of this tiny answer set in that run, not equal selection probabilities. Even the invented 99%-versus-1% sampler can return both. Distinguish what was observed from a claim about how future draws are distributed.

Evidence boundary. The SAT-sampling paper connects rewritten logical structure to GPU execution and valid solutions. Its local evaluation review gives the tested settings. The examples below teach dependencies and constraint meaning; they do not reproduce the paper's full transformation or sampler.

Review: Compiler structure · Legal parallel work

2. Design for the shapes and conditions that can occur

A design can work in an ideal model yet fail when its manufactured shape or operating conditions differ. Include those limits while choosing the design. Checking one typical case does not establish that all required cases work.

Which shapes can the process make?
Include feature-size and other stated manufacturing rules before ranking candidates. Rechecking a repaired drawing is necessary because changing its shape can change its behavior.
Apply it

Compare choosing among buildable candidates with repairing the highest-scoring ideal candidate after selection.

Where it fails: Repairing an unbuildable feature can change performance enough to reverse the original ranking.

Evidence boundary: BOSON-1 includes fabrication restrictions during search. The 30/50/60 nm example is invented, not a process specification.

Inspect the named source

Which variations does the evidence cover?
Distinguish a typical setting, sampled variations, and a bound covering every allowed combination. State the relations between quantities before combining their limits.
Apply it

List the allowed timing intervals and any separately justified relation between logic and wire delays.

Where it fails: A midpoint or a set of favorable samples does not exclude the failing combination allowed by the model.

Evidence boundary: BOSON-1 evaluates sampled process variations. The 2.1 ns worst case and 1.9 ns joint bound are original teaching values.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching timing model: a path's logic delay lies between 1.1 and 1.4 nanoseconds, its wire delay between 0.2 and 0.5, and the receiving element requires another 0.2. Treat every combination within these intervals as allowed and ignore other timing effects. Using the interval midpoints gives 1.25 + 0.35 + 0.2 = 1.8 nanoseconds, apparently below a two-nanosecond requirement.

The allowed worst case is 1.4 + 0.5 + 0.2 = 2.1 nanoseconds, which misses the requirement. A design that works at the midpoint is therefore not guaranteed to work throughout the stated range. Sampling ten favorable combinations would not remove the remaining unfavorable combinations from the model.

The relation between the quantities matters too. If separate evidence established that logic delay plus wire delay never exceeds 1.7 nanoseconds, the total bound would instead be 1.9. That stronger joint constraint excludes some combinations admitted by the separate intervals. It cannot be inferred merely because those combinations were absent from a small sample. Neither kind of bound supplies a manufacturing success rate without a distribution of actual devices and conditions.

BOSON-1 applies this concern to photonic devices, which guide light through shaped material. The paper includes designs that turn a light path and let paths cross. Its search accounts for the shapes its fabrication model can produce and for variations in that process. This changes the choice being made: the goal is not just good performance for the ideal drawing, but performance that stays within the stated loss and delay limits after the modeled manufacturing changes. The evaluation uses sampled variations; the local review does not establish a guarantee for every manufactured device.

Why not choose the best ideal shape and repair it afterward? In an original two-candidate example, a process cannot make features narrower than 50 nm. Design A requires a 30 nm feature and scores 95 in the ideal model; design B uses 60 nm and scores 90. Suppose widening A's feature to 50 nm reduces its score to 70. Choosing A first and repairing it loses to choosing B. The repair changes the behavior, not just the drawing. These widths and scores are invented; they illustrate why a search over buildable candidates can differ from repairing an unconstrained winner.

The BOSON-1 paper compares related choices about when to include manufacturing limits and which variations to sample. It reports that sampling choices affect the optimization result. A sample set that produces a better design is not automatically proof that untested conditions are harmless. Keep three claims separate: the shape meets the specified manufacturing rules, the evaluated variations give acceptable performance, and every required condition is covered by a justified bound. Evidence for the first two does not by itself establish the third.

Check your reasoning

A redesigned wire route is guaranteed, within this model, to take no more than 0.35 nanoseconds. Keep the logic bound and receiving requirement unchanged. What timing margin remains, and what is still outside the calculation?

Read the reasoning

The bound is 1.4 + 0.35 + 0.2 = 1.95 nanoseconds, leaving 0.05 before the two-nanosecond limit. The guarantee is conditional on the stated bounds and omitted timing effects remaining appropriate. It does not establish acceptable power, legal geometry, functional correctness, or behavior outside the stated operating range.

Evidence boundary. BOSON-1 connects manufacturing-aware search to variation testing. The linked local review states its photonic benchmarks and process-model limits. The timing intervals and feature-width example below are teaching assumptions, not paper measurements or real process specifications.

Review: Physical constraints and evidence · Fault assumptions

3. Ask what shared-memory delays reveal

Two programs can affect each other without reading the same data. If they use the same memory connection, one can make the other wait. That delay can reveal activity or even carry a message. To explain the effect, identify the shared resource, who controls its use, and who can measure the resulting wait.

Which service rule determines the wait?
Draw arrivals, occupied intervals, and reserved slots. State whether transfers can be split and whether another user can borrow unused time.
Apply it

Compare continuous service with reserved slots, including the changed assumption that transfers can be split into blocks.

Where it fails: Borrowing unused slots can reintroduce dependence on another user’s activity even when it improves completion time.

Evidence boundary: MC3 measures effects of shared memory contention. The seven-versus-four-millisecond reservation example is original.

Inspect the named source

Is the activity a message or an unintended clue?
Distinguish a cooperating sender and receiver from an observer inferring a victim's activity. Neither timing effect implies that stored bits were corrupted.
Apply it

Identify who deliberately sends a signal and who observes it before describing the security result.

Where it fails: A demonstrated cooperative channel does not by itself establish extraction of an unwilling victim’s secrets or corruption of stored data.

Evidence boundary: MC3 evaluates covert communication on three Orin platforms. The exact timing inference and fixed-slot comparison are original.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching schedule: a shared connection transfers one block per millisecond and serves requests in arrival order without interruption. A probe request arrives at time 1. If the connection is empty, it finishes at time 2. If another user started a four-block transfer at time 0, the probe waits until time 4 and finishes at time 5. Its response time is either one or four milliseconds, despite identical probe data.

Under the deliberately narrow assumptions that these are the only two possible states and timing is observed exactly, the probe distinguishes whether the earlier transfer occurred. The same three-millisecond delay is both a performance cost and an observation about another user's activity. In a real system, other traffic or measurement noise could produce overlapping times; this example supplies no measured attack success rate.

Now change the service rule: split transfers into one-block pieces and reserve alternating one-millisecond slots for the two users, with the probe's user owning the slot from time 1 to 2. Assume splitting adds no cost and no unfinished transfer crosses a slot boundary. If unused slots cannot be borrowed, the probe finishes at time 2 in either case, but its user cannot exploit the other user's idle slots. This removes the difference in this timing observation at the cost of usable capacity. It does not establish protection against every other observation, nor does a waiting-time model describe physical corruption of stored bits.

MC3 provides a measured paper example of communication through shared memory traffic. One program deliberately changes memory use; another observes the resulting contention, meaning competition for the same transfer capacity. The paper evaluates this on three NVIDIA Orin platforms without requiring a shared last-level cache or elevated access to the system. The key distinction is cooperation: a sender chooses activity to encode a message and a receiver tries to decode it. That is a covert channel, not automatically an attack that reads an unwilling program's secrets.

The local review records a tradeoff between communication rate and accuracy under the tested platform and workload conditions. Faster signaling does not help the task if the receiver cannot distinguish the signals reliably. The exact one-versus-four-millisecond distinction in the teaching example avoids this difficulty by assumption; real measurements need to account for other traffic and timing variation. Likewise, the fixed-slot schedule above is an invented comparison, not an evaluated MC3 defense.

Allowing unused slots to be borrowed changes the observation again. A probe might then finish sooner when the other program is idle than when it is active. Even if borrowing lowers average completion time, the claim that the probe's service is independent of the other program no longer follows from the fixed-slot argument. The timing change and information revealed must be evaluated together under the actual service rule.

Check your reasoning

With alternating reserved slots starting with the other user at time 0, when do four probe-user blocks ready at time 1 finish? Compare this with an otherwise empty unreserved connection, counting elapsed time from arrival.

Read the reasoning

The probe-user slots are 1–2, 3–4, 5–6, and 7–8, so completion is at time 8, seven milliseconds after arrival. On an empty unreserved connection, continuous service from 1 to 5 takes four milliseconds. The reservation sacrifices three milliseconds in this trace. Its observation benefit relies on enforcing the fixed schedule rather than secretly lending idle slots in a way the probe can notice.

Evidence boundary. MC3 connects shared memory contention to measured covert communication. Its local evaluation review states the platform and workload limits. The arrival-order and fixed-slot schedules below are original teaching models, not measured MC3 timings or a validated mitigation.

Review: Memory state · Observation and influence

4. Check whether the test can catch the mistake

A generated test can run without errors and still check the wrong thing. Start with the required behavior, choose inputs that distinguish correct from incorrect behavior, and inspect what the test actually compares. A successful run counts as evidence only if a relevant mistake would make it fail.

Checking the checker
Identify the reference used to judge a generated test. A test that always passes supplies no evidence that the design meets its requirement.
Apply it

Compare ordered output sequences, not sorted values, when the requirement is to preserve queue order.

Where it fails: Sorting can hide reordered outputs; using sets can additionally hide a lost duplicate.

Evidence boundary: CorrectBench evaluates generated testbench reports against a reference. The 7,2,7 queue trace is original.

Inspect the named source

Repair and independent checks
After a repair, repeat affected checks and use cases beyond those that prompted the repair. Matching one failure case can hide a new mistake elsewhere.
Apply it

After a repair, test cases beyond the triggering example and inspect the benchmark’s exact acceptance rule.

Where it fails: Passing an eight-of-ten agreement threshold permits disagreements; bounded repair can stop without producing a correct checker.

Evidence boundary: CorrectBench separates functional repair from mutant-based Eval2 evaluation. The all-ten-reference-rejections scenario is original.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching requirement: a queue must return accepted values in the same order they entered. Enqueue 7, then 2, then 7, with sufficient space and no simultaneous operations. The next three removals must return 7, 2, 7. A generated checker that sorts the input and output lists before comparing them accepts the wrong output 2, 7, 7. It checks the values and their counts but throws away the order required by the specification.

Adding a check of just the first value is not enough. Output 7, 7, 2 has the correct first value and the same value counts, but is still wrong. For this completed trace, comparing the entire output sequence with the accepted input sequence detects both mistakes. Keeping duplicates matters: checking only the set of values would also miss losing one copy of 7.

This repair still does not check what happens when the queue fills, when a removal is attempted on an empty queue, after reset, or during overlapping insertion and removal. Those cases need their own specified rules. Deliberately wrong implementations can reveal a weak checker, but catching a selected set of mistakes is not a proof that every possible implementation satisfies the requirement.

CorrectBench applies this question to generated hardware testbenches: programs that supply inputs to a simulated circuit and judge its responses. Its validator reports scenarios as correct, wrong, or uncertain. A controller then chooses whether to repair the testbench, generate a fresh one, or stop. The paper limits the number of repair and restart attempts. This is a bounded process that can give up, not a guarantee that enough retries eventually produce a correct checker.

The benchmark's acceptance rule needs its own explanation. The paper's Eval2 criterion compares a generated testbench's pass/fail reports with a reference testbench on ten modified circuit implementations, called mutants. Agreement on at least eight of the ten counts as passing that criterion. It does not mean every mutant was rejected, that every comparison agreed, or that all possible circuit bugs were detected. The modified implementations are used to evaluate the method, not as the repair process's supplied answers.

Suppose, in an original example, the reference rejects all ten mutants. A testbench that rejects eight and accepts two meets that 80% agreement threshold but misses the two tested faults. If the reference instead accepts a mutant, agreement requires accepting it too: the score measures agreement with the reference, not simply the number of rejections. Read the rule behind a reported pass rate before turning it into a claim about correctness. The reference and the selected faults also need to match the behavior the reader cares about.

Check your reasoning

List the distinct orderings of 7, 2, 7. How many does the sorted-list checker accept, how many pass an added first-value check, and how many satisfy the required order?

Read the reasoning

The three distinct orderings are 7,2,7; 7,7,2; and 2,7,7. Sorting accepts all three. Requiring the first value to be 7 still accepts the first two. Exact sequence comparison accepts only 7,2,7. These counts describe this input trace, not an overall detection rate across arbitrary queue bugs.

Evidence boundary. CorrectBench connects generated tests to functional validation, bounded repair, and a separately defined evaluation rule. The local review records its task and model limits. The queue trace and ten-rejected-mutant scenario below are teaching examples; the eight-of-ten agreement threshold is the paper's Eval2 rule.

Review: Testing and specification · Preserving meaning

5. Keep more detail where the answer needs it

Rounding two numbers by the same amount need not change the final answer equally. Their importance depends on how later operations use them. Choosing precision separately can save storage, but the choice itself may need tags, extra calculation, or a recovery path. Count those costs too.

Which values share one precision choice?
Name the group, the information needed to describe its format, and the values excluded from the smaller format. Count the full stored representation.
Apply it

Compare coarse and fine error-control units, including metadata and the decisions made at each unit.

Where it fails: Finer control can cost more metadata or coordination than the numerical error it removes.

Evidence boundary: Cocktail selects precision per context chunk and retains higher-precision exceptions. The three-byte payload plus one-byte tag is original.

Inspect the named source

What establishes acceptable output?
Separate a derived error bound from observed model quality. If rejected results trigger a fallback, include its time and state requirements.
Apply it

Specify the fallback’s time, memory, and output-quality obligations before treating it as a safety net.

Where it fails: A fallback that misses the deadline or changes the accepted answer is not equivalent to the primary path.

Evidence boundary: Cocktail quality tests are model/workload evidence, not the linear example’s worst-case bound. The 3 ms plus 4 ms fallback is original and not attributed to Cocktail.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching calculation: the required output is 10x + y. A coarse stored value has absolute error at most 0.1; a fine stored value has error at most 0.01. Assume these bounds hold for the input range and that subsequent arithmetic is exact. Coarse values for both inputs allow output error up to 10 × 0.1 + 0.1 = 1.1. Fine x and coarse y reduce that bound to 0.2. Coarse x and fine y give 1.01. Giving the same extra precision to a different input changes its value to the final calculation.

If the allowed output error is 0.25, fine x and coarse y suffice under these assumptions. Suppose coarse storage costs one byte per value and fine storage two. That mixed choice uses three bytes rather than four for both fine. If identifying which value is fine requires a separate one-byte tag for this tiny record, total storage returns to four bytes. A precision policy needs its description as well as its stored numbers.

A fallback also needs a time budget. Suppose the mixed calculation and its check take 3 milliseconds. On a rejected result, an exact fallback takes another 4. Success on the first path costs 3; fallback completion costs 7. With a five-millisecond deadline, fallback may recover the required numerical answer while still failing the delivery requirement. An available recovery path is not automatically an acceptable one.

Cocktail applies selective precision to information a language model keeps so it can use earlier context while generating an answer. This stored information is called the key-value cache. The paper splits the input context into chunks, chooses how many bits each chunk's cached values use, and rearranges the chunks for access on the GPU. Choosing fewer bits and choosing a layout that lowers storage or access cost are different changes: one changes the represented numbers, while the other changes how they are stored and reached.

The paper does not apply its lower-precision choice to every cached value. It keeps the cache for newly generated output at 16-bit floating-point precision. A context remainder shorter than a full chunk also stays at that precision. The remainder is not discarded from the task. These exceptions matter when counting memory: multiplying the entire cache size by one advertised bit ratio would miss the values that remain in the larger format. The local review also notes that searching for the precision settings has a cost, especially at small batch sizes.

The linear example above has an explicit error bound because the output is exactly 10x + y under the stated arithmetic assumptions. Cocktail's model-quality tests are evidence for its evaluated models and inputs, not that same kind of bound for every answer. Likewise, keeping some values at higher precision is not an exact fallback for an already unacceptable output. A reader needs to know which values retain detail, how the policy is selected, and what test establishes acceptable final quality.

Check your reasoning

Change the required output to x + 10y, retaining the same error bounds, storage costs, and 0.25 output-error limit. Which input should use fine storage? Does the earlier choice remain justified?

Read the reasoning

Fine y and coarse x give 0.1 + 10 × 0.01 = 0.2, within the limit. Keeping fine x and coarse y gives 0.01 + 10 × 0.1 = 1.01 and cannot certify it. The importance of a stored value follows its later use, not its name or a permanently assigned precision label. The three-byte payload and possible one-byte tag costs are unchanged.

Evidence boundary. Cocktail connects chunk-level precision, cache layout, and selection overhead. The linked local review states the evaluated models and workloads. The linear error bounds, byte counts, and fallback timings below are original teaching assumptions, not Cocktail measurements.

Review: Numerical detail · Decision costs · End-to-end quality

6. Simplify the search without losing the answer

Choosing each part of a design separately can be quicker than checking every combination. But the parts may compete for the same space or depend on one another's timing. Before splitting the problem, identify which shared constraints must survive the split.

What lets the parts be solved separately?
State the shared constraints and the assumptions that make the split valid. An arbitrary division of resources can discard combinations the full problem allows.
Apply it

Draw the boundary between independently optimized blocks and the coupling that returns when they share timing, power, or data.

Where it fails: Two locally best choices can be incompatible when combined.

Evidence boundary: The CGRA paper separates time then placement under a neighbor-register-access assumption. The equal-area split is an original counterexample to arbitrary decomposition.

Inspect the named source

What does a faster search establish?
Separate tool runtime, success before timeout, and the resulting design's performance. State which cases are included in the comparison.
Apply it

Compare the time to find a design separately from its execution time, and retain cases where the search times out.

Where it fails: A fast average over completed comparisons does not describe success on every benchmark or equal improvement in application speed.

Evidence boundary: The CGRA paper uses a 4,000-second timeout and excludes cases with either tool timing out from its average compilation-time comparison.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching design: two components must share an area budget of 10 square millimeters. For each component, a small implementation uses 4 square millimeters and takes 6 milliseconds; a large one uses 6 and takes 3. Assume their work is sequential, with no transfer or switching costs. Choosing the fastest implementation separately for each component produces area 12 and time 6: fast but outside the budget.

There are four combined choices. Small–small uses area 8 and takes 12 milliseconds. Small–large and large–small each use area 10 and take 9. Large–large uses area 12 and takes 6. Under the original area constraint, the two mixed choices are tied for fastest. The shared budget is the relationship that prevents independent local choices from solving the full problem.

Dividing the area allowance equally in advance gives each component a limit of 5. That leaves only the small choice for each, producing a valid 12-millisecond design but excluding both valid 9-millisecond designs. Restricting search can therefore preserve feasibility while losing the best permitted answer. A later check can confirm that the selected design fits; it cannot recover an excluded choice unless the search is allowed to reconsider the restriction.

DATE's monomorphism-based mapping paper separates two choices for a configurable array of processing units: when each operation runs and which unit runs it. Such an array is called a CGRA. Its units calculate and pass values through a limited set of connections, so a schedule is not executable unless the required values can reach the assigned units in time. The paper first finds a time solution under its constraints, then searches for a placement that preserves the required connections. Monomorphism here names the connection-preserving graph mapping used in that second search.

This separation is justified for the paper's stated hardware model, not for every possible array. The paper proves that its constrained time solutions admit the required mapping, and identifies a restriction: each processing unit must be able to read its neighbors' internal registers, the small stores holding their intermediate values. Removing that access changes the problem. The proof cannot simply be carried over to a different connection arrangement. This contrasts with the arbitrary equal-area split above, for which the example directly shows lost solutions.

The evaluation also separates the time to find a mapping from the quality of the resulting mapping. A large reduction in compilation time means the tool finds a placement and schedule faster; it does not mean the application itself runs that many times faster. The reported average compilation-time comparison excludes benchmarks where either tool times out. That rule matters: the average describes completed comparisons, while timeout cases need separate reporting. The local review and this lesson do not claim an independent reproduction.

Check your reasoning

Suppose the full design must also finish within 10 milliseconds. Does the equal five-square-millimeter allocation find a valid solution? Does its failure establish that the original problem has no solution?

Read the reasoning

The equal allocation permits only small–small, which takes 12 milliseconds and fails the new time limit. It does not prove the original problem impossible: either mixed choice uses exactly 10 square millimeters and finishes in 9 milliseconds. Failure inside a restricted search is not failure of the larger problem unless the restriction is known to preserve all relevant solutions.

Evidence boundary. The CGRA-mapping paper connects problem separation to an explicit hardware assumption and proof. Its local review records the benchmark and timeout limits. The two-component area and execution-time examples below are original, not CGRA measurements.

Review: Search and preparation · Constraint preservation

7. Decide what happens after a fault is detected

A detector can report a problem without preventing a wrong result from escaping. Ask which changes it detects, when it checks, and what stops or repairs the affected work. These are separate requirements; satisfying one does not establish the others.

Which changes can the check detect?
Name the checked property and a change that leaves it satisfied. Unchanged bits, an allowed return address, and intended circuit behavior are different properties.
Apply it

Compare a check for changed stored bits with a check that the generated circuit implements the intended behavior.

Where it fails: Unchanged maliciously generated bits can pass an integrity check; detecting corruption is not the same as checking the original design.

Evidence boundary: RTL-Breaker evaluates poisoned generation under selected triggers and tasks. The parity counterexample is original.

Inspect the named source

Does the check happen before the harmful action?
Place checking, release, and recovery on a timeline. Include the trusted state used by the check and the time needed to respond.
Apply it

Identify the protected reference used at a function return and place validation before the action it guards.

Where it fails: Checking an allowed control-flow target does not certify every numerical output or exclude every allowed-but-unwanted target.

Evidence boundary: EILID checks return state and selected call targets under its stated threat model. The publish-at-4/check-at-5 timeline is original.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching system: a stored result contains a four-bit unsigned value and one extra bit chosen so the total number of ones is even. Value 5 is 0101, with extra bit 0. Flipping its least significant data bit produces 0100, value 4. The total is now odd, so the stated parity check detects the change. Detection alone does not say whether the system should retry, restore another copy, stop, or publish the value anyway.

Flipping the two least significant data bits instead changes 0101 to 0110, value 6. The total number of ones stays even, so the same check accepts the changed value. For this code, every single-bit flip in the five stored bits changes parity, but every two-bit flip preserves it. A claim about single-bit detection must retain that fault assumption when carried into a complete-system argument.

Suppose a result is computed by time 3 milliseconds, published at time 4, and checked at time 5. Even detection of a covered fault happens after the result is visible. To promise that detected corrupt results are not published, the release decision must wait for the check, or publication must have a precisely specified reversible meaning. If a later retry takes 3 milliseconds, completion at time 8 also misses a time-6 deadline. Detection coverage, release order, and recovery timing are separate obligations.

EILID provides a concrete example of checking at the point of use. It adds instructions around function calls and returns on small processors. Before a call, it records the expected return address in a protected shadow stack: a separate record of where execution should resume. Before returning, it checks the current return address against that record. The check concerns the path execution takes, not whether every calculated value is correct. Protecting return addresses would not, by itself, detect the changed numerical value in the parity example.

The paper also checks indirect calls against a table of allowed function entry points. It explicitly notes a limit: redirecting a call to another valid entry can still satisfy this function-level check. A detector must therefore be described by the set of changes it excludes, not by a general claim that execution is safe. The local review records an FPGA-based implementation and runtime overhead on the tested applications; the added checks are not free and do not cover every attack on the device.

RTL-Breaker concerns an earlier stage: a model trained on poisoned hardware examples can generate unwanted circuit behavior in response to a trigger. That does not require a later bit flip in stored data. A parity check could correctly confirm that the generated bits are unchanged while the circuit itself does the wrong job. The local review limits the reported attack to tested models, triggers, and tasks. Generation-time checks, runtime control checks, and physical-error detection address different failure causes; combining their names is not evidence of a tested complete defense.

Check your reasoning

How many one-bit and two-bit error patterns exist for the five stored bits? Which does the parity rule detect? Why do these counts not establish how often a real machine returns an incorrect result?

Read the reasoning

There are five one-bit patterns, all detected. There are 5 × 4 / 2 = 10 two-bit patterns, all undetected by this parity rule. Real error rates require evidence about which faults occur, their frequency, when checks run, and what follows an alarm. Counting possible patterns does not assign probabilities to them or prove the response policy is safe.

Evidence boundary. EILID connects execution checks to protected reference state; RTL-Breaker connects training data to unwanted generated behavior. Their local review states the tested systems. The parity patterns and publication/retry timeline below are original examples, not paper measurements.

Review: Threat boundaries · Detection and recovery

8. Compare the time to finish the same required job

Before comparing numbers, write down what counts as a finished result. Does every input need an acceptable answer? Must it arrive before a deadline? Does the clock include preparation, checking, and recovery? A faster component matters only to the extent that it helps meet the stated requirement.

Are both methods delivering the same result?
Keep the required outputs, quality rule, and deadline visible. State changed hardware or settings rather than silently treating different experiments as the same job.
Apply it

Write the exact acceptance rule before comparing pass rates, and record any change to inputs, settings, or hardware.

Where it fails: Agreement on selected tests is not the same requirement as detecting every fault; partial delivery is not completion of a mandatory batch.

Evidence boundary: CorrectBench supplies a concrete reference-agreement rule. The ten-answer deadline example is original.

Inspect the named source

Which work and failures are included?
Count preparation, execution, checking, and recovery for the claimed job. Report unfinished or timed-out cases separately instead of treating them as successful completions.
Apply it

Count preparation, successful execution, checks, failures, and recovery through completion of the required batch.

Where it fails: Dropping unfinished searches or failed outputs changes the population described by an average.

Evidence boundary: The CGRA review records timeout exclusions and compilation-time scope. The batch fallback totals are original, not a combined DATE system.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Original teaching batch: method A handles ten independent inputs sequentially, spending 2 seconds to prepare, 3 to calculate, and 1 to check each. Every output passes the same required check. It delivers ten acceptable results in 60 seconds. Method B spends 1 second calculating and 1 checking each input, with no other initial costs, but four outputs fail. Its first pass ends after 20 seconds with only six acceptable results.

Suppose each of B's four failed inputs can be handled by a fallback that always passes and takes another 12 seconds, including all preparation and checks. Completing all ten inputs then takes 20 + 4 × 12 = 68 seconds. Reporting B's threefold faster calculation would miss both its initial checking cost and the cost of finishing the failed inputs. Reporting six results after 20 seconds would answer a different question from completing the specified batch.

If the fallback instead takes 8 seconds, B completes the batch in 52 seconds and wins. The conclusion depends on the failed-input count and recovery cost, not just the preferred path. These are stipulated outcomes for one batch, not an expected failure distribution or a measured comparison between DATE papers. Changing the accuracy requirement to accept the failed outputs would also change the task being compared.

Now add a deadline: all ten answers must be ready by time 60. A meets it exactly. B with the 12-second fallback finishes its fourth recovery at time 68, so it misses the requirement; with the 8-second fallback it meets it at time 52. Reporting B's six accepted answers at time 20 could satisfy a partial-delivery requirement, but it is not evidence that all ten are ready on time. State which of those services the reader actually needs.

The earlier DATE lessons illustrate why a common word such as 'pass' needs a definition. CorrectBench's Eval2 pass means sufficient agreement with a reference on selected modified circuits, not detection of every possible defect. The CGRA paper's compilation speed describes how quickly a mapping is found, not how quickly the mapped program runs. Cocktail's memory saving concerns a cache with both reduced-precision chunks and higher-precision exceptions. These are meaningful results, but they count different things and cannot be combined by multiplying their headline improvements.

A comparison record is short and specific: required outputs; inputs and machine; settings allowed to change; start and stop events; failed or timed-out cases; recovery costs; and how each result was measured or estimated. For example, a faster compiler may reduce preparation while leaving execution unchanged. Test generation may produce more cases without making every generated test correct. Follow the changed step into the complete job, and retain costs or unresolved failures instead of dropping them from the denominator.

Check your reasoning

At 12 seconds per fallback, what is the largest number of failed inputs for which B still finishes all ten strictly sooner than A? Keep the initial 20-second pass and sequential recovery assumptions.

Read the reasoning

Require 20 + 12f < 60, so f < 10/3. At most three inputs may need fallback: total time is 56 seconds. Four give 68 and lose. This is a break-even count for the given batch, not a guarantee that an unmeasured workload will stay below it.

Evidence boundary. Read this closing lesson alongside CorrectBench in theme 4, Cocktail in theme 5, and the CGRA mapping study in theme 6. Their local reviews establish different comparison rules, not a jointly measured system. All ten-input batch and deadline numbers below are original teaching assumptions.

Review: Whole-path accounting · Measurement stage

Practice reading a paper

A generated testbench accepts 100 known-good designs and also accepts 20 deliberately faulty versions that violate the target property. Passing the good cases does not compensate for missing those faults. Ask whether the test actually observes the required output or event, whether the injected faults exercise that requirement, and whether repair is checked on independent cases. Even catching all 20 would establish coverage of that selected fault set, not a proof for all incorrect implementations.

Back to the lessons

VLSID 2025: connect a representation to the device that realizes it

Four-theme route with two full walkthroughs (TimeFloats and the pulse-bit study). One other locally reviewed paper informs the small sample; energy-accounting discrepancies remain unresolved and conference coverage is incomplete.

A stored bit pattern, a pulse duration, and a circuit connection are different ways of making an intended operation physical. Their failure modes differ. Begin by asking what physical quantity represents the value, what can disturb it, and which later operation interprets it. The small local VLSID sample provides examples of this connection; it does not establish the dominant ideas across the whole conference.

Evidence boundary

The synthesis uses three papers with locally extracted text and detailed written reviews of their evaluations; two of those records now have full learner walkthroughs here. The other 95 records have only abstracts or titles. No independent reproduction was performed. The four themes below draw on that small sample. When a study evaluated only a model, the route does not present its result as a measurement of manufactured hardware.

Paper walkthrough: TimeFloats: follow a number through time, charge, and stored state

Paper walkthrough: Pulse-bit errors: count what a changed control bit does

1. Follow a physical error into the answer

A number can be stored as bits or represented by how long a signal lasts. The same-sized disturbance need not have the same effect in each representation. First translate the disturbance into a changed value; then check how the next calculation or decision uses that value.

How much does the stored value change?
Apply the decoding rule to the disturbed bits or signal duration. Count the numerical change, not just the number of disturbed bits.
Apply it

Use the duration decoder in the worked example: convert a physical timing error into the corresponding value error before judging it.

Where it fails: A small duration error can cross a decision threshold when the true value is close to that threshold.

Evidence boundary: The pulse-bit-error review distinguishes control fields with different simulated consequences. Both linear duration rules are original teaching models.

Inspect the named source

Does that change affect the required result?
Follow the changed value into the later calculation or decision. An error bound may preserve one decision while leaving another uncertain.
Apply it

Follow the value error into the final yes/no decision, as with 1.9 being decoded as 2.1 in the worked example.

Where it fails: A bound on a local number does not preserve a task result when the downstream rule has a nearby boundary.

Evidence boundary: The pulse-bit study evaluates simulated output changes, not physical fault occurrence rates. The 1.9-to-2.1 threshold example is original.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Use an invented time encoding: a value x is represented by a duration t = 10 + 2x ns for x between 0 and 4. The decoder subtracts 10 and divides by 2. A duration error of at most 0.4 ns therefore gives a decoded-value error of at most 0.2, provided the same rule applies and no clipping occurs. If a later decision asks whether x is at least 2, a true value of 1.9 can be decoded as 2.1 and change the decision. A bounded local error does not imply an unchanged task output.

Contrast that with an ordinary unsigned four-bit encoding. Starting from 0011, changing the last bit changes 3 to 2, while changing the first changes 3 to 11. Both are one-bit changes but their numerical consequences differ eightfold. Neither example is a model of all errors in a physical circuit. The encoding, disturbance, and downstream decision must all be specified before an error rate becomes informative.

There is a cost to making a duration less sensitive to the same timing error. Change the invented rule to t = 10 + 4x ns, keeping x between 0 and 4. The same 0.4 ns disturbance now changes the decoded value by at most 0.1, but the largest duration grows from 18 ns to 26 ns. In this model, more time separates neighboring values. That improves tolerance to a fixed absolute timing error while increasing the longest signal duration; it does not establish a free improvement in speed or energy.

The VLSID pulse-bit-error study examines bits stored in the ordinary electronics that control a quantum processor. Those bits describe pulse amplitudes and phases, meaning the pulse's size and position within its oscillation. A changed stored bit alters the pulse description, which can alter the simulated gate output. The local review records much larger effects for some high-significance fields than for other tested bits. These are faults in classical control data, not interchangeable with an abstract error applied directly to a qubit.

The review limits the detailed evidence to Qiskit simulations using an IBM device model, rather than physical quantum-hardware measurements. That permits a bounded question: under this representation and simulated setup, which bit changes most disturb the output? It does not establish the frequency of those faults in manufactured control memory or the same sensitivity on every device. Counting possible errors, measuring their consequences, and estimating how often they occur remain separate tasks.

Some plotted values need a further qualification. Section 3.2 of the pulse-bit preprint says two tested bit positions produced invalid pulses. The authors filled the missing graph values by drawing straight lines between neighboring results; those filled values are estimates, not simulated outcomes for the invalid pulses. They also assume that the system detects these pulses and stops transmission. Section 4.1 relies on that assumption when excluding those bits from correction. A proposed safeguard is therefore part of the reasoning, but its operation is not established by the neighboring simulation results.

Check your reasoning

A decoded value is 2.3 and the time-encoding example's justified absolute error bound is 0.2. Can its true value be below 2? What if the decoded value is 2.1?

Read the reasoning

For 2.3, the true value lies between 2.1 and 2.5, so it cannot be below 2 under the stated bound. For 2.1, the interval is 1.9 to 2.3 and crosses the decision threshold; the bound cannot settle the decision. This uses a worst-case bound, not a typical or mean error, and assumes the decoder and range conditions remain valid.

Evidence boundary. The local pulse-bit-error review connects ordinary control-memory faults to simulated quantum outputs. TimeFloats supplies a different time-domain representation discussed in theme 2. The linear duration rule and four-bit values below are teaching models, not either paper's implementation.

Review: Representation error · Fault models · Physical conditions

2. Count the work around near-memory arithmetic

Calculating where values are stored can avoid sending them to a separate processor. But inputs may need conversion, outputs must be readable by the next stage, and training changes stored parameters. Follow that whole path before comparing energy.

What work remains besides multiplication?
Count loading, scale alignment, conversion, updates, and output handling. Explain which work is done once and which repeats for each input.
Apply it

Trace one value through loading, storage, arithmetic, update, and output conversion; the recurring-cost example counts every stage.

Where it fails: Removing one transfer does not remove conversion, update, or output work, so the claimed saving can disappear.

Evidence boundary: The inspected TimeFloats preprint describes timing and alignment hardware; this course keeps the complete value path as an original teaching model.

Inspect the named source

Do the energy and error accounts cover the same operation?
Check component totals, units, device assumptions, and output quality. Keep unresolved accounting differences visible.
Apply it

Compare the one-time parameter load with the number of later uses in the energy break-even calculation.

Where it fails: If parameters change every vector, the one-time cost becomes recurring and the apparent near-data advantage reverses.

Evidence boundary: The paper’s modeled energy accounting is reported with an unresolved component-sum discrepancy; no full training result is claimed.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Consider invented energy costs for repeatedly using one fixed set of stored parameters. A reference path uses 6 nJ per input vector, including movement and calculation. A proposed near-data path uses 0.5 nJ for input conversion, 1 nJ for calculation, and 0.5 nJ for output conversion: 2 nJ per vector. Loading its parameters costs 30 nJ once. After n vectors, the comparison is 6n versus 30 + 2n nJ. Seven vectors lose at 42 versus 44; eight win at 48 versus 46. The benefit depends on reuse, not only on the central operation.

Now suppose the parameters change after every vector and each change costs the same 30 nJ. The proposed path needs 32 nJ per vector and loses to the 6-nJ reference. Real update costs need not equal initial loading, but omitting them would conceal the question. Reusing old parameters when the algorithm requires new ones is not a valid way to recover the saving. Keep parameter version and permitted update timing attached to the energy comparison.

TimeFloats computes sums of input-weight products using signal durations and memory circuitry. Floating-point values have a magnitude part and an exponent that sets its scale. Products with different scales cannot simply be added as though their magnitude parts used the same units. The paper's five-step path includes combining exponents, finding a shared scale, adjusting inputs, computing products and their sum, and converting the result back to a digital floating-point value. A cheap multiplication leaves these supporting steps to be counted.

Conversion also affects the answer. The source describes modeled device variation when converting bits to timing signals and converting results back to bits. It evaluates a specified statistical perturbation model; the result is not a guarantee over every manufactured circuit. Under the tested model, exponent computations are more sensitive than magnitude computations. That supports examining where to spend limited correction resources, not treating every physical error as having the same consequence.

The energy account needs caution too. Section IV-B lists component costs of 1.28, 3.25, 0.023, 1.32, and 2.421 pJ, which sum to 8.294 pJ, while stating a total of 5.8 pJ. The focused walkthrough also records different entries in Table I. These differences remain unresolved. Do not silently choose a preferred total or use the headline efficiency to predict full training energy. The implementation evidence is synthesis and circuit simulation, not a measured fabricated chip.

Check your reasoning

If output conversion instead costs 1.5 nJ per vector, with all other invented costs unchanged and one initial load, how many vectors are needed for a strict energy win?

Read the reasoning

The recurring cost becomes 0.5 + 1 + 1.5 = 3 nJ. Require 30 + 3n < 6n, so n > 10: ten vectors tie and eleven are the first strict win. Additional idle energy, loading time, quality differences, or supporting components could change the full-system decision and are not included in this toy account.

Evidence boundary. TimeFloats connects stored weights to time-domain arithmetic, alignment, conversion, and updates. Its focused walkthrough records an unresolved energy-accounting discrepancy. The nJ costs below are invented and do not repair or validate the paper's reported pJ totals.

Review: Placement and movement · Conversion costs · Energy and evidence

3. Choose the device that can finish the required job

Starting sooner is not the same as finishing sooner. A device may need extra operations to move values between its connected units, or may produce a less accurate answer. Count waiting, preparation, execution, and checking before choosing where to run.

After translation and mapping
Evaluate the program after it is adapted to the target's supported operations and connections. The source-level operation count may omit work introduced by that mapping.
Apply it

Use the A-versus-B timeline: include queue, preparation, execution, and acceptance rather than comparing execution alone.

Where it fails: A target device can have shorter execution but lose after translation, routing, or acceptance work is included.

Evidence boundary: QuaLITi evaluates target-specific translated circuits in noisy simulation. The A/B timeline is original.

Inspect the named source

Queue, noise, and acceptance
Compare arrival-to-accepted-result time under the task's quality condition. A quicker start does not guarantee an earlier usable result.
Apply it

Compare arrival-to-accepted-result time and the uncertainty interval, not just the time until a device starts.

Where it fails: A quicker start or lower central estimate does not guarantee an earlier acceptable answer when intervals overlap.

Evidence boundary: QuaLITi measures real-device queue behavior separately and estimates full inference waits. The 20-second prediction and 50-second trace are original.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

In a generic invented device-selection problem, A has a 2-ms queue, 3-ms transfer and translation preparation, 8-ms execution, and 1-ms acceptance check. B has a 5-ms queue, 1-ms preparation, 4-ms execution, and 1-ms check. With sequential stages and both results accepted, A takes 14 ms and B 11. Choosing the shortest queue selects the later answer. This is not a quantum-device benchmark; it isolates the difference between starting sooner and finishing sooner after target-specific work.

Suppose instead that total-time predictions are A = 12 ms with a justified uncertainty range of ±3 ms, and B = 13 ms with ±0.5 ms. Their possible intervals, 9–15 and 12.5–13.5, overlap. The smaller central prediction does not guarantee an earlier result. B has the smaller worst-case bound in this example; A has the smaller prediction. Which criterion matters depends on the requested promise and on whether those bounds actually apply to the current job.

QuaLITi considers quantum circuits running on devices with different available connections and error characteristics. If an operation needs two quantum states that are not suitably connected, adapting the circuit can introduce extra operations to move those states. A source-level count omits that work. The paper therefore examines the circuit after translation for each target, alongside operation errors and errors in reading out the result. Choosing a device changes the implementation being evaluated, not just its place in a queue.

The evidence comes from different stages. The training and inference experiments use three noisy Qiskit simulators built from device-calibration data, with selected eight-qubit connection patterns. Separately, the paper observes queues on real IBM devices and submits a small dummy circuit to measure waiting. It then estimates inference waiting time by applying that measured wait to every data point. That calculation assumes future requests experience the same wait; it is not a measurement of the full model serving every input on those devices.

An original example shows the estimate's sensitivity. Multiplying a 2-second observed wait by ten separately queued requests predicts 20 seconds of waiting. If the first five instead wait 2 seconds each and the next five wait 8 seconds each, total waiting is 50 seconds. If requests are batched, they may not even incur ten separate waits. Queue observations can inform a decision, but the arrival pattern, submission method, and changing queue must match the model used to turn them into a completion-time claim.

Check your reasoning

A new measurement reduces A's justified interval to 10–11 ms, while B remains 12.5–13.5 ms. What ranking follows? What could invalidate that inference before execution?

Read the reasoning

Every time in A's interval is less than every time in B's, so A is faster under those stated bounds. A queue that changes after measurement, a different mapped program, or changed operating conditions can make the bounds inapplicable. This inference concerns time only; the accepted-result requirement must still hold for both devices.

Evidence boundary. QuaLITi connects circuit structure and device noise to simulated model accuracy, and separately studies real-device queues. Its estimated full inference waiting times are not measured complete inference runs. The A/B timings and uncertainty intervals below are invented examples.

Review: Connections · Waiting · Worker selection

4. Label how each result was obtained

A simulation answers a question about a model. A measurement records what happened in a particular test. They answer different evidence questions; combining them does not make the whole result measured. Name the evidence for each part, the conditions it covers, and any unresolved discrepancy.

What is modeled
Name the process, timing, variation, error, and surrounding-system assumptions. Identify which conclusion depends on each assumption.
Apply it

For each term in the additive error example, write down the process and operating condition that justifies its bound.

Where it fails: If the final computation is nonlinear or a component bound does not hold jointly, adding the bounds is not a valid certificate.

Evidence boundary: TimeFloats uses synthesis and circuit/process models. Its unresolved energy accounting is separate from the original additive-error example.

Inspect the named source

What is measured
State which components were physically present and tested. Keep mixed measured and estimated quantities labeled within the same result.
Apply it

Separate a simulated timing or error value from a value observed on a fabricated device when reading the evidence.

Where it fails: Measuring one stage cannot silently convert modeled neighboring stages into measurements.

Evidence boundary: QuaLITi combines simulated accuracy and separate measured queue observations; full inference waits are estimates. The table retains this split.

Inspect the named source

Worked teaching example

Take a deliberately linear teaching model: the final numerical error equals the sum of encoding error, calculation error, and readout error. Suppose justified absolute bounds are 0.2, 0.15, and 0.1. The largest permitted absolute total is at most 0.45, because the errors can have the same sign. That bound does not meet a required limit of 0.3. It also does not prove every run fails: errors can be smaller or cancel. The model cannot certify the requirement from these bounds alone.

Do not silently replace worst-case bounds with an average-case combination. Any statistical claim needs assumptions about distributions and dependence. Nor does measuring the encoding stage convert modeled calculation and readout terms into measurements. A mixed result should identify its measured and modeled parts, their operating conditions, and why their combination is justified. If the final computation is nonlinear, even this simple additive account may not apply.

What the three reviewed records support—and what they do not establish.
StudyWhat was checkedWhat remains open
Pulse-bit errorsControl-bit changes in a quantum simulatorHow often real faults occur; effects on other devices
TimeFloatsCircuit design and variation modelsNo chip tested; energy totals disagree
QuaLITiModel simulations and separate device wait testsFull waiting time estimated, not timed

The three reviewed records need different next checks. For the pulse-bit study, the simulated sensitivity does not supply a physical rate of memory faults. For TimeFloats, the inconsistent energy entries need reconciliation before the reported total can support a reliable energy comparison. For QuaLITi, measuring a representative full inference workload would test the assumption that a dummy circuit's wait can be applied to every data point. These are missing pieces of evidence, not experiments this course has performed.

Keep a paper-reported number separate from a number whose accounting you have checked. Adding the TimeFloats prose components verifies what those listed values sum to; it does not determine which conflicting entry is correct. Similarly, observing a queue verifies that observation, not a future wait. A careful writeup can explain a mechanism and its limits while leaving the unresolved claim unresolved.

A missing result also needs a reason. A run that stops because its input is invalid differs from a run that finishes with a wrong answer. Connecting nearby points in a graph does not tell us which would happen on the real device. For the pulse-bit study, the next check would exercise the assumed stop mechanism: does it recognize the invalid pulse, prevent transmission, and report the interruption? Then record whether the requested computation is retried or left unfinished. This is a proposed test, not evidence supplied by the graph.

Check your reasoning

The calculation bound improves from 0.15 to 0.05 and the readout bound from 0.1 to 0.04. Is the same 0.3 requirement certified by the linear model? Does this establish the behavior of a manufactured chip?

Read the reasoning

The combined bound becomes 0.2 + 0.05 + 0.04 = 0.29, so the requirement follows within this model if each bound is valid jointly for the operating conditions. It does not independently establish real-chip behavior: the implementation must match the model, and omitted effects or invalid component bounds can defeat the conclusion. Keep the model-level result and physical evidence separate.

Evidence boundary. The three-record evaluation review separates pulse-bit simulations, TimeFloats circuit modeling, and QuaLITi's mixed simulation/queue evidence. The table summarizes those limits, not a new experiment. The additive error bounds below are original teaching assumptions.

Review: Evidence stages · Scope of validation

Practice reading a paper

In a deliberately simple unsigned four-bit encoding, 0011 represents 3. Flipping the last bit produces 0010, or 2: an error of 1. Flipping the first bit produces 1011, or 11: an error of 8. Both are one-bit faults. Explain why reporting only a bit-flip count misses value sensitivity, and why even value error is insufficient without knowing how the next operation uses the number. This example concerns ordinary binary encoding, not a numerical result from the VLSID papers.

  • Pulse-bit study — preprint sections 3.2 and 4.1: invalid pulses, estimated plot values, and assumed stopping behavior
  • Hashem and colleagues, TimeFloats — inspected preprint; sections III–IV support the focused walkthrough
  • VLSID 2025 publication record — conference identity; final text not compared here
  • VLSID three-record bounded synthesis and unresolved coverage
